摘要 端午食粽是中国传统节日端午节最具代表性的传统习俗之一. 民间传说认为该习俗形成于祭祀屈原. 长期
以来, 中国粽子用于祭祀的历史及其与屈原的关系主要依据传世文献, 未曾获得出土的实物史料证据. 河南省信阳
市城阳城址八号墓和安徽省淮南市武王墩一号墓均出土了植物包. 通过古DNA分析, 鉴定2座战国楚墓出土植物包
的包裹叶片来源于壳斗科栎属(Quercus)栎亚属白栎组(sect. Quercus)植物的叶片, 结合叶片边缘缺刻特征推断包裹
叶片来源于槲树(Quercus dentata Thunb.)的叶片; 通过形态学、淀粉粒以及有机残留分析, 发现信阳市城阳城址八
号墓植物包内容物主要含有果壳的稻(Oryza sativa L.)和黍(Panicum miliaceum L.), 是迄今发现最早的类粽子遗存.
淮南市武王

  内容提要：山东济宁东贾柏遗址出土的北辛文化中期的两件小口双耳罐和两件磨棒上的残留物
中发现较多的淀粉粒、植硅体、霉菌和酵母细胞。分析结果显示，两件陶罐曾用于酿酒，酿酒原料以稻
米为主，并加入粟黍、小麦族、栝楼根和橡子。酿酒方法可能包括两种：一种为曲酒，利用发霉谷物，并
且可能加入植物茎叶制曲酿造，其中根霉可能是曲中的主要发酵剂；另一种为口嚼酒，通过咀嚼谷物
利用人的唾液糖化淀粉。北辛文化酿造曲酒的方法可能是受到了中原地区文化的影响，但口嚼酒是
目前最早的考古学证据。口嚼酒是否起源于海岱地区，需要进一步研究。
  关键词：北辛文化 东贾柏遗

evidence.quote:
费专项资金(ZZXT202403)
资助


摘要 端午食粽是中国传统节日端午节最具代表性的传统习俗之一. 民间传说认为该习俗形成于祭祀屈原. 长期
以来, 中国粽子用于祭祀的历史及其与屈原的关系主要依据传世文献, 未曾获得出土的实物史料证据. 河南省信阳
市城阳城址八号墓和安徽省淮南市武王墩一号墓均出土了植物包. 通过古DNA分析, 鉴定2座战国楚墓出土植物包
的包裹叶片来源于壳斗科栎属(Quercus)栎亚属白栎组(sect. Quercus)植物的叶片, 结合叶片边缘缺刻特征推断包裹
叶片来源于槲树(Quercus dentata Thunb.)的叶片; 通过形态学、淀粉粒以及有机残留分析, 发现信阳市城阳城址八
号墓植物包内容物主要含有果壳的稻(Oryza sativa L.)和黍(Panicum miliaceum L.), 是迄今发现最早的类粽子遗存.
淮南市武王

figures.caption_en: Figure 6. Examples of starch types and damage morphologies in Shangshan pottery. 1. Type I compound rice starch with extinction crosses; 2. Type I compound rice starch without extinction crosses but retaining birefringence; 3. Type I compound rice starch showing weak birefringence; 4. Separated Type I rice starch grains; 5. Type II Job’s tears starch grains of various shapes; 6. Type III panicgrass tribe (Paniceae) starch, possibly barnyard grass, with deep channels caused by enzymatic digestion; 7. Type IV wheat tribe (Triticeae) starch with deep channels and micropitting; 8. Type V acorn starch resembling ring-cupped oak (Cyclobalanopsis fleuryi); 9. Type V acorn starch resembling oak (Quercus fabri); 10. Type V compound acorn starch resembling stone oak (Lithocarpus glaber) or ring-cupped oak (Cyclobalanopsis fleuryi), also showing loss of material due to enzymatic digestion; 11. Type V acorn starch resembling stone oak (Lithocarpus brevicaudatus); 12. Type VI lily starch; 13. Gelatinized starch mass; 14, 15. Gelatinized starch clusters stained with trypan blue, resembling compound rice starch.

  内容提要：山东济宁东贾柏遗址出土的北辛文化中期的两件小口双耳罐和两件磨棒上的残留物
中发现较多的淀粉粒、植硅体、霉菌和酵母细胞。分析结果显示，两件陶罐曾用于酿酒，酿酒原料以稻
米为主，并加入粟黍、小麦族、栝楼根和橡子。酿酒方法可能包括两种：一种为曲酒，利用发霉谷物，并
且可能加入植物茎叶制曲酿造，其中根霉可能是曲中的主要发酵剂；另一种为口嚼酒，通过咀嚼谷物
利用人的唾液糖化淀粉。北辛文化酿造曲酒的方法可能是受到了中原地区文化的影响，但口嚼酒是
目前最早的考古学证据。口嚼酒是否起源于海岱地区，需要进一步研究。
  关键词：北辛文化 东贾柏遗

·研究报告·


  基于人牙结石的淀粉粒证据探讨裴李岗遗址
       先民植物性食物来源

                      陶大卫
                                                                           ( 郑州大学历史学院考古系，河南郑州  450001)


   摘要: 人牙结石淀粉粒分析是开展古代居民食物来源研究的有效途径之一。用此方法对河南新郑裴李岗遗址仅
  存的两具裴李岗文化人骨牙齿上的结石开展了淀粉粒分析，成功提取出38 颗淀粉粒，其中可鉴定种属的淀粉粒主

牙结石完整、避免植物微体损伤的前提下，提取并分析其中的植物微体遗存。本研究共提取8 份样本，

  摘要：河旁贝丘遗址是广西新石器时代早中期的一种重要文化遗址类型，目前对其生业状态和定居模式的研究还

  相对薄弱。本研究使用综合性植物考古学研究方法，对邕江流域豹子头、石船头和那北咀这３个河旁贝丘遗址进

   行了大遗存分析、薄壁组织（ｐａｒｅｎｃｈｙｍａ）遗存分析、炭屑分析以及淀粉粒和植硅体等微体遗存分析。本研究的分

  析结果与以往的研究成果表明，邕江流域河旁贝丘群体的食谱范围非常广泛，且包含了多种回报率档次差异极大

摘要 吐鲁番地区降水稀少﹑气候干燥, 大量考古遗址得以保存. 这些考古遗址中粮食作物  关键词
的遗存为揭示吐鲁番地区农业发展的历程提供了直接的证据. 本文以洋海古墓群﹑胜金店墓  吐鲁番

Body-text clarification (editorial addition from the cited PDF):
1–5 (A): Most likely from one or more Triticeae genera; not a species-level diagnosis of domesticated wheat or barley. (PDF pp. 3).
6–9 (B): The authors consider a mixture of panicoid starch and starch from Triticeae stems possible; these panels are not all identified as foxtail millet or grass seeds. (PDF pp. 5).
10–11 (C): Small-grain aggregates assigned by the authors to Triticeae on their association with Type A and the bimodal size distribution; not a species identification from small-grain shape alone. (PDF pp. 5).
12 (D): A single grain, left taxonomically unidentified by the authors. (PDF pp. 5).

figures.caption_en:
Figure 2. Starch types in Shangshan jar residues compared with modern references. 1, Type I starch (suspected rice) with deep pits attributed to amylase damage; 2, damaged rice starch from modern rice wine; 3, Type I gelatinized aggregates (suspected rice), with a few recognizable grains; 4, Type II panicoid starch; 5, Type III Triticeae starch with deep grooves attributed to enzymatic damage; 6, wheat starch from modern daqu starter with deep grooves attributed to enzymatic damage; 7, Type II gelatinized aggregates with faint grain outlines and dark-red rounded objects possibly representing Monascus; 8, gelatinized wheat starch in modern daqu, with red rounded Monascus cleistothecia; 9, Type II Triticeae aggregates with intact grain shapes; 10, wheat starch aggregates in modern daqu; 11, Type III water-caltrop starch; 12, modern water-caltrop starch. Specimens 8 and 10 are from high-temperature daqu made by Yangshao Winery. Scale bars: 7–10, 20 μm; others, 10 μm.

Editorial source-check note:
The caption codes conflict with the body: panel 4 is captioned Type II Panicoideae, panel 5 Type III Triticeae and panel 11 Type III water caltrop, while the body assigns these plant groups to Types III, II and IV respectively. The printed legend is retained with this discrepancy disclosed.

body_evidence.quote: 通过实验分析, 13 件石器的26 个样品中一共提 取出478 粒淀粉粒. 除21 粒表面模糊、无法鉴别外, 其余的457 粒可以分为8 大类13 亚类(表2). 库房尘 土样品中未提取出淀粉粒. A 类: 共观察到192 粒, 其共同特点是呈多边形, 脐点居中, 无层纹. 根据粒径大小可分为2 个亚类: A1 类164 粒(图2(a)), 粒径范围8.99~24.86 μm, 均值 15.72 μm. 该类淀粉粒呈多面体状、脐点开放、有通 过脐点的T 型或X 型裂隙、无层纹. 已有的研究成 果[25,31]表明粟(Setaria italica)、黍(Panicum miliaceum)、

高粱(Sorghum bicolor)、玉米(Zea mays)和薏米(Coix chinensis)的淀粉粒一般呈多面体状, 但是粟、黍淀粉 粒的粒径均值都小于10 μm, 起源于美洲地区的玉米 传入东亚的时间较晚, 所以仅从粒径范围上考虑, A1 类淀粉粒与薏米或高粱相一致. 但是高粱淀粉粒部 分可见层纹[30], 而本次实验所观察到的所有A1 类淀 粉粒都未见层纹, 故A1 类淀粉粒很可能是来自薏苡 属某种(Coix spp.)植物. A2 类28 粒(图2(b)), 粒径范 围4.03~10.07 μm, 均值6.75 μm. 呈多边形、夹角尖 锐, 表面较为光滑、无裂隙、无层纹, 部分表现为3~5 粒组合在一起的复粒淀粉. 该类淀粉粒的表面形态 和粒径范围与很多稻族植物相一致, 如稻(Oryza sativa)和菰(Zizania latifolia). 稻与菰都有部分由多个 淀粉粒组成的复粒淀粉, 但淀粉粒的排列方式各不 相同(图2(c), (d)中箭头所示区域). 因此A2 类淀粉粒 很可能来自稻(Oryza spp.). B 类: 共观察到40 粒, 其共同特点是淀粉粒由 半圆形和扇形组合而成, 脐点偏心. 可分为2 个亚类: B1 类28 粒(图2(e)), 由两个半圆组合而成的复粒淀 粉粒, 部分单粒为复粒受外力解体而成, 粒径范围 9.77~23.49 m, 均值15.42 m. B2 类12 粒(图2(f)), 由三个扇形组合而成的复粒淀粉粒, 部分单粒为复 粒解体而成, 粒径范围8.74~17.56 μm, 均值12.64 μm. 现代植物淀粉粒形态数据库表明, 很多块根块 茎类植物, 如我们在现代样品中分析时发现莲藕 (Nelumbo nucifera)、睡莲(Nymphaea tetragona)、裂果 薯(Schizocapsa plantaginea)淀粉粒具有这种由2~3 个 淀粉粒组合而成的半圆形或扇形复粒淀粉粒. 虽然 暂不能确定具体的种属, 但可以将B 类淀粉粒鉴定

为根茎类植物淀粉粒. C 类: 共观察到74 粒, 其共同特点是淀粉粒呈 椭圆形或近圆形, 脐点居中, 消光臂相互垂直. 可分 为3 个亚类: C1 类30 粒(图2(g)), 淀粉粒呈椭圆形或 近圆形, 表面比较光滑, 无裂隙和层纹. 粒径范围 7.04~19.49 m, 均值11.53 m. C2 类26 粒(图2(h)), 呈椭圆形, 大部分表面有裂隙或小坑. 粒径范围 9.59~18.70 m, 均值14.22 m. C3 类18 粒(图2(i)), 呈圆形、表面较光滑、脐点非常开放. 粒径范围 8.39~16.11 m, 均值11.66 m. 由于很多植物生长 过程中都会产生部分圆形和椭圆形的淀粉粒, 因此 本文将此类淀粉暂时不作具体分类. 即便如此, 该类 淀粉粒在进行考古器物的功能分析、判别器物上提取 的淀粉粒是否来自污染、以及说明古人类植物利用多 样性等方面有着重要意义[10].

D 类: 共观察到26 粒(图2(j)), 呈椭圆形, 层纹 明显, 偏光下层纹尤为清晰, 大部分有通过脐点的纵 贯裂隙. 粒径范围15.84~45.23 m, 均值29.12 m. 该类淀粉粒在形态上具有明显的豇豆属(Vigna)植物 淀粉粒特征. 通过与现代植物淀粉粒形态数据库相 比对, D 类淀粉粒与很多豇豆属植物, 如赤豆(V. angularis)、豇豆(V. unguiculata)和绿豆(V. radiata)等 相一致, 很可能是其中的一种或几种. E 类: 共观察到31 粒, 分为2 个亚类. E1 类9 粒 (图2(k)), 呈正六边形, 部分可见脐点, 表面有凸起 的挤压面. 粒径范围12.03~20.86 m, 均值15.48 m. E2 类22 粒(图2(l)), 一边为弧形的多边形, 粒径范围 12.37~30.68 m, 均值17.75 m. 篦齿苏铁(Cycas pectinata)茎髓淀粉粒以及其他一些根茎类植物淀粉 粒如: 葛(Pueraria lobata)、黄磨芋(Amorphophallus

body_evidence.quote: 通过实验分析, 从3 颗牙齿上提取淀粉粒共48 颗, 其中从T1 上提取10 颗, T2 上提取22 颗, T3 上提 取16 颗. 其中, 6 颗淀粉已被破坏, 其他的淀粉粒可 以分为7 类. 第1 类: 6 颗. 淀粉粒成多边形, 脐点居中, 开放, 有放射状裂隙, 无层纹. 长轴在13.3~18.5 μm 之间变 化, 短轴在12.1~16.4 μm 之间变化(图3(a)和(b)). 已 有的现代植物淀粉粒数据表明, 多边形的淀粉粒大 多来自于禾本科植物种子, 比如粟 (Setaria italica)、 黍(Panicum miliaceum)、稻 (Oryza sativa)、高粱(Sorg- hum bicolor)和玉米 (Zea mays)[1~8,19~22]. 另外, 荞麦 (Fagopyrum esculentum)和山楂(Crataegus pinnatifida) 等的淀粉粒也是多边形. 但是稻、燕麦、荞麦和山楂 等植物的淀粉粒平均粒径小于该类淀粉; 高粱虽然 与此类淀粉粒粒径相近, 但高粱大多具有放射状或 者线形裂隙, 而且高粱的淀粉粒粒径较大者具有层 纹(图2(d)); 玉米起源于美洲, 直到大约16 世纪初期 传入我国[23], 而黍淀粉粒平均粒径7 μm, 单颗最大 粒径11.08 μm, 并且大多表面没有裂隙. 根据我们对
来自中国北方6 个现代粟样品的淀粉粒分析结果, 粟 的淀粉粒平均粒径在9~12 μm, 单颗最大值19.34 μm, 特征粟淀粉粒表面光滑, 裂隙明显(图2(a)). 此类淀 粉与粟类淀粉在形状大小和表面特征上均吻合, 所 以将此类淀粉粒鉴定为粟. 第2 类: 5 颗. 淀粉粒也成多边形, 脐点居中, 开

接近, 但只有1 颗, 暂存疑. 第7 类: 1 颗. 圆形, 中间有一线状痕迹, 脐点居 中, 闭合. 旋转成椭圆形、半球形、扇形等形状, 椭 圆形时有一纵向裂隙. 无层纹. 长轴为11.4 μm, 短 轴10.1 μm(图3(o)). 该淀粉粒特征与现代块茎类淀 粉比较相似, 此淀粉粒可能来自块茎类.

  水洞沟遗址(SDG)是中国北方典型的旧石器时代晚期遗址，大量的年代数据表明遗址

数。由于残留物分析需要消耗大量时间，很难完成全部标本的处理，因此选择部分适当标本

摘要  为了揭示4000a BP前后地理条件封闭的忻定盆地考古学文化大发展与传统粟黍农业及外来麦类种植和牛

骨骼为研究对象, 运用碳氮稳定同位素分析和人牙结石上植物微体化石分析的研究方法, 还原了先民的食物结构

Body-text clarification (editorial addition from the cited PDF):
a–c (A1): Similar to foxtail-millet starch and considered possibly derived from foxtail millet by the authors. (PDF pp. 2).
g–h (A1): Comparable to panicoid starch, with broomcorn millet not excluded; larger grains might also derive from Triticeae stems. The exact taxon is unresolved. (PDF pp. 2, 3).
d–e (A2): Possibly Sorghum, Coix or another grass; not assigned to a single genus or species. (PDF pp. 3).
i (B): Non-diagnostic spherical or ellipsoidal grains; some could derive from Setaria, but that assignment does not apply to the entire group. (PDF pp. 3, 3).
k (C1): Tuber-type morphology, comparable to Dioscorea starch. (PDF pp. 3, 4).
l (C2): A form common among tuber starches, without a diagnostic genus or species assignment. (PDF pp. 3, 4).
f (E): Overall morphology comparable to legumes (Fabaceae), without a genus or species assignment. (PDF pp. 4, 4).
j (F): Lacks diagnostic features; the genus and species are unidentified. (PDF pp. 4).

body_evidence.quote: mays L.)等 [17-19]。另外,荞麦(Fagopyrum esculentum Moench.)、燕麦(Avena sativa L.) 和山楂(Crataegus pinnatifida)等的淀粉粒的二维形状也是多边形,但是稻、燕麦、荞麦和 山楂等植物的的淀粉粒的平均粒径要小于该类淀粉粒 [17];玉米在16 世纪初才传入中国 [23]; 高粱的淀粉粒与粟、黍的淀粉粒在粒径和形态上有部分的重合,但高粱的淀粉粒表面裂隙 多呈放射状,消光臂则呈现弯曲特点且多有层纹 [17]。该类淀粉粒表面较光滑或有“ 一” 字 形或“Y” 字形裂隙,消光臂清晰且多为相互垂直,因而不应来自高粱,很可能来自粟、黍 或者薏苡。根据相关的研究 [21,24-25] ,粟的淀粉粒粒径范围为6.23~19.35μm,平均粒径为9.32μm, 脐点居中,其中粒径较大的颗粒有穿过脐点的裂隙;黍的淀粉粒,平均粒径为8.42μm,粒 径范围为5.96~10.99 μm,大多表面没有裂隙,只有少数淀粉粒具有穿过脐点的微弱裂隙 [24]。 该类淀粉粒中有10 颗粒径大于19 μm 的淀粉粒不应来自粟和黍,它们有横向或“Y” 字形裂 隙,不能排除来自薏苡属的可能,但薏苡属淀粉粒的消光臂呈现“Z” 字形,而该类淀粉粒 的消光臂为十字形,故排除薏苡属的可能 [22]。故综合上述的形态和大小等特征,我们认为 该类淀粉粒为禾本科粟类淀粉粒,但是也不排除粒径较小者有来自黍的可能。 B 类:该类淀粉粒为近圆形或椭圆形,其中大部分淀粉粒聚合在一起,无法准确的 统计其具体数量,其中,轮廓较清楚的淀粉粒数量大约有33 颗,脐点居中,脐点开放, 表面层纹不明显,消光呈“X” 字形,粒径范围在3.27~36.1μm(图2- c、c’、d、d’)。轻 轻敲击盖玻片,淀粉粒发生翻转后侧面呈梭形,类似于凸透镜状,中间有一裂沟。综合以 上的特征,并参考国内外关于小麦族淀粉粒的研究成果 [26-28],我们认为该类淀粉粒来自禾 本科小麦族植物淀粉粒。 C 类:10 粒,该类淀粉粒的特征是卵圆形,少数复粒淀粉,或有“Y” 字形裂隙,消 光呈“X” 字形,无层纹,粒径范围在12.22~24.25μm(图2- e、e’、f、f’)。该类淀粉的 形态与坚果类特征比较一致 [14,19],卵圆形淀粉粒多见于坚果类植物中的栎属、栗属(Castanea spp.)以及银杏(Ginkgo biloba L.) 等,其中银杏淀粉粒以卵圆形为主,兼有三角形和肾 形的变体,脐点居中,层纹不明显,消光臂呈消光呈“X” 字形交叉,且可见有中央指向 边缘的放射线,故排除银杏的可能 [29];而栗属植物如板栗,有层纹,且粒径较小,故不 符合该类淀粉粒的特征 [19]。综上,认为该类淀粉粒应来源于壳斗科栎属类植物,但本次 实验提取到的栎属植物淀粉粒较少,难以进一步鉴定种属。 D 类:2 粒,该类淀粉粒呈椭圆形,脐点居中,消光臂呈“ 十” 字形,脐点开放,表 面层纹不明显,粒径较大,粒径范围在9.52~22.55μm(图2- g、g’)。根据形态特征来看 [16], 可能来自块根块茎类植物。但由于仅发现两粒,缺乏典型鉴定特征,暂存疑。 E 类;1 粒,该类淀粉粒呈肾形,表面有凹坑,层纹较明显,有裂隙,偏光下层纹也 较明显,“X” 字形消光,粒径较大,长径29.μm,短径22.53μm(图2- h、h’)。豆科植 物的淀粉粒大多呈椭圆形、肾形或圆三角形,层纹明显,表面有树枝状、“Y” 字形、线形、 翼状裂隙等 [29]。根据其形态和大小等特征来看,该类淀粉粒应来自于豆科植物。

body_evidence.quote: M68:55和M77:9, 黍稃壳在M30:1、M30:2、M30:3、 M30:5和M68:69有发现。根据树枝状纹饰、乳突直 径和凹点数量等鉴定指标(Tubb et al., 1993; Ball et al., 1999), M90:5麦类稃壳植硅体极有可能来自小 麦。目前仅在七份样品中发现作为水稻茎叶指标的 水稻扇型植硅体, 暂未发现稻壳双峰型植硅体。此 外在M68:56、南III区M95:6样品中发现密集的不规 则多边疣粒板型、不规则多边平滑板型、导管型、 双层嵌套板型的植硅体类型(图3-q−s), 属于大麻 内果皮部位的典型植硅体类型(王聪等, 2022)。而 其他样品的不规则多边疣粒板型较少且分散, 未 发现有拼合而成的片状平面拼图形结构, 难以进一 步判断。选取M68:56与M95:6样品的500个不规则多 边疣粒板型的植硅体进行测量, 长度分别为 15.24±2.83 μm、15.08±2.60 μm, 宽度分别为9.56± 2.00 μm、9.92±2.18 μm, 与现代大麻样品平均数值 相比(长度15.4±2.3 μm、宽度10.8±1.7 μm)较小。 2.3 淀粉粒 通过对41份样品进行实验分析, 仅在20件陶 仓中提取出99颗淀粉粒。91颗淀粉粒按可鉴定的形 态可以分为3(A-C)大类; 其余3颗淀粉粒由于形态 不具备明显鉴定特征, 无法鉴定, 而归为D类; 5颗 淀粉粒受到一定程度损伤, 归为E类(图6)。 A类: 58颗, 占据淀粉粒总数的58.6%。多面体 形, 脐点居中, 大部分有裂隙, 裂隙多为横断性, 偏光下十字消光臂多相互垂直。A类淀粉粒长度范 围在2.65~18.91 μm, 平均粒径为13.20±3.85 μm。在 现代淀粉粒数据库中, 多面体型的淀粉粒大多来 自禾本科植物种子, 如粟、黍、狗尾草、水稻等, 但 水稻的淀粉粒长度范围在2.71~8.26 μm, 粒径远小 于本次实验提取到的A类淀粉粒。结合已有研究和 植硅体分析, A类淀粉粒应来自粟、黍等粟类植物。 A类淀粉粒在陶仓的出现概率为80%(16/20)。 B类: 27颗。呈凸透镜状, 脐点居中, 平面光滑, 侧面有纵向裂隙, 在偏光下观察其十字消光臂呈 狭长“X”型, 且从内向外加宽。B类淀粉粒长度范 围在2.34~30.71 μm, 平均粒径为9.82±8.45 μm。根 据现代植物淀粉粒图谱, 同时参照小麦族淀粉粒 的研究(Yang & Perry, 2013), 认为该类淀粉粒应来 源于禾本科普通小麦族植物。M68:56淀粉粒样品 在观察、鉴定中发现了小麦稃壳, 所以其5颗淀粉 粒很有可能是小麦; 同时结合麦类植硅体的发现, M68:6淀粉粒粒群也可能来自小麦。B类淀粉粒在 陶仓的出现概率为25%(5/20)。 C类: 6颗, 均来自M68:82样品中。多呈椭圆形

和圆三角形, 脐点可见, 偏于一侧, 表面光滑有 “一”字形裂隙, 轮纹清晰, 在偏光下消光强烈, 消 光臂弯曲。C类淀粉粒长度范围在9.75~16.15 μm, 平均粒径为13.87±2.37 μm。根据这些鉴定特征, 现 代淀粉粒数据库中块根块茎类淀粉粒的形态特征 与C类相似, 而且可能来自薯蓣科植物。C类淀粉 粒在陶仓的出现概率为5%(1/20)。 D类: 3颗。由于形状不具备鉴定特征, 暂无法 对比确定。 E类: 5颗。该类淀粉粒因受一定程度损伤而无 法进一步鉴定。主要表现为淀粉粒由边缘向内产生 裂隙, 消光区域的扩大, 推测是碾磨加工所造成 的损伤(葛威, 2010; Ma et al., 2019)。

figures.caption_en:
Fig. 3 Starch grains from pits of the Fengtai Site in Qinghai Province. They can be divided into 6 groups. The first group: (a) and (b); the second: (c) and (d); the third: (e) and (f); the fourth: (g); the fifth: (h); and the sixth: (i).

Body-text clarification (editorial addition from the cited PDF):
a–b (第一类): One or more Triticeae taxa; wheat and barley are not individually distinguished. (PDF pp. 2).
c–d (第二类): Possibly foxtail millet and/or sorghum in the authors’ interpretation; sorghum requires further evidence and is not a confirmed cultivated crop here. (PDF pp. 2).
e–f (第三类): Legumes: some compare with Vigna or Pisum, another with Cicer; not all identified as mung bean or adzuki bean. (PDF pp. 2, 2).
g (第四类): Possibly a root or tuber, without a precise taxonomic assignment. (PDF pp. 2, 3).
h (第五类): Similar to lily starch; the authors suggest Liliaceae, not a particular lily species. (PDF pp. 3).
i (第六类): A large grain whose plant origin remains unidentified in the source. (PDF pp. 3).

body_evidence.quote: We examined six phytolith samples from the sediment that had filled the bowl, and used them to diagnose their plant of origin. Three samples from the noodle layer near the bottom of the bowl contained abundant husk phyto- liths of the types known as dendriform-1 (Fig. 1b) and dendriform-2 (Fig. 1c) at con- centrations of 9.81104 and 4.36104 grains per gram, respectively. Their shape and pat- terning allowed us to diagnose them as millets, and they were identified as belonging to Pan- icum miliaceum and Setaria italica, respec- tively (see supplementary information). The starch grains found in the noodle sample (Fig. 1d) closely resemble those of millets, based on our comparison with modern refer- ence samples from different cereal grains.

To determine the taxa of foxtail millet and common millet, we analyzed the phytoliths of 46 grain crop samples stored in 5 newly excavated storage pits (CS-I to CS-V) at the Cishan site, and 1 sample (BWG) preserved in a storage bottle from the Culture Museum of Cishan. These grain crop samples are dated between ca. 10,300 and ca. 7,500 cal yr BP based on new 14C dating measurements (Fig. 3, Table S1). All 47 archaeological samples we analyzed contained abun- dant diagnostic husk phytoliths that can be divided into 2 groups according to their phytolith assemblages and 14C dating results. The first group, including 27 samples from CS-I, III, and IV, is dated between ca. 10,300 and ca. 8,700 cal yr BP. All of the husk phytoliths present are diagnostic of common millet based on their shapes,  patterns (Fig. 2 A, C, and E), and average R value (0.7) (Fig. 2I). The second group, including 20 samples from CS-II, V, and BWG, is dated between ca. 8700 and ca. 7,500 cal yr BP. More than 97% of the husk phytoliths are also diagnostic of the common millet (97.2% for CS- II, n  1,273; 97.5% for CS-V, n  1,000; 99.6% for BWG, n  1,000), but a small quantity (0.4–2.8%) of the husk phytoliths in the second group can be attributed to S. italica (Fig. 2 G and I). Group A (Figure 3(a)-(c)): nine spherical or po- lygonal starch grains with combinations of attributes that only occur in seeds of foxtail millet (Setaria italica) were recovered from the slab. Seven starch grains had centric and open hila, and no demonstrable lamellae. They often had deeply crossed, winged to Y-shaped, or stellated fissure, surfaces with short lines radiating from the centre to edges, and they measure more than 14 μm in length. These features are highly diagnostic and are

Group B (Figure 3(d)): two ovoid starch grains had centric, open hila, demonstrable lamellae, and a linear or small Y-shaped fissure. The lamellae were clearer under polarized light than under unpolarized light. The sizes of the two grains are 23.19m and 23.95 μm, respectively. Starch grains of this type are unknown in species other than adzuki bean (Vigna angularis).

Group C: four ovoid starch grains were characterized by an X-shaped Maltese extinction cross visible under polarized light. Group C had two subgroups, C1 and C2. Group C1 had two normal oval grains. They had centric and open hila, longitudinal fissures, no lamellae, but dense radiations vertical to the longitudinal fissure on the surface of the grains (Figure 3(e)). The sizes are 15.01 and 16.99 μm, respectively. The features of starch grains in group C1 correspond to those from modern Q. mongolicus[22]. The remaining two starch grains belong to group C2. One is rounded-angular oval; the other is drop-shaped (Figure 3(f)). They had eccentric and closed hila, no lamellae, no fissure, and measured 17.93 and 8.78 μm in size, respectively. These two grains are defi- nitely from seeds of Q .acutissima[22].

Group D (Figure 3(g), (h)): the slab contained seven rounded starch grains, which had centric, open hila, de- monstrable lamellae, small Y-shaped fissures, and measured 18.11-29.15 μm in size. This group cannot be identified at this time because no starch grains similar to them are currently in worldwide mod- ern comparative collections, including references collec- tions from America and Australia.

Body-text clarification (editorial addition from the cited PDF):
a (A1): Interpreted by the authors as Job’s-tears-type starch; other modern grass comparators are not additional archaeological identifications. (PDF pp. 5).
b (A2): Very possibly Oryza; cultivated rice is suggested, but the authors explicitly call the identification tentative. (PDF pp. 5, 5).
c (B): Compared by the authors with acorn starch from other sites; no particular oak species is assigned here. (PDF pp. 6).
d–e (C): Lenticular morphology, but the discussion explicitly leaves Group C unidentified; shape alone is not used here to reassign it to Triticeae. (PDF pp. 6).
f (D): Unidentified in the source; no modern comparator is promoted to a diagnosis. (PDF pp. 6).
g–h (E): Similar to Chinese horse-chestnut/buckeye (Aesculus chinensis) seed starch; based on one grain and explicitly tentative. (PDF pp. 5).
i (F): Considered very possibly derived from Job’s tears by the authors. (PDF pp. 5).
j–o (正文G；原图注j–l误列D): The body assigns j–l (unpolarized) and m–o (polarized) to Group G, compares them with adzuki bean and discusses Vigna. The caption calls j–l Group D, conflicting with the body. (PDF pp. 4, 4, 5).

Editorial source-check note:
The source also has inconsistent counts: total 42, but sample totals K1=21, K2=4 and K3=20; the K3 components sum to 19. No revised total is silently substituted. The Chinese version S093 also contains a related discrepancy.

through the hila in some grains (Figure 3j–l). The grains in group G were very large in size. The mean size was almost 40 μm, but the Maltese extinction crosses were not very intact (Figure 3m–o). Besides starch grains, Softwood tracheids with bordered pits were also seen using microscopy1) (Figure 4a, b). Bor- dered pits, like starch grains, appeared to have an extinction cross under polarized light (Figure 4c, d), which often con- fused researchers.

The grey-yellow sample, in contrast, contained clay miner- als which could be seen using microscopy. There were more damaged starch grains recovered from these charred residues than from the stone tools analyzed from the Shangzhai site [14]. Though the major morpho- logical characteristics of starch grains were still intact, the Maltese extinction crosses were not (Figure 3m–o), proba- bly due to damage from heating. But, as was previously mentioned, because starch grains from different plants have different gelatinization temperatures, and because the pot- tery could have been broken when the food was cooking, starch grains which did not reach the gelatinization tem- peratures could survive and preserve. Modern reference collections show that starch grains with polygonal shapes are almost always derived from seeds

body_evidence.quote: Therefore, the following protocol was used. (1) Slide and cover containing dental calculus were taken apart by forceps, and placed into beakers. (2) The beakers were shaken in an ultrasonic water bath for 10 min at a power of 500 W×50%. (3) A 5% solution of sodium hexametaphosphate (Calgon) was added to each sample to deflocculate the calculus and ease dispersal, and then rinsed twice by using ultrapure wa- ter. (4) Starch was isolated using a solution of CsCl at a density of 1.3 and 1.8 g/cm3. (5) The recovered residue was mounted on a slide. (6) In addition, we placed tooth T2 into beaker, and then retrieved starch grains repeating (2)–(5) again. A protocol used to tooth T3 was revised partly after summary of aforementioned protocols in order to perfect the protocol and make it more effective. 1) The tooth was brushed with a soft toothbrush in ultrapure water to remove adherent soil and other particles. 2) The tooth was shaken in an ultrasonic water bath for 15 min at a power of 500 W×50%. 3) A 5% solution of Calgon was added to sample to deflocculate the calculus and ease dispersal for 10 hours, and then rinsed it twice in ultrapure water. 4) The calculus was dissolved in a 10% solution of HCl for 12 hours, and then rinsed it twice in ultrapure water. 5) The retrieved re- mains were mounted on a slide. The length of the major axis is 13.3–18.5 μm, and the minor axis is 12.1–16.4 μm. Modern reference collections show that starch grains with polygonal shapes are usually derived from seeds in the grass family, Poaceae. Plants in our comparative collection include fox- tail millet (Setaria italica), broomcorn millet (Panicum miliaceum), rice (Oryza sativa), sorghum (Sorghum bicolor), oat (Avena sativa), and maize (Zea mays). body_evidence.quote: We compared starches from unprocessed seeds (Fig. 2) with those from the ground flour of foxtail millet, broomcorn millet and wheat. Since the process of grinding creates pressure on the seeds, the starch granules of cereal flour may show some morphological changes (Babot 2003). We noticed that starches from unprocessed millets tended to cluster into groups, while starches from ground millet flour often appeared as disjoined single grains with the occurrence of some fissures radiating from the hilum (see arrows in Figs 3 (1a) and 3 (2a)). The starch granules from commercial wheat flour showed even more severe alterations on the surface. Incomplete and fractured granules were present (Fig. 3 (6a)), and striations in different directions appeared on the surface of some granules (Fig. 3 (3a)). In other cases, the outline of the granule had become irregular, and the surface rough in texture (Fig. 3 (4a)). The lamellae became unusually distinc- tive in some areas on the granule (see arrow in Fig. 3 (5a)). Meanwhile, these damaged granules also showed alterations in extinction crosses, as the arms became wider and the centre became a large dark circle (see arrows in Figs 3 (1b), 3 (2b), 3 (4b) and 3 (5b)). These alterations reflect damage to the crystal structure. Our observation of these characteristics is consistent with research on maize starch granules after ball-mill treatment, which shows that granules lost flatness and smoothness and became rough on the surface, with a final disruption of starch components (Tamaki et al. 1998). body_evidence.quote: We compared starches from unprocessed seeds (Fig. 2) with those from the ground flour of foxtail millet, broomcorn millet and wheat. Since the process of grinding creates pressure on the seeds, the starch granules of cereal flour may show some morphological changes (Babot 2003). We noticed that starches from unprocessed millets tended to cluster into groups, while starches from ground millet flour often appeared as disjoined single grains with the occurrence of some fissures radiating from the hilum (see arrows in Figs 3 (1a) and 3 (2a)). The starch granules from commercial wheat flour showed even more severe alterations on the surface. Incomplete and fractured granules were present (Fig. 3 (6a)), and striations in different directions appeared on the surface of some granules (Fig. 3 (3a)). In other cases, the outline of the granule had become irregular, and the surface rough in texture (Fig. 3 (4a)). The lamellae became unusually distinc- tive in some areas on the granule (see arrow in Fig. 3 (5a)). Meanwhile, these damaged granules also showed alterations in extinction crosses, as the arms became wider and the centre became a large dark circle (see arrows in Figs 3 (1b), 3 (2b), 3 (4b) and 3 (5b)). These alterations reflect damage to the crystal structure. Our observation of these characteristics is consistent with research on maize starch granules after ball-mill treatment, which shows that granules lost flatness and smoothness and became rough on the surface, with a final disruption of starch components (Tamaki et al. 1998). body_evidence.quote: widened at the edge of the cross in some cases. Second, the features of these granules, particularly the extinction crosses, are similar to some mineral grains that we have often encountered when examining ancient samples. For example, there are many such grains in the samples we collected from Shizitan in Jixian county, Shanxi province (Fig. 5). They show cross-like bire- fringence under polarized light, and the maximum lengths of the granules are similar to those of millet starches. These grains may easily be mistaken for starches. But when observed under a DIC view, they look very flat on the surface, unlike the three-dimensional characteristics of starch granules. In addition to mineral grains, fungal spores and gypsum spherulites may also be misidentified as starches. Both are common in soils and show extinction crosses under polarized light (Haslam 2006; Loy 2006). In any case, the Lajia noodle ‘starches’ need to be re-examined. In conclusion, our research shows that, first, as determined by the property of millets, it is very difficult, if not impossible, to make pure millet noodles and it is even more unlikely to make noodles from millet with husks. Second, it is unclear from the original report whether the residues from the Lajia noodle remains were actually derived from the noodles themselves. Third, starch morphology after cooking shows distinctive alterations, particularly the loss of the extinction cross, a phenomenon that does not fit with the original interpretation of the granules said to be from the Lajia noodles. body_evidence.quote: From our investigations, starch grains of P. miliaceum with husk from the Yingpan Tomb are completely unchanged in morphology resembling modern reference samples (Fig. 4b), which exclude the possibility that starch grains from the Subeixi samples changed with age. Starch grains ground then soaked in water at room temperature hardly changed or changed very little, with a slight swelling of only a few grains. However, varied cooking methods produced some different changes among the starch grains of P. miliaceum. Compared with the uncooked samples, the gelatiniza- tion of the starch grains in the cooked P. miliaceum is very obvious. Heating in the presence of water causes a most remarkable swelling and distortion of the starch grains. When boiled whole, some grains retained their angular shape and extinction crosses for longer than 10 min, becoming fully gelatinized after 20 min. Ground P. miliaceum starch grains, however, tend to be more vulnerable and

and Europe (Lu et al., 2009a). Other early charred grains of common millet have been found at Xinglonggou (8000e7500 cal yrs BP) (Zhao, 2008), Yuezhuang (6060e5750 cal yrs BC) (Crawford et al., 2006), Dadiwan (7800e7350 cal yrs BP) (Liu and Kong, 2004), and Shangzhai (7500e7000 cal yrs BP) (Yang et al., 2009). During the Middle and Late Neolithic, foxtail millet (S. italica) surpassed common millet, becoming the most common cereal in North China. However, common millet was still significantly more common in inland areas than in those regions further east (Lee et al., 2007). The historical crop distributions indicate that common millet has a stronger drought resistance, and could grow better in poor soil (Crawford et al., 2005), thus it is no wonder that the common millet predominated over other crops in the extremely arid Turpan District. To date, the earliest P. miliaceum found in Xinjiang was nearly 4000 cal years BP at the Xiaohe Cemeteries (unpublished data), and later 2800 cal years BP at the Yanghai Tomb inTurpan, and it already was the main cereal crop in Turpan (Jiang et al., 2007b). Our research at the Subeixi Cemeteries proves that P. miliaceum was an important crop untill 300 BC. Moreover, it had been ground and made into noodles and cakes as a staple food. Aging can be one possibility for the changes of starch grains in ancient food remains. However, a large number of ancient starch grains are morphologically unaltered in many cases (Piperno et al., 2000, 2004; Pearsall et al., 2004; Fullagar et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2009). The starch grains of both whole and ground ones collapsed at the centre, producing in the majority of cases fissures radiating from the hilums and a small portion becoming hollow inside (Fig. 7a, b). Longer boiling times caused more extreme swelling and loss of features till all of the grains gelatinized completely. Compared with other cooking methods, baking results in less damage to starch grains. After 20 min of baking many starch grains still remain unchanged with clear or damaged extinction crosses. The most distinct difference of baked P. miliaceum starch grains is that nearly all the grains disintegrated with visible shadows or hollows at the centre, while fissuring is extremely rare (Fig. 7c). Steaming, like boiling, causes extensive swelling and gelatini- zation of the starch grains in a short time. The ground P. miliaceum, kneaded to dough, and then steamed produced starch grains which are almost all completely damaged, although a small portion of the starch grains still retained their characteristic shape and extinction crosses. The partly damaged grains appear to break down from the centre displaying hollows or fissures, with the former pattern being a little more common. Based on cooking experiments, all the grains can be classified into five different morphological categories which are (I) unchanged

(III) and a relatively high proportion of damaged grains with fissures (V) (Fig. 7b, e). Ancient caryopses produce more starch grains belonging to Category V, while the proportion of completely damaged grains decreases to a certain extent, resembling the starch grains of whole-boiled P. miliaceum (Fig. 7a, d). The starch grains of all the ancient cakes are characterized by the highest rate of intact grains (I), a relatively low proportion of totally damaged grains (III), rather high percentage of damaged grains with shadows or hollows (IV), and extremely few grains with fissures at the centre (Fig. 7c, feh). In order to clarify the relation of ancient samples and modern cooking-experimental samples, cluster analysis of SPSS was applied to the proportion of five different morphologies from modern and archaeological samples in Table 6. A dendrogram of the five morphologies in 9 samples was constructed (Fig. 9). There were 2 groups when the threshold is about 14. The modern boiled and steamed samples clustered together with ancient noodles and caryopsis samples. Within this group, moreover, the ancient noodles and modern ground-boiled samples composed one small group, while the of ancient caryopses and modern whole-boiled samples were similar. body_evidence.quote: Type I starches (n 1⁄4 47) are mostly triangular with round corners or are irregularly oval in shape. The fissure is linear and sometimes appears as a deep depression; the arms of extinction crosses are often bent, lamellae are rare, and the hilum is either centric or eccentric (Fig. 3.1e4). These features clearly resemble several Quercus species (SI Figure 2.1e3), which grow in north China today (Yang et al., 2009b). When size ranges are compared to those in our reference collection, Type I starches (5.45e24.61 mm) show best matches to Quercus variabilis and Quercus fabri (Fig. 4.A). The deep depressions visible in some grains may have been caused by grinding, as similar damage to starch grains was noted in ground acorn flour (Q. variabilis), which was milled with a millstone for 12 min in our experimental study (SI Figure 2.4).

Eighty starch grains are classified to Type II, including 22 indi- vidual granules (4.5e24.09 mm) observed as isolated granules or as small granule clusters. A group of small granules (range 1.71e5.08 mm) bound within a cell wall (n 1⁄4 58 measured) are also included in this tally. The isolated granules are characterized by having facetted shapes with either angular or round edges; the numbers of facets vary from four to six; the hilum is centric, and often appears as a deep depression; pronounced star fissures often radiate toward the periphery; and the arms of extinction crosses are mostly straight. In several cases lamellae are visible on a part of the granule (Fig. 3.5e8).

Type III starches (n 1⁄4 5) are characterized by a larger granule size (19.11e38.21 mm), an eccentric hilum, lack of fissures, irregular triangular or oval shapes, and bent extinction crosses (Fig. 3.9e12). These granules show strong similarities in morphology and size with the Chinese shanyao yam (Dioscorea opposita Thunb.) in our reference samples. D. opposita is represented by numerous culti- vated varieties in different regions across China. The wild forms can also be found in mountainous areas. Starch grains from five D. opposita samples (wild and cultivated) in our reference samples show some notable variations in shape within a specimen as well as between specimens, and this is an area of future research. Shizitan Type III starch grains are similar to a yam reference specimen collected from Luoyang, Henan, and referred to as tiegun shanyao by the locals (SI Figure 2.11, 12, Fig. 4.C). Yam starch grains are rare in the Shizitan assemblage. Since tubers do not have to be ground prior to consumption, processing tubers was probably not the main function of these tools.

Type IV starches (n 1⁄4 4) are irregularly oval or facetted in shape. Fissures and lamellae are not visible and the extinction cross often has many arms. The center of the cross sometimes appears as a large dark area (Fig. 3.13e16), consistent with bean starch grains damaged by grinding (see Babot, 2003). body_evidence.quote: This handstone is an elongated slab with two use surfaces which were heavily ground; the cross-section is trapeziform and dimen- sions are: 17 cm long, 5.2 cm wide and 5 cm thick (Fig. 2A). It was found on the house floor of House No.64 which belongs to the Xiaohexi Culture (before 6200 BC) (Suo, 2005), west of the hearth (Fig. 3A). The white macroscopic residue can be observed on the use surfaces (Fig. 2A). Samples F64A and F64B yielded nineteen and seven starch grains respectively (Table 3). Three starch grains from F64A were polygonal. Their sizes are 8, 9 and 8 mm respectively. They have circular hila with a smooth surface (Fig. 4A). These starch grains show similarities to Panicum miliaceum (Fig. 5A), but the

sample of these type of starch grains is too small to make a convincing identification. One ovoid starch grain from F64A is 18 mm and has a longitudinal fissure that is characteristic of Quercus sp. (Fig. 4B) (compared with Fig. 5CeG, Yang et al., 2009a, 2009b).

This grinding stone which had a concave use surface is 34 cm long, 18 cm wide and 3e7.4 cm thick (Fig. 2B). It was uncovered from the house floor of No.63 which belongs to the Xinlongwa Culture, southwest of the hearth (Fig. 3C). Samples F63A and F63B yielded 245 and 9 starch grains respectively (Table 3). Forty-seven of the starch grains extracted from F63A are spherical or polygonal (Fig. 4C). The starch grains range in size between 5 and 11 mm. They

have smooth surfaces without fissures. These starch grains are from the grass family Poaceae, and most likely from broomcorn millet (Panicum miliaceum) (Yang et al., 2009a, 2010a). We also found twenty-four polygonal starch grains from F63A (Fig. 4D). They have centric and open hilum and deep fissures. Seven grains measured more than 14 mm in length. Yang et al. (2009a, 2010a) indicated that this kind of starch grains is possibly from Setaria italica. The size of another ten starch grains are between 11 and 14 mm. Setaria italica and Setaria viridis have starch grains that fall into this size range (Yang et al., 2010a). The ten grains cannot be identified to species but are probably from Setaria. The remaining seven grains had the same morphological features as the other seventeen grains, but range in size between 8 and 11 mm. These grains are also possibly from Setaria. body_evidence.quote: clearly observed on all of four artifacts. Our reference collection includes examples of Setaria italica, Panicum miliaceum and different nuts including Quercus, Lithocarpus, Cyclobalanopsis and these are discussed in detail. Starch grains from millets are polyg- onal in shape (Fig. 5A, B). Yang et al. (2010a) has conducted morphological characterization of starch grains from two domes- ticated millets (Setaria italic and Panicum miliaceum) and their wild relatives including green foxtail grass (Setaria viridis), Panicum bisulcatum and Eriochloa villosa in North China. This study showed that starch grains from broomcorn millet have smooth surfaces, mostly without fissures, whereas starch grains of foxtail millet mostly have open hila with characteristic fissures. It is also indi- cated by Yang et al. (2010a) that starch grains whose sizes are smaller than 11 mm might be either of broomcorn millet if they have more than 40% grains without fissures or of Setaria if they have more than 30% of starch grains with fissures. The starch grains from acorns have different morphologies depending on their species. Starch grains from Quercus are mostly oval shaped and some have longitudinal fissures across the hila (Yang et al., 2009b; Fig. 5D). Starch grains from Lithocarpus and Cyclobalanopsis are oval and irregular, bigger than those from Quercus and some have shallow fissures (Table 2; Fig. 5H, I; Liu et al., 2010a, 2010b). Starch grains from Cyclobalanopsis are semi-compound (Fig. 5I).

This handstone is an elongated slab with two use surfaces which were heavily ground; the cross-section is trapeziform and dimen- sions are: 17 cm long, 5.2 cm wide and 5 cm thick (Fig. 2A). These starch grains show similarities to Panicum miliaceum (Fig. 5A), but the

sample of these type of starch grains is too small to make a convincing identification. One ovoid starch grain from F64A is 18 mm and has a longitudinal fissure that is characteristic of Quercus sp. (Fig. 4B) (compared with Fig. 5CeG, Yang et al., 2009a, 2009b).

measurements and features of this starch assemblage are similar to Quercus. One starch grain had eccentric hilum and longitudinal fissure (Fig. 4F). Starch grains with eccentric hila are only found in Quercus acutissima. The morphology and size of this starch grain are very close to starch grains from Quercus acutissima that were identified previously (Fig. 5E; Yang et al., 2009a, 2009b).

body_evidence.quote: All starch grains from wild millets within the genus Setaria have wrinkled surfaces and coarse edges (Fig. 2aeh). Starch grains from green foxtail grass (S. viridis) are the largest in maximum length fol- lowed by those of S. pumila. Starch grains from S. pumila and S. parviflora are mainly spherical in shape with short lines that radiate from the center to the edges of the grains. Grains from S. viridis often have fissures through the hila which vary in form, while those from other species seldom have strongly-defined fissures.

Starch grains from foxtail millets have a basic polyhedral shape with occasional spherical or oval grains, and the surfaces are smooth (Fig. 2iel). These observations are in line with those re- ported previously (Reichert, 1913). The hila of starch grains from foxtail millets are centric, and the majority of grains have hila that are traversed by deep, linear, transverse, Y-shaped or stellate fissures. Radiating lines occur commonly from the center to the edge on the surface of grains. 987 starch grains from 9 samples were measured. The mean maximum length measurements of 9 samples are 9e12 mm with the largest starch grains occurring in the sample collected in Inner Mongolia, and the smallest from the sample collected in Hebei Province. The mean of 987 starch grains is 9.9  2.3 mm, 95% CI is 9.7e10.0 mm.

Polyhedral starch grains dominate the sample (Fig. 2meo), an observation that is in line with previous research (Reichert, 1913). The hila of starch grains from broomcorn millets are centric, and almost 70% of the grains are unfissured. The remaining 30% grains have slight fissures through the hila, and a very few starch grains have transverse or Y-shaped fissures. The mean maximum length measurements of 9 samples are 6.5e7.5 mm, and, notably, starch grains that are larger than 10 mm in length make up less than 2% of the population. Only 3 of 923 grains measured more than 10 mm and the largest size is 11.9 mm. The mean maximum length of the 923 starch grains from broomcorn millets is 7.3  1.4 mm and the 95% CI is 7.2e7.4 mm.

The wild ancestor of broomcorn millet is still unknown. Panicum bisulcatum, a wild grass and congeneric species with broomcorn millet, has similar morphological features in its starch grains in both size and surface features. The differences lie in the size classes and fissure patterns. The ration of length to width of wild grass starches measure 1.0e1.7 um larger than those of broomcorn millet (w1.0) (Fig. 2p), and starch grains from P. bisulcatum have fissures even less frequently than the starches of broomcorn millet.

body_evidence.quote: The tribes and genera within the Poaceae are easily distin- guishable from one another using very basic morphological traits and assemblage characteristics (Reichert, 1913; Tateoka, 1962). Fig. 4 shows the starch grains extracted from the seeds of plants within the genera Oryza, Zizania, Sorghum, Coix, Eriochloa, Avena as well as 8 genera from the Tribe Triticeae. Starch grains from the Tribe Triticeae are lenticular, a morphology that is very different from others which are typically dominated by polyhedral shapes.

body_evidence.quote: Starch grain analysis The starch grains extracted could be divided into two distinctive types. Type 1 were large simple grains (10–40 mm) (Table 3) (Figs. 4, 5), circular/oval in outline, with centric and faint hilum. When rotated into side view, they assumed a lenticular form. Some had demonstrable lamellae (Fig. 6A, B). All cakes and dumplings possessed this type of starch grain. According to modern reference collections and published references [17,21,24,25] (Fig. 4A–C), this type of starch grain could be interpreted as one of the crops belonging to Triticeae. It is most likely that they were derived from Triticum aestivum, Hordeum vulgare, or H. vulgare var. coeleste. Type 2 was smaller (4–10 mm) (Table 3) (Figs. 4, 5), sub-rounded and polygonal overall in shape, with a central and faint hilum, and occasional fissures, with no lamellae. Most of the extinction crosses were bilaterally symmetrical. Starch grains extracted from the ancient porridge fell into this type, which could be identified as belonging to Panicum miliaceum (Fig. 6C) (compared with Fig. 4D, [22,26])

body_evidence.quote: Starch grain analysis The starch grains extracted could be divided into two distinctive types. Type 1 were large simple grains (10–40 mm) (Table 3) (Figs. 4, 5), circular/oval in outline, with centric and faint hilum. When rotated into side view, they assumed a lenticular form. Some had demonstrable lamellae (Fig. 6A, B). All cakes and dumplings possessed this type of starch grain. According to modern reference collections and published references [17,21,24,25] (Fig. 4A–C), this type of starch grain could be interpreted as one of the crops belonging to Triticeae. It is most likely that they were derived from Triticum aestivum, Hordeum vulgare, or H. vulgare var. coeleste. Type 2 was smaller (4–10 mm) (Table 3) (Figs. 4, 5), sub-rounded and polygonal overall in shape, with a central and faint hilum, and occasional fissures, with no lamellae. Most of the extinction crosses were bilaterally symmetrical. Starch grains extracted from the ancient porridge fell into this type, which could be identified as belonging to Panicum miliaceum (Fig. 6C) (compared with Fig. 4D, [22,26])

Phytolith analysis All husk phytoliths extracted from porridge had smooth surfaces without any papillae; the epidermal long cell walls were g- undulated. Moreover, the ending structures of the epidermal long cells were of the cross-finger type (Fig. 6E). In addition, the average R value (ratio of the width of endings interdigitation to the amplitude of undulations) was 0.82, which is in accordance with that of Panicum miliaceum (0.7960.12) [20] (Table 4). In this case the husk phytoliths extracted from the porridge belonged to Panicum miliaceum. This scenario agrees well with the results of the starch grain analysis. However, the phytolith morphology of the ancient dumpling revealed that the epidermal long cell walls were V-undulated and the ending structures of epidermal long cells were of the cross-wavy type (Fig. 6F). Fifty phytoliths extracted from the dumpling were also measured and statistically analyzed and found to have an average R value of 0.38, which fit quite well with that of S. italica (0.3360.11) [20] (Table 4). The phytoliths from the dumpling were consequently identified to be from S. italica.

body_evidence.quote: Our comparative work with modern specimens indicates that to distinguish domesticated millet starch grains from wild, and foxtail millet from broomcorn millet, there are two key factors to be considered. One factor is morphological and applies to single- starch grains, and the second is an assemblage-based approach. The basic morphological form of all studied wild and domesti- cated millet starches is a polyhedral shape with occasional spherical forms present (Fig. 2). Starch grains from wild millets within the genus Setaria are characterized by wrinkled surfaces and rough edges, and the mean size is typically <10 μm, much smaller than both domesticated foxtail millet and green foxtail grass (17). The starch grains from green foxtail grass are the largest among the wild millets, and their range of sizes (<14 μm) and morphology overlap somewhat with foxtail millet.

body_evidence.quote: No starches were recovered from the three control specimens. More than 400 starch grains were recovered from the tools (Table 1), and 255 were identified as starch grains from grasses. Some 205 of the 255 grass starch grains have the polyhedral or spherical shape (Fig. 3) characteristic of millet starches. When the assem- blage is viewed as a whole, starch grains with wrinkled surfaces and rough edges, wild characteristics, comprise at least 38% of the millet starches, and starch grains measuring >14 μm in size, characteristic of domesticated seeds, make up about 46.8% of the millet starches (Fig. 4). Of the remaining starch grains in the as- semblage, the remaining 50 grass starch grains are derived from grasses in the tribe Triticeae, several species of which occur locally, and 13 starch grains are characteristic of geophytes. Studies to identify and interpret these other residues are ongoing.

No starches were recovered from the four control specimens. More than 793 starch grains were recovered from the tools, carbonized residue, and cultural deposits (Table 1), 742 of which were identified as starch grains from grass seeds. Subsequent analyses and comparative studies have led to the identification of 525 of the 742 grass starches as derived from millets, and the remaining 217 from grasses classified within the tribe Triticeae (Fig. 3). Additionally, 50 starch grains characteristic of geophytes were identified. During the early occupational phase, the starch grains with wrinkled surfaces and rough edges, characteristics of

All millet starch grains >14 μm bear morphological features consistent with those of domesticated foxtail millet. The remaining starch grains, which measure <14 μm, vary in mor- phologies. Some have wrinkled surfaces like those from wild millet grass, and some have smooth surfaces that are the same as starch grains from both wild and domesticated foxtail and broomcorn millets (Fig. 3). Because the broomcorn millet phy- toliths were recovered from the late phase occupation at Donghulin, this assemblage of starch grains (<14 μm) bearing smooth surfaces is very likely derived from broomcorn millet. We are not yet comfortable making a secure identification of these starch grains because they also occurred in the early phase occupations at Donghulin and Nanzhuangtou when there is no supporting phytolith evidence, and the starch grains from both wild and domesticated foxtail and broomcorn millets overlap with one another in this size zone (17).

body_evidence.quote: The starch grains from species within the grass family are typically, but not always, polyhedral (Fig. 1). Of the 38 studied species, 23 are characterized by simple, polyhedral starch grains, e.g. foxtail millet (Setaria italica) (Fig. 1-9), but compound starch grains occur in some species, e.g. naked oat (Avena nuda) (Fig.1-37). Lenticular or discoidal starch grains occur in 11 of the studied species in the tribes Triticeae and Bromeae. The remaining 4 species contained spherical grains. The hila of starch grains from the studied grasses are centric with occasional fissures. The sizes range widely (Table 2), from a few microns to more than 40 mm in maximum length. The mean of starches from seeds of forage grasses are often less than 5 mm, while the mean of starch grains from rye is greater, up to 28.9  13.3 mm (Table 2).

lenticular grains are recovered with regularity, and they possess unique diagnostic characteristics. The identification and differen- tiation of archaeological starches from this group, therefore, will necessarily depend upon the larger, lenticular grains (Piperno et al., 2004; Henry et al., 2011; Perry and Quigg, 2011). For these reasons, the large size class of starches was measured and studied for this investigation while the small class was disregarded. Typical morphological characteristics of the starch grains from the tribe Triticeae are a lenticular or discoid shape, an olivary side view (Fig. 2c) and pressure craters on the surfaces of grains that appear as small depressions (Fig. 1-21e27). The mean maximum length of measurements of 10 species in this group ranges from 12.1 mm to 28.9 mm and the largest starch grain, with a maximum dimension of 45.2 mm, comes from rye. Viewed with a polarizing microscope, the starch grains show strong birefringence, with the extinction crosses appearing strongly black against a bright, white background. Some starch grains from the tribe Triticeae are unique in that the four bright white areas divided by the extinction cross change from brighter at the center of the grain, to dark, then brighter again at the edge (Fig. 2d).

body_evidence.quote: Starches that occur in the seeds of species within the tribe Tri- ticeae typically have a bimodal assemblage with two distinct size classes, small and large (Lindeboom et al., 2004) (Fig. 2a, b). The small grains tend to be rather uniform in morphology when observed at a magnification of 400. Previous studies demonstrate that these small grains are difficult to detect via compound light microscopy, are rarely diagnostic to taxa, and occur in many plant tissues (Moss, 1976; Czaja, 1978; Barton, 1991; Loy et al., 1992; Therin et al., 1997; Perry and Quigg, 2011). In contrast, the larger

lenticular grains are recovered with regularity, and they possess unique diagnostic characteristics. The identification and differen- tiation of archaeological starches from this group, therefore, will necessarily depend upon the larger, lenticular grains (Piperno et al., 2004; Henry et al., 2011; Perry and Quigg, 2011). For these reasons, the large size class of starches was measured and studied for this investigation while the small class was disregarded. Typical morphological characteristics of the starch grains from the tribe Triticeae are a lenticular or discoid shape, an olivary side view (Fig. 2c) and pressure craters on the surfaces of grains that appear as small depressions (Fig. 1-21e27). The mean maximum length of measurements of 10 species in this group ranges from 12.1 mm to 28.9 mm and the largest starch grain, with a maximum dimension of 45.2 mm, comes from rye. Viewed with a polarizing microscope, the starch grains show strong birefringence, with the extinction crosses appearing strongly black against a bright, white background. Some starch grains from the tribe Triticeae are unique in that the four bright white areas divided by the extinction cross change from brighter at the center of the grain, to dark, then brighter again at the edge (Fig. 2d).

body_evidence.quote: 3.4.1. Starch grains from rye (Secale) Starch grains that are larger than 20 mm make up 77.8% of the population. Diagnostic rye starch grains bear Y-shaped or stellate fissures through the hila, and they are sometimes surrounded by very faint concentric lamellae and delicate radiating lines (Fig. 4a). The craters on the surface often appear in reticulate patterns.

3.4.2. Starch grains from crested wheatgrass (Agropyron cristatum) These starches are the second largest in size following rye, and grains larger than 20 mm make up 70.3% of the population. Diag- nostic granules have four to six well-defined concentric, equidis- tant lamellae from hilum to edge (Fig. 4b). Craters often occur scattered on the surface of the grain (Fig. 4c).

3.4.5. Starch grains from barley and naked barley (Hordeum) Seven species within the genus Hordeum were examined in previous archaeobotanical studies (Piperno et al., 2004; Henry et al., 2011; Perry and Quigg, 2011). Of them, two species, Hor- deum spontaneum and Hordeum bulbsom, are present in China. Starch grains from the previously studied seven species always measure less than 30 mm when lamellae are absent, which is similar to our samples of barley (H. vulgare) and naked barley (H. vulgare var. coeleste), where the largest grain measured 27.4 mm. Starch grains from naked barley are a little larger than barley, and 35.0% of the starch grains are larger than 20 mm; while 57.1% of starch grains from naked barley are larger than 20 mm. The granules from barley and naked barley often present as deformed, lenticular shapes in plan view including ellipses, subcircles, semicircles, rounded- corner triangles and others (Fig. 1-22 and 23, Fig. 4d). Some starches from both samples have faint craters in reticulate patterns on their surfaces. Lamellae are extremely rare to absent.

3.4.7. Starch grains from wildrye (Elymus) Starches from seeds of 12 species of Elymus native to North America have been previously described (Reichert, 1913; Messner, 2008; Perry and Quigg, 2011). Perry and Quigg (2011) analyzed the crater (depression) patterns on the surfaces of starch grains and were able to use these criteria to identify archaeobotanical samples to species. Since no wildrye remains have been reported from archaeological sites in China, here we chose only two spe- cies, Elymus dahuricus and Elymus kamaoji, to study. The largest starch grain from seeds of these two species measures less than 20 mm. The craters of starch grains from E. dahuricus occur in reticulate patterns throughout the surface (Fig. 4g and h), while the craters on of starch grains from E. kamaoji are rare or absent (Fig. 1-19).

body_evidence.quote: The following factors should be considered in both these and other contexts in which these taxa may occur. 4) Ancient starch residues recovered from grinding stone tools almost always exhibit damage. Our experiments grinding seeds demonstrate that damaged starch grains within three genera, Aegilops, Triticum and Hordeum, are not distinguishable from each other at the genus level. 5) Perry and Quigg (2011) noted that surface craters do not occur on every starch grain from any species of grass in the tribe Triticeae, and secure identifications may require larger assemblages of microfossils. Therefore, depending upon the size of the assem- blage, and whether or not diagnostic grains are present, genus-level identifications may be more secure than species-level IDs. In- vestigators should note when diagnostic forms are present. We applied these principles as we identified starches that were previously recovered from the early occupation (11,150e10,500 cal kyr BP) of the Donghulin site located at the edge of the North China Plain (Yang et al., 2012b). Of the 137 grains initially believed to be derived from grasses in the Triticeae, 78 starch grains from two lithic mullers can now be securely identified as derived from the Tribe Triticeae. Using the data derived from the new modern comparative studies, and with application of the dichotomous key, we are now able to make further identifications. body_evidence.quote: A total of 153 starch grains were retrieved from the study sample. Of these, only 25 could not be identified at either the genus or the species level. The remaining starch granules were classified into five broad categories, described in detail below. Twenty-two starch grains could not be classified in any way due to post- or pre-depositional damage that had altered the granule morphology. The starch granules were not evenly distributed on all sampled stone knives. The majority was derived from the edges of these artifacts, and a small number were recovered from the back and the adhering sediments (Table 2). Group 1 (Fig. 4aec): This group contained seventy-nine starch grains. Seventy-eight of them had an oval form, with centric hila and no visible lamellae or fissures. The length of the starch grains was between 8.6 and 42.5 mm, and the width (taken at 90 at the mid-point of the length) was between 7.9 and 24.1 mm. The features are most similar to starch grains from chickpea, Cicer arietinum. One granule with an oval form had a centric hilum and visible lamellae, with a distinct longitudinal fissure. This is believed to be from a species of Vigna, such as the red bean, Vigna umbellate, or the mung bean, Vigna radiata. Group 2: Twenty-five starch grains had a circular to sub-circular shape in plane view (Fig. 4def), a lenticular cross-section, a central hilum (usually marked with a thin line), and distinctive dimples (Henry et al., 2011). The size of the length was between 12.4 and

22.8 mm, and the width was between 10.3 and 20.2 mm. When the starch grain was rotated, it had an oblong shape, central hilum and longitudinal fissure. These starch grains were definitely from the Triticeae tribe. Some starch grains had characteristic crater-like dimples that have been noted in a wide number of species within this genus, such as modern bread wheat, Triticum aestivum, and most other wild wheat species, such as Triticum monococcum, Tri- ticum urartu, Triticum vavilovii, and Triticum turgidum (Henry et al., 2011). Other starch granules had several features consistent with those from Hordeum spp. (barley). Group 3 (Fig. 4gei): This group contained twelve polygonal starch grains with centric and open hila, no lamellae, and radial fissures. The length was 8.5e18.3 mm, and the width was 7.6e 16.4 mm. Our modern reference collections show that starch grains with polygonal shapes are often derived from seeds in the grass family, Poaceae. Plants in our comparative collection include foxtail millet, Setaria italica, broomcorn millet, Panicum miliaceum, rice, Oryza sativa, sorghum, Sorghum bicolor, oat, Avena sativa, buckwheat, Fagopyrum esculentum, whitethorn, Crataegus pinnati- fida, (Torrence and Barton, 2006; Perry, 2002; Perry et al., 2007; Piperno et al., 1985, 2000, 2004; Piperno and Holst, 1998; Piperno and Dillehay, 2008; Zarrillo et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2009; Yang and Jiang, 2010; Li et al., 2010b). There are several likely candi- dates to have produced these starches, including sorghum, broomcorn millet, and foxtail millet. The length of sorghum is 5.7e 2

Group 5 (Fig. 4kel): The shape of five starch grains was oval, with an eccentric hilum. The starch grains had visible lamellae and a radiating fissure. The length is between 23.4 and 40.4 mm, and the width is between 18.4 and 30 mm. Based on our modern reference collection, these are most likely derived from roots or tubers. body_evidence.quote: (Caryota sp.) were recovered from six stone tools (Table 2). These granules, ranging 12.1–25.8 mm in size, are typically sub-ovate wide shouldered at the hilum, tapering toward the distal end that sometimes contains a conical concavity with a wide or narrow internal channel running from the distal end to the hilum (Figure 3a). Our reference material includes the species of Burmese fishtail palm (C. mitis) (Figure 4a), solitary fishtail palm (C. urens) (Figure 4b) and Philippines fishtail palm (C. cumingii), and there are strong morphological similarities to the first two, though size is closest to solitary fishtail palm. Six starch granules, ranging12.1–25.8 mm in size (Figure 3b), recovered from six stone tools are identical with modern reference talipot palm (Corypha umbraculifera) (Figure 4c). These typically have a sub-spheroid form with characteristic overlapping concentric rings that appear as surface features. A single granule (Figure 3c), 11 mm in size, is narrow at the hilum and elongate with a narrow channel or depression running from the hilum to the distal end (Figure 4d). The physical features are a good match for Arenga undulatifolia from our reference collection, but the lack of other Arenga sp. from our reference material and other archaeological granules necessarily lowers the certainty of this identification. Seventeen starch granules from banana (Musa sp.) were recovered from three tools recovered from ancient living surface

one (Table 2). These can be sub-divided into two groups. Seven starch granules (Figure 3d–h), ranging 25.1–55.6 mm in size, with an irregular or triangular ovoid, well defined lamellae and a wrinkled texture, were recovered from two stone tools on the same living surface, and most closely match those found in the hybrid banana type according to Lentfer [12]. Ten starch granules with a sub-circular to sub-triangular shape (Figure 3i–j), 11.7–18 mm in size, similar to the starches from one of domesticated banana’s progenitors, wild seeded banana (M. acuminata) (Figure 4e–f). In total of 48 starch granules from several freshwater roots and tubers were also recovered. Two granules from lotus root (cf. Nelumbo nucifera), 31.8 mm and 28.2 mm in length respectively, are

distinct elongate ovate with well-defined lamellae and a highly eccentric hilum in the form of a small vacuole (Figure 3k and 4g). Seventeen granules from Chinese arrowhead (Sagittaria sp.), ranging 14.2–18 mm in size, are sub-ovate with a centric or slightly offset hilum that is often stellate (Figure 3l and 4h). Twenty-nine granules from water chestnut (cf. Eleocharis dulcis) are small (ranging 8.8–12 mm in size), in triangular, oval or irregular shape, sometimes with light fissures through the centric hila (Figure 3m, 4i). From tool #8 (Figure 2) 38 starch granules from the terrestrial fern (Angiopteris sp.) were recovered (Figure 3n–o), which includes edible varieties such as Angiopteris yunnanensis [19]. Starch granules from this species are typically irregular compound

granules with complex extinction crosses under cross polarised light (Figure 4j–k). Job’s-tear (Coix spp.) also seems to have been a common resource exploited at Xincun (Figure 3p). Fifty three granules of Job’s-tear were recovered, typically spheroid or polyhedral, with two to three flat facets, centric hilum that normally has a T-shaped fissure (Figure 4l). Five starch granules from acorns (Quercus sp.) were also identified (Figure 5). Phytoliths extracted from residues adhering to the stone tools coincide with the starch results at the family level (Figure 6), except for the presence of rice (Oryza) phytoliths. Of the identified 1,950 phytoliths, 56% were globular echinate phytoliths from palm (Aracaceae) (Figure 6a–b and Figure 7). Also recorded were polygonal cones from sedge (Cyperaceae) (Figure 6c), which includes water chestnuts, and elongate triangular prisms from ferns (Figure 6d). About one percent of the phytoliths were identified as belonging to the rice (Oryza) among which some fan-shaped, two- peak glumes and scale decorated bulliforms were recovered (Figure 6e–g and Figure 7).

In total of 48 starch granules from several freshwater roots and tubers were also recovered. Two granules from lotus root (cf. Nelumbo nucifera), 31.8 mm and 28.2 mm in length respectively, are

granules with complex extinction crosses under cross polarised light (Figure 4j–k). Job’s-tear (Coix spp.) also seems to have been a common resource exploited at Xincun (Figure 3p). Fifty three granules of Job’s-tear were recovered, typically spheroid or polyhedral, with two to three flat facets, centric hilum that normally has a T-shaped fissure (Figure 4l). Five starch granules from acorns (Quercus sp.) were also identified (Figure 5). Phytoliths extracted from residues adhering to the stone tools coincide with the starch results at the family level (Figure 6), except for the presence of rice (Oryza) phytoliths. Of the identified 1,950 phytoliths, 56% were globular echinate phytoliths from palm (Aracaceae) (Figure 6a–b and Figure 7). Also recorded were polygonal cones from sedge (Cyperaceae) (Figure 6c), which includes water chestnuts, and elongate triangular prisms from ferns (Figure 6d). About one percent of the phytoliths were identified as belonging to the rice (Oryza) among which some fan-shaped, two- peak glumes and scale decorated bulliforms were recovered (Figure 6e–g and Figure 7).

Body-text clarification (editorial addition from the cited PDF):
1–4 (I): Comparable to several Triticeae genera; the authors explicitly allow more than one genus, not a species diagnosis of crested wheatgrass. (PDF pp. 3).
5–8 (II): Comparable to Phaseoleae, particularly Vigna; explicitly difficult to identify to species. (PDF pp. 4).
9–14 (III): Similar to multiple Paniceae genera; the authors propose wild grasses and enlargement through grinding, not a diagnosis of domesticated millet. (PDF pp. 4).
15–18 (IV): Most comparable to Chinese yam (Dioscorea opposita), particularly wild reference samples; this does not establish cultivated yam. (PDF pp. 4).
19–23 (V、VI): Both morphological types compare most closely with Chinese snake-gourd root (Trichosanthes kirilowii); they are not two separate plant taxa. (PDF pp. 5).
24–28 (跨遗址比较): 24–25 are from Shizitan S9; 26 from Shigu; 27–28 from Egou. They are comparison images and must not be counted as Shizitan S14 finds. (PDF pp. 3, 3).

body_evidence.quote: Type I Starch. Type I starch granules (n = 45; 33% of the total starch) are round or oval in shape and relatively large in size (14.56–39.21 μm). The surface is rather flat, the hilum is centric, lamellae are visible on large granules, and the extinction cross is shaped as either “×” or “+.” Most of the type I granules appear damaged (33; 74%), showing broken edges, deep fissures, pro- nounced lamellae, and/or a dark central area on the extinction cross (Fig. 3, 1–4). These starch granules, in morphology and size, resemble many taxa in the Triticeae tribe of the grass family indigenous to north China and still found in Shanxi today (27). This includes many genera of Agropyron, Elymus, Roegneria, and Leymus in our references, as well as those reported in other studies (ref. 28, figure 4). The characteristics of damaged gran- ules are also consistent with those found in ground Leymus and Agropyron from our references (Fig. 4, 1–4).

Type II Starch. Type II starch granules (n = 20; 15% of the total starch) are irregularly oval or nearly kidney-shaped and relatively large in size (17.31–40.76 μm). Fissures and lamellae are visible in most cases, and the extinction cross often exhibits many arms. Seven granules (35%) are damaged, characterized by broken edges and/or a large dark area at the center (Fig. 3, 5–8), con- sistent with bean starch granules damaged by grinding (23). Type

central depression with or without a small circular protrusion in the middle, pronounced fissures, widened extinction cross, and/ or visible lamellae on part of the granule (Fig. 3, 9–14). Type III starch granules are similar in shape to several genera within the Paniceae tribe. Some genera in our reference samples, such as Setaria, Panicum, Echinochloa, Pennisetum, and Digitaria, all exhibit both faceted and spherical granule shapes, the presence of fissures, a centric hilum, and straight cross shape, similar to type III starch granules. However, the damaged type III granules particularly resemble, in morphology, those from green foxtail grass (S. italica ssp. viridis), which is the wild ancestor of do- mesticated foxtail millet (S. italica ssp. italica), and barnyard grass (Echinochloa crusgalli) Fig. 4, 9–14).

Type IV Starch. Type IV starch granules (n = 24; 18% of the total) are characterized by a large granule size range (19.33–59.05 μm), irregular triangular or oval shapes, an extremely eccentric hilum, the presence of lamellae in most cases, and an extinction cross with bent arms (Fig. 3, 15–18). One granule appears to be damaged, showing broken edges, rough surface, and a dark area in the center of the extinction cross. These starch granules most resemble the D. opposita yam, which has many cultivated and wild variations in north China (Fig. 4, 15 and 16). Among five D. opposita samples we collected from Henan, the domesticated ones show smaller granule size ranges (8.83–33.16 μm, 14.01– 53.16 μm, 11.16–48.22 μm) than those of two wild ones (16.27– 63.08 μm, 22.9–70.62 μm). Type IV starch is more comparable with wild yam in morphology and size (Fig. 5, 4).

The surface is rather flat, the hilum is centric, lamellae are visible on large granules, and the extinction cross is shaped as either “×” or “+.” Most of the type I granules appear damaged (33; 74%), showing broken edges, deep fissures, pro- nounced lamellae, and/or a dark central area on the extinction cross (Fig. 3, 1–4). These starch granules, in morphology and size, resemble many taxa in the Triticeae tribe of the grass family indigenous to north China and still found in Shanxi today (27). This includes many genera of Agropyron, Elymus, Roegneria, and Leymus in our references, as well as those reported in other studies (ref. 28, figure 4). The characteristics of damaged gran- ules are also consistent with those found in ground Leymus and Agropyron from our references (Fig. 4, 1–4).

central depression with or without a small circular protrusion in the middle, pronounced fissures, widened extinction cross, and/ or visible lamellae on part of the granule (Fig. 3, 9–14). Type III starch granules are similar in shape to several genera within the Paniceae tribe. Some genera in our reference samples, such as Setaria, Panicum, Echinochloa, Pennisetum, and Digitaria, all exhibit both faceted and spherical granule shapes, the presence of fissures, a centric hilum, and straight cross shape, similar to type III starch granules. However, the damaged type III granules particularly resemble, in morphology, those from green foxtail grass (S. italica ssp. viridis), which is the wild ancestor of do- mesticated foxtail millet (S. italica ssp. italica), and barnyard grass (Echinochloa crusgalli) Fig. 4, 9–14).

Type IV Starch. Type IV starch granules (n = 24; 18% of the total) are characterized by a large granule size range (19.33–59.05 μm), irregular triangular or oval shapes, an extremely eccentric hilum, the presence of lamellae in most cases, and an extinction cross with bent arms (Fig. 3, 15–18). One granule appears to be damaged, showing broken edges, rough surface, and a dark area in the center of the extinction cross. These starch granules most resemble the D. opposita yam, which has many cultivated and wild variations in north China (Fig. 4, 15 and 16). Among five D. opposita samples we collected from Henan, the domesticated ones show smaller granule size ranges (8.83–33.16 μm, 14.01– 53.16 μm, 11.16–48.22 μm) than those of two wild ones (16.27– 63.08 μm, 22.9–70.62 μm). Type IV starch is more comparable with wild yam in morphology and size (Fig. 5, 4).

It is possible that type I starches belong to more than one genus in the Triticeae tribe, although the large granules are particularly similar to Agropyron cristatum and Agropyron desertorum in form (Fig. 4, 2 and 3) and size (Fig. 5, 1).

Type A grains can be divided into three subtypes (types A1, A2 and A3) based on differences in size, surface morphology and fissure type. (1) Type A1 starch grains. Type A1 starch grains (n = 171) commonly have deeply crossed, winged to Y-shaped, or stellated fissures, and surfaces with short lines radiating from the centre to the edges (Fig. 2a, b); their mean diameter is 11.7 lm (range 5.2–19.8 lm). According to diagnostic morphological characteristics, the mean diameter of starch grains in modern reference collections, and comparisons of ancient starch grains with those in 31 modern samples of millets derived from the seeds of seven species of the genus Setaria and two species of the genus

Panicum [32], we determined that the type A1 grains are from foxtail millet and broomcorn millet. (2) Type A2 starch grains. Type A2 starch grains (n = 6) have a mean diameter of 16.3 lm (range 11.8–18.0 lm). The diameters of some type A2 grains overlap with those of type A1 grains, but type A2 grains exhibit a smooth surface and radial fissures, with the lon- gest fissures radiating from the centre to half the diameter of the grain (Fig. 2c). Type B starch grains (n = 85) are characterized by biconvex shapes and a centric hilum. The starch grains are olivary and possess a longitudinal dent when rotated (Fig. 2k). Type B grains can be divided into two subtypes (types B1 and B2) on the basis of surface morphology and lamellae. Type B1 grains (n = 63) have irregular biconvex shapes, including those that are semicircular (Fig. 2f) and ellipsoidal (Fig. 2g), possess faint craters arranged in reticulate patterns on their surfaces, and lamellae are absent. The mean diameter of type B1 grains is 20.9 lm (range 14.5–25.7 lm); 24 of the 63 grains are larger than 20 lm in diameter. Type B1 grains are similar to the starch grains from Hordeum spp. studied by Yang and Perry [27], and we therefore infer that type B1 grains are from Hordeum spp. Type B2 starch grains (n = 22) are featured with generally round, regular biconvex shapes, a centric hilum, faint lamellae and reticulate patterns craters on the starch grain surface (Fig. 2h–j). The mean diameter of type B2 grains is 28.1 lm (range 8.3–36.2 lm); 8 of the 22 grains are larger than 30 lm in size. According to mor- phology and size, type B2 grains at least contain starch grains from those of Triticum spp., as reported by Yang and Perry [27] and Piperno et al. [33].

Type C grains include three elliptical starch grains char- acterized by a centric hilum. Two starch grains show stellated fissures and no lamellae (Fig. 2l). The third grain shows radiating fissures with demonstrating lamellae (Fig. 2m), especially under polarized light. The lengths of the three starch grains are 45.0, 36.6 and 23.6 lm. Their features are consistent with those of starch grains from the food legumes such as Cajanus spp., Cicer spp. and Phaseolus spp. in our comparative collection. Thus, we infer that type C grains are from food legumes.
