body_evidence.quote: The starch grains that occur in wheat seeds are well documented in the literature. Starch grains (diameter < 5 mm) begin to be produced in the parenchyma cells of ovaries the day before flowering (Sheng et al. 2004). By the time the plant has mature seeds, two typical starch morphotypes are present, Types A and B (Evers 1971). Type A starch grains begin to appear 4 days after flowering and their size keeps increasing until 19 days after flowering. These grains are discoidal or lenticular in form and range between 10 and 35 mm in size. Type B starch grains develop 12–14 days after flowering and range between 1 and 10 mm in size. Type B starch grains have a spherical or polyhedral shape (Evers 1973; Dengate and Meredith 1984; Peng et al. 1999; Wilson et al. 2006). Previous studies demonstrate that grains less than 5 mm are difficult to detect via compound light microscopy, are rarely diagnostic for taxa and occur in many plant tissues (Moss 1976; Czaja 1978; Barton 1991; Loy et al. 1992; Therin et al. 1997). Therefore, in this study we define Type A starch grains as lenticular in shape, with a mean size more than 10 mm; and Type B starch grains as spherical or polyhedral in shape, with a mean size ranging from 5 to 10 mm. Thirty-eight starch grains from immature wheat seeds were studied. They have an ovate or spherical shape, and are 3.3 1 0.8 mm in mean size (Fig. 4 (a)). The morphological characteristics on the surfaces of these starches were not clear at a magnification of 400¥. In the mature wheat seeds, a total of 101 starch grains, including 78 Type A (Fig. 4 (b)) and 2

One hundred and fifteen starch grains from rice seeds were studied. These have a polyhedral shape, and a few have one curved margin and one concave margin (Fig. 4 (g)), but more detailed morphological characteristics were not visible due to the small size of the starches. The largest grain is 6.9 mm in size (Table 1), though the record for the largest grain can reach 11.27 mm (Yang et al. 2012b). Forty-four starch grains were extracted from mature rice stems, 40 of which are morphologically similar to seed starches, at less than 11.3 mm. The remaining four grains were much larger than the maximum size of those recorded in rice seeds, being between 11.3 and 22.5 mm (Fig. 4 (h)). The percentage of the new type of starch grains in the entire assemblage is 9.1% (Table 1). The Group C flakes, which were used to harvest rice, yielded 282 starch grains of the typical seed morphotype, ranging in size from 4.2 to 11.3 mm. Thirty starch grains from the newly described stem type, ranging from 11.3 to 21.9 mm, were much larger than the seed morphotype, making up 9.6% of the population.

One hundred and eight starch grains from millets were measured in this study. The morphological features of starch grains from seeds of foxtail millet are in line with those reported previously (Yang et al. 2012b), including a basic polyhedral shape, centric hila and deep, linear, transverse, Y-shaped or stellate fissures (Fig. 4 (i)). The mean size was 11.3 1 1.9 mm, ranging from 7.1 to 17.5 mm (Table 1). Fifty-five starch grains typical of those from seeds were extracted from mature foxtail millet stems, three of which are polyhedral and spherical starch grains, larger than 20 mm in size (Fig. 4 (j)). The largest one was 32.3 mm in maximum length, much larger than has ever been recorded for the morphotype found in foxtail millet seeds (Yang et al. 2012b). The percentage of starch grains larger than 20 mm is 5.5% in this assemblage (Table 1). Three hundred and twenty-seven starch grains of foxtail millet were recovered from flakes of Group D: 320 of these measured less than 20 mm, the size of the largest starch grains from seeds (Yang et al. 2012b), while the remaining seven were larger than 20 mm, making up 2.1% of the assemblage.

wheat stems, we found 23 Type A, two Type B and two polyhedral starch grains that belong to the new type, with these grains measuring 16.9 and 18.0 mm in size. The previously undescribed stem type of starch grain makes up 9.1% and 7.4% of the starch assemblages from immature and mature stems, respectively (Table 1). No starch grains were recovered from the control samples (A1, B1, C1 and D1), or from the unused edge of the flakes used in the harvesting experiments. In contrast, fairly large numbers of starch grains were recovered from the working edges of all used flakes. Group A flakes, which were used to harvest immature wheat, yielded 71 Type A and 13 Type B starches. The assemblage also included seven polyhedral starch grains from the new stem type, ranging from 12.8 to 23.4 mm (Table 1). Group B flakes yielded 355 Type A and 88 Type B, and 30 of the new type, ranging from 11.3 to 25.2 mm, were recovered (Table 1). The new type makes up 7.7% and 6.3% in the two starch assemblages, respectively.

body_evidence.quote: A wealth of starch grains was found in the prehistoric noodle fragments (Fig. 6b–e) and, furthermore, a consid- erable number of starch grains were extracted from the three samples (serial numbers , ` and ́) taken from the

lower strata within the earthenware bowls (Fig. 6a). No starch grains were extracted from samples taken from other strata. Starch grains found in the noodle sediment strata and within noodle fragments all evince a definite pasted char- acter, partly heavily gelatinized, and displaying a gradually tapering and fading cruciform birefringence shape (Fig. 6d); once the starch forms have been partly gelati- nized, these cruciform structures become not obvious (Fig. 6e). On some of the noodle fragments, however, a great number of rounded or quasi-rounded edges, with umbilical points in the centre, can still be found on the starch granules, and the cruciform birefringence structure remains relatively apparent (Fig. 6b). The starch grains extracted from the noodle sediment strata are typical of a relatively large average grain size. The weights of the complete starch granules found in the sedimentary strata and in noodle fragments were measured and found to be, on average, 8.2 ± 2.8 lm. Comparing this with the size and morphology (Fig. 7) of starch granules taken from modern plants grown in northwest China (Table S1), the archaeological noodle samples had starch granules which, in size, appeared smaller than those of barley

by gelatinization. Nonetheless, the residual starch grains still possessed clear outlines. The morphology of some of the starch grains within the noodle fragments was apparent, and some of the starch grains extracted from the noodle sediment strata had relatively clear cruciform extensions. Millet starch surficial radiation patterns could also be seen often on the surface of some starch grains (Fig. 6c). In addition to using a polarizing microscope to observe and identify these starches, Congo Red dyeing, fluores- cence microscopy and many other simple iodine dyeing methods can be employed [40–42]. These allow the starch grains within the noodle fragments, as opposed to other mineral grains, to be easily determined. There is no need to use any analytical methods [such as scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS)] to infer whether or not grains are minerals. Some scholars consider that both ‘‘gypsum sphaerocrystal’’and ‘‘fungal spores’’ have cruciform extinction [43]; in fact, gypsum crystals are monoclinic and cannot form sphaero- crystal. Out of all the minerals found naturally, these can be grouped into three major crystal categories, seven major crystal systems and 32 crystal types; none of these can form sphaerocrystal. Even isometric crystal minerals, there was no comprehensive crossextinction. The so-called gypsum sphaerocrystal exists nowhere in the natural world. body_evidence.quote: Starch granules from Job's tears and millets are generally small in size; facetted, round, or oval in shape; and exhibit linear-, V-, Y- shaped or radiated fissures (Fig. 1). We selected four predictor variables that are potentially diagnostic for identification. These variables include: (1) size of the granule (SG), meaning the maximum length of a starch granule measured through the hilum; (2) eccentricity of the hilum (EH), meaning the ratio of the linear distance between the hilum and the edge of the granule on both sides (long arm/short arm); (3) presence or absence of a Z-shaped arm (ZA) on the extinction cross, meaning that under the polarized filter, a clearly defined angular and double-curved shape is present on one (or more) of the four arms; and (4) presence or absence of curved arm(s) (CA) on the extinction cross, which differs from the Z-shaped arm in that only one curve is present on an arm (Fig.1; see also Supplementary fig. 1 for more detailed illustration). These variables on each granule were measured and recorded in Excel, and then transferred to SPSS for statistical analysis.

body_evidence.quote: Morphotype 1: The round lenticular starch grain resembles starch from Triticeae, a tribe in the Poaceae (Reichert, 1913; Piperno et al., 2004; Li et al., 2010). According to the compara- tive collections, barley (Hordeum), wheat (Triticum), and rye (Secale) starch are all lenticular with straight distinct extinction crosses and visible lamellae (Fig. 6). Because the modern col- lections comprise only domesticated species, the size of the starch may differ compared to the wild species. Additionally, the age of the granule and the nutritional status of the plant will

influence starch size (Oliveira et al., 1994; Gott et al., 2006). Additionally, the artifact residues were buried for more than 20 ka and then went through the extraction procedures, which may have changed the original size of the starch grains. Thus, we did not apply the size parameter for identification. In addition to Hordeum, Secale and Triticum, the genera Aegilops and Agropyron also belong to the Triticeae. The wild species of these plants have a broad distribution in Ningxia and Northwest China (Dong and Zheng, 2006; Ma et al., 2007; Li et al., 2009). We conclude that morphotype 1 starch may be from the seeds of a wild species in the Triticeae. Morphotype 2: The ovate grain resembles starch from under- ground storage organs of Dioscorea, Maranta, Lilium, and Fritil- laria (Reichert, 1913; Emiola and Delarossa, 1981; Erdman, 1986; Moorthy, 1994; Gebre-Mariam and Schmidt, 1998; Hoover, 2001; Pérez and Lares, 2005; Chandler-Ezell et al., 2006; Full- agar et al., 2006; Yang and Jiang, 2010). Based on the compar- ative collections, the starch from the residue samples is more like modern Dioscorea, Lilium and Fritillaria starch concerning the ovate shape, relatively large size (diameter: 44e56 m), bent extinction cross and visible lamellae (Fig. 6: g, h). Lilium and Fritillaria species, as well as other genera in the Liliaceae, are broadly distributed in Ningxia, including wild and cultivated species, which are still consumed by locals (Ma et al., 2007). body_evidence.quote: Type I starch grains (N = 82) are spherical or regular oval in shape, Type II (N = 11) is characterized by a bell or semi-sphere shape, and Type III (N = 13) consists of compound grains of twins, triplets, and quadruples (Figure 3 and Table 3). Types I–III starch grains are most comparable in morphology and size with the root of snakegourd (Trichosanthes kirilowii in the Cucurbita- ceae family) in our reference data. The starch grains from this plant are varied in shape, and include spherical, oval, semi-spher- ical, bell-shaped, and polygonal morphologies. Compound starch is composed of various numbers of grains, mostly between two and four. The hilum is eccentric in most cases, fissures in various forms are sometimes present, lamellae are visible on some large grains, and the extinction cross often has bent arms (Figure 4). When sizes are compared, Types I–III also closely resemble the range of ground T. kirilowii dry root (Figure 5). Types I–III grains together, therefore, are identifiable as T. kirilowii root, accounting for 22% of the starch assemblage (N = 106).

These plants have both wild and culti- vated variations in North China. In Inner Mongolia today, only cultivated D. opposita grows in Wulanchabu, but five wild spe- cies of Lilium are widely distributed (Ma, 1985), and at least two species (L. concolor var. and L. pumilum) are found in the Daihai area (Ma, 1985; Xiao et al., 2004). We therefore identify Type IV starch as Lilium sp. and/or D. opposita (lily/yam).

Four grains (1% of the total) are classified as Type VI starch, which are either triangular or irregularly oval in shape (Figure 3 and Table 3). These features mostly resemble several Quercus species (Figure 4), such as Q. variabilis, Q. liaotungensis, and Q. mongolica, which grow in North China today (Yang et al., 2009b). body_evidence.quote: The phytolith counts for most of the artifacts were quite low (<30 per sample). In most cases, the phytoliths were not diagnostic. The dominant phytolith type was the hair cell, in several different forms (Table 4 and Figure 6a–c). Hair cells were most common on the SHSII artifacts, specifically GS4, R3, and R4, but SHSI- GS2 had a comparable number. R3 also had a few more diagnos- tic hair cells (‘armed hair cells’) that in some cases are consistent with the Trichosanthes sp. identifications based on the starch grains (Kealhofer and Piperno, 1998); however, armed hair cells are present in a variety of other taxa (also present in the regional pollen profiles). Both R3 and R4 had hair base phytoliths that also are consistent with Cucurbitaceae types, but occur in other taxa as well (e.g. Kealhofer and Piperno, 1998; Morris et al., 2009: Plate 1; Piperno, 2006). Small pieces of unidentified tissue were also

common on several of the artifacts. The remaining phytolith types included smooth spheres, tissue fragments (Figure 6d), tracheids, and long cells (Figure 6f). While, in general, tracheids are not particularly diagnostic, those found on GS2 are very similar to Typha sp. tracheids (Guo et al., 2012). Very few grass-related phytoliths (particularly from glumes) were identified. The plant ‘fibers’ present are not specifically diagnostic (Fig- ure 6g; https://fril.osu.edu/index.cfm, Fiber Reference Image Library); however, their distribution is strongly patterned. Their morphology, in most cases, is consistent with root hairs (e.g. Typha sp., see Acharya et al., 2013), while others are similar to fungal hyphae. Comparisons with reference material from Typha, Trichosanthes, Lilium, and Dioscorea, all of which produce fibers, indicate that all but Lilium are likely sources of the archeo- logical fibers. However, other sources cannot be ruled out. Fibers are present on all of the SHSI artifacts, but most abundant on GS2. They are also present on all SHSII artifacts, but clearly dominant on R3. A few broken raphides were found in association with the grinding stones. Both Dioscorea yam and Typha rhizome produce abundant raphides. The presence of both root hairs and raphides, likely in association, support the processing of USOs on these grinding stones. In terms of intensity, GS2 and R3 reveal the most evidence for USO processing.

In addition to phytoliths and starch, a variety of other types of microfossils are present on tools, particularly pollen, lichen types, and other spores. The pollen assemblage includes one Pinaceae grain, a few grass pollen grains (Poaceae), and a high frequency of 3C3P type pollen (Figure 6i). Several different types of spores are common on nearly all of the grinding stones from both sites (Table 4). Given the long-term storage of these artifacts in a field station near the site before being moved to the museum, it seems likely that most of these are not related to their mid-Holocene use.

Type I starch grains (N = 82) are spherical or regular oval in shape, Type II (N = 11) is characterized by a bell or semi-sphere shape, and Type III (N = 13) consists of compound grains of twins, triplets, and quadruples (Figure 3 and Table 3). Types I–III starch grains are most comparable in morphology and size with the root of snakegourd (Trichosanthes kirilowii in the Cucurbita- ceae family) in our reference data. The starch grains from this plant are varied in shape, and include spherical, oval, semi-spher- ical, bell-shaped, and polygonal morphologies. Compound starch is composed of various numbers of grains, mostly between two and four. The hilum is eccentric in most cases, fissures in various forms are sometimes present, lamellae are visible on some large grains, and the extinction cross often has bent arms (Figure 4). When sizes are compared, Types I–III also closely resemble the range of ground T. kirilowii dry root (Figure 5). Types I–III grains together, therefore, are identifiable as T. kirilowii root, accounting for 22% of the starch assemblage (N = 106).

body_evidence.quote: According to previous work by Henry et al. (2009), gelatinization could only occur in systems with an excess of water and heating, which would cause a most remarkable swelling and distortion of the starch grains, which could even become gelatinoids. The cooking process would make the starch grains lose the properties of cross-extinction under the polarized microscope (Fig. 5). In our experiments, although modern crop grains were ground and soaked in water at room temperature, the extracted starch grains changed hardly or very little, with a slight swelling of only a few grains in the microscope observations. In addition, the morphology of the starch granules of an ancient barley specimen (Fig. S2) resembles that of modern unprocessed reference samples, and the proportion with a completely unchanged morphology exceeds 90%, while this percentage is very low in the foodstuffs, indicating that a spontaneous damage process with age

has virtually not happened at all. Therefore, the possibility of damage due to starch extraction, processing and spontaneous ageing can be excluded, which leaves cooking as the best explana- tion for the destruction of the starch granules in the specimens. The morphology of the ancient extracted starch grains is relatively simple, and can be divided into two forms by size. Most of the large grains are nearly, but not absolutely, circular in plane view and lenticular in side view, and their diameter ranges from 10 to 40 μm; while the small ones, whose diameter lies between 1 and about 10 μm (Fig. 5 and Table 3), are rounded or round-polygonal. The morphology of the starch granules can be used to exclude the possibility of the flour originating from Paniceae crops, because the morphology of their granules is smaller in size, ranging from about 4 to 10 μm, simple, sub-rounded and faceted (Gong et al. 2011). body_evidence.quote: Shizitan 14 (ca. 23,000-18,000 cal. BP) was occupied primarily during the LGM. Three sandstone slabs, dating to ca. 23,000-19,500 cal. BP, were subjected to residue and usewear analyses. The total of 136 starch grains re- covered were dominated by Triticeae tribe grasses (33%), followed by Dioscorea sp. yam (18%), beans of the Faba- ceae family (15%), Paniceae grasses (13%), and Tricho- santhes kirilowii snakegourd root (11%) (Liu et al. 2013a) (Figure 3).

Shizitan 9 (ca. 13,800-8,500 cal. BP) was occupied during a period of transition from the Pleistocene to the Holocene, when the climate changed from cold-dry (YD) to warm-wet conditions (Holocene). Carbonized seeds of wild millets (Setaria and Echinochloa spp.) and goosefoot (Chenopodium sp.) are present in flotation samples, dating to 13,800-11,600 cal BP (Bestel et al. 2014). Four grind- ing stones (two slabs and two handstones), dating to 12,700-11,600 cal BP, were analyzed for plant residues. A total of 212 starch grains were recovered, with most being derived from a tool unearthed from a later occupation stratum dating to the onset of Holocene. The great majori- ty of starch grains are from grasses, including Panicoideae (most likely Paniceae) (38%) and Triticeae tribe grasses (26%); Quercus sp. acorns (26%) appeared for the first time; and small proportions of starch belong to tubers (snakegourd root, 2%; and yam, 2%) and beans (2%) (Liu et al. 2011) (Figure 3).

Grinding stones from the Peiligang culture Grinding stones from seven Peiligang culture sites have been subjected to residue analysis. These include five sites located on the floodplains of central Henan (Egou, Shigu, Peiligang, Shawoli, and Gangshi) (Liu et al. 2010a; Zhang 2011; Zhang et al. 2011b) and two sites situated on the southern bank of the Yellow River in Mengjin county, western Henan (Zhaigen and Bangou) (Liu et al. 2013b). A total of 25 grinding stones from these sites were ana- lyzed and more than 2800 starch granules recovered, identifiable to eight taxa. The predominant starch grains belong to acorn, Triticeae grasses, snakegourd root, Job’s tears (Coix lacryma-jobi), and millet, while only a few grains are identifiable as beans, Dioscorea sp. yam, and other tubers (Table 2; Figure 3).

Results More than 400 starch grains were recovered from fifteen subsamples of residues extracted from lithic tools (Fig. 4 and Table S3). No starch granules were recovered from the associated sediment samples indicating a likelihood that the ancient starches were associated with tool use. 118 grains were classi- fied as unidentifiable, and this group includes 43 tiny (less than 5 μ m), spherical granules which often occur in immature seeds (Fig. S2a), 23 clusters of compound starch grains (Fig. 2h and Fig. S2b), and 52 granules that are damaged to the point that their origin cannot be determined. Though the clusters of compound starch grains are characteristic of those that occur in immature seeds of barnyard grasses (Fig. 2d) and in both mature and immature rice (Oryza sp.), similar forms have been noted in many other grasses so these cannot be securely identified13,22. The single starch grains from rice have polyhedral

shape with sharp angles, but they cannot be detected easily and identified securely because of their tiny size13. Only a small number of starches from other grass (Triticeae), acorns (Lithocarpus/Quercus sensu lato) and water chestnut (Trapa) were recovered (Fig. S2c–f). Both acorns and Trapa are documented as important food resources alongside cultivated rice at later sites in the region with better preservation of plant macro-remains23. More than 270 starch grains in the assemblage are of a basic polyhedral and spherical morphology (Table S3). Of these, 261 grains fall into the size zone of 5–17 μ m, and are characterized by a fissured cavity. Within this subgroup of remains, 54 starch grains, 21% in this assemblage, have pits on their surfaces (Fig. 2f–h). These morphological features are characteristic of barnyard grasses based on the material we have examined. As rice produced starch grains at the smallest end of the starch size range around 5 μ m they are much harder to recover and to positively identify. In addition, if rice were boiled as whole grains it would be less likely to be found on groundstone surfaces. Therefore the starch evidence may underrepresent rice, but nevertheless it confirms the importance of Echinochloa, another wetland grass with edible grains, which was apparently processed with groudstones. More than 3400 starch grains were recovered from the tools exca- vated from the Nanzhuangtou site (Table 3). Of them, 63 were identified as starch grains from millets with the polyhedral or spherical shape (Figure 3Ba–c), ranging 6.6–22.6 μm in size (Yang et al., 2012b). The ubiquity of millets on the lithic tools and potsherds is 100% (Table 3), suggesting that millet consumption was quite common here; seven lenticular starch grains (Figure 3Bd,e), ranging 17.4–25.3 μm in size, were identified as the tribe Triticeae (Yang and Perry, 2013), and they occur occasionally (Table 3). The overwhelming majority of starch grains, ranging

6.5–23.8 μm in size, identified on a mullers (S7:F7) are from water caltrop (Figure 3Bf–h), from which starch grains present large group and small group, and characteristic starch grains are compounded by two single granules (Figure 3Af–i). The starches of water caltrop consistent with the pattern are revealed by macro- plant identification. Two types (A and B) of geophyte starch grains are also found (Figure 3Bi–l; Table 3). Subtype A is similar to starch grains from Chinese yam (Dioscorea opposita) of our modern reference collections (Figure 3Ah–j), and subtype B is consistent with the features of snake gourd (Trichosanthes kirilowii) root described by other studies (Liu et al., 2013, 2014). It is important to note that each of the pottery sherds examined contains some millet starch grains and very occasionally some unidentifiable ones (Table 3). While this evidence is not sufficient to suggest that ceramic pots were used exclusively for cooking seeds of grasses as other types of foods might not be preserved or preserved in other forms, it is possible that water caltrop was less likely or less frequently processed in pots. But here again, there is another possibility that we cannot entirely rule out. In Southern China today, water caltrop is boiled with shells in pots, which could prevent starches being left on the pottery. body_evidence.quote: of the total), characterized by broken edges, rough surface, deep fissures, pronounced lamellae, or a dark area in the center of the extinction cross. These features are consistent with the morphological changes after grinding based on experimental studies (Ge et al., 2010; Henry et al., 2008). The morphology of the starch types is described in SI Text (available online). The significance of the plants identified is presented in the ‘Discussion’ section. Type I starch grains (n = 136; 17% of the total; from 17 tools) resemble those from Lilium sp. bulbs. At least eight lily species are widely distributed in Northeast China today (Ma, 1985a; Yang et al., 1996). When compared with our reference data, Type I

starch grains best match to Lilium pumilum DC and Lilium tigri- num; both can be found in the region. Type II starch grains (n = 3; 0.4% of the total; from two tools) resemble those from yams including Dioscorea polystachya. Wild yam is distributed widely in China, growing in forests, scrub for- ests, herb communities, mountain slopes, along rivers, and road- sides. It is also commonly cultivated (Wu and Raven, 2000). It is unclear whether wild yam grew in the Liao River area during the Neolithic period due to the lack of data. Only cultivated yam grows in the region today (Ma, 1985a). Type III starch grains (n = 15; 1.9% of the total; from five tools) are most comparable with the root of snake

gourd (Trichosanthes kirilowii in the Cucurbitaceae family). This particular root has been known as an edible plant since antiquity (see discussion below). Snake gourd is widely distributed in northern and southern China, growing in open forests, shrub lands, grasslands, and fields beside villages in many regions of China (Wu et al., 2011). It is unclear, however, whether or not snake gourd was native to the Liao River region. It is cultivated in Inner Mongolia today (Ma, 1980). Type IV starch grains (n = 322; 40.3% of the total; from 20 tools and 1 calculus sample) best match to the seed of Job’s tears (Coix lacryma-jobi). Job’s tears grow near streams, in marshy valleys, moist fields, and by houses. The cultivated forms are widely distributed in China, but the wild ones grow mainly in tropical and subtropical areas (Wu et al., 2006). It is cultivated in Inner Mongolia today (Ma, 1983). Only 89 individual phytoliths were observed; however, additional plant-derived material, such as fibers and vascular tissue, was noted (Figure 4; Table 2). Most vegetal fibers and vascular tissue lack diagnostic taxonomic value (Piperno, 2006); however, silicified tracheary elements (n = 21) from USOs appear in residues of tools used for the processing of USOs. Tracheary elements are relatively abundant in these sam- ples (n = 21), comprising 23.6% of the phytolith assemblage. The largest percentage (55.5%) of phytoliths in this assem- blage is composed of hair cells, silicified appendages from the epidermal surfaces of leaves produced in eudicot plant families (Kealhofer and Piperno, 1998; Piperno, 2006). Hairs were classi- fied into four categories (Figure 4; Table 2). Type 1 (n = 46) hairs are simple, unicellular, lanceolate cells. Type 2 (n = 2) hairs are simple, unicellular, lanceolate hair cells that are armed, having spine-like surface projections. Type 2 hairs are consistent with Boraginaceae. Type 3 (n = 1) includes a single multicellular hair with blunt tip observed with a cistolith inclusion at its base. Finally, Type 4 (n = 1) hairs are multicellular with pointed tip lack- ing cistolith inclusion. Only Type 2 hairs are identified at this time to the family level, and these are consistent with hairs observed in the borage family, Boraginaceae. Two small pieces of charred archaeobotanical remains from Xin- glonggou of unknown botanical origin were examined for starch content. A significant number of starch grains of similar morphol- ogy were visible in both samples, but also exhibit damage due to heating, that is, gelatinization and morphological change. The starch grains can be grouped into three types: (1) two grains that were round or polygonal in shape with a faint extinction cross; (2) mostly polygonal or round grains with damaged surfaces bearing deep fissures and no visible extinction cross although the grains are florescent under the polarized light; (3) grains with a granulate surface, some having fused to large pieces (Figure 6). body_evidence.quote: Because of a lack of fauna results and to supply comple- mentary information concerning plant consumption, teeth from four individuals (M5:E, M6:B, M6:C and M11:D) were analysed for microfossils in dental calcu- lus. A total of four different kinds of microfossils were recovered from the dental calculus of the tooth samples belonging to M11:D and M11:E, including phytoliths (Figure 3a), parasite (Figure 3b), pollen (Figure 3c and d) and starch grains (Figure 3e–g). Here, we mainly focus on the identification of the starch grains because they play a significant role in revealing the types of plants consumed. A total of 14 starch grains were extracted from the four teeth. Six of these were readily identified to two different plant taxa according to diagnostic morphological features (Yang et al., 2005; Ge, 2010; Yang & Jiang, 2010; Wan et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2014). The first type of starch grains was characterised as having a flat and circular form with centric and closed hila on their stationary surface. The length of the major axis is between 10.4 and 38.9μm, while the length of the minor axis is between 8.8 and 36.4μm. Some of these starch grains have visible lamellae and craters, but no obvious fissures were present in the front view (Figure 3e1 and e2). However, these starch grains were observed to have an oval shape with a longitude fissure from the side view after compression and rotation (Figure 3e3 and e4). When these starch grains were

compared with the modern reference collections (Figure 4a1–a4), they were consistent with Triticeae, including wheat (Triticum aestivum), barley (Hordeum vulgare) and/or highland barley (H.vulgare L var. nudum), and so on (Ge, 2010; Li et al., 2010; Yang and Jiang, 2010; Ma et al., 2014). body_evidence.quote: A total of 797 starch granules were recovered from the 28 tools examined. The starch grains are classified into ten types based on morphology and size (Figs. 3 and 4; Table 3). Many of these types are identifiable to plant taxa when compared with our reference material (Fig. 5). The morphological characteristics of starch types are described in Table 4. Most of the starch grains show signs of damage (n = 453; 56.8% of the total), characterized by broken edges, rough surfaces, deep fissures, pronounced lamellae, or a dark area in the center of the extinction cross. Such a high percentage of damaged grains in the assemblage is not natural in native starch, but more likely caused by grinding, a scenario consistent with the function of grinding stones (Babot, 2003). Type I starch grains (n = 86; 10.8% of the total; from 16 tools of all phases with 57.1% ubiquity) are consistent with starches from lily (Lilium spp.) bulbs. In comparison to our reference material, Type I starch grains best match to Lilium pumilum DC and Lilium tigrinum. Both species can be found in Inner Mongolia today (Ma, 1985a; Yang et al., 1996). Type II starch grains (n = 14; 1.8% of the total; from seven tools of the XLW and HSH phases with 25% ubiquity) are most comparable with the root of snake gourd (Trichosanthes kirilowii in the Cucurbitaceae

family). It is unclear if snake gourd is native to the Liao River region, however it is cultivated in Inner Mongolia today (Ma, 1980). Type III starch grains (n = 7; 0.9% of the total, from three tools of the XLW and ZBG phases with 10.7% ubiquity) are comparable to starches from yam, including Dioscorea polystachya. It is also unclear if wild yam grew in the Liao River area during the Neolithic period. Only cultivated yam grows in the region today (Ma, 1985a). Type IV starch grains (n = 154; 19.3% of the total; from 17 tools of all phases with 60.7% ubiquity) are identified as Job's tears (Coix lacryma-jobi). Starch grains from Job's tears and foxtail millet share some common characteristics and are difficult to separate. Our identifica- tion is based on a statistical model which achieved a success rate of 80% in a blind test (Liu et al., 2014). The cultivated forms of Job's tears are widely distributed in China, including Inner Mongolia (Ma, 1983), but wild variants are native to tropical and subtropical areas of southern China (Wu et al., 2006). We have hypothesized previously that Job's tears was introduced to the Liao River region as a cultivated plant (Liu et al., 2015a).

Type VIII starch grains (n = 88; 11% of the total; from one tool of the HSH phase with 3.6% ubiquity) appeared in three clusters composed of numerous very small compound granules, consistent with rice (Oryza sp.) starch. Rice was not an indigenous plant in the temperate climate of Northeast China, therefore the rice starch at Baiyinchanghan certainly represents a domesticated rice variety that originated in the south. Type IX starch grains (n = 2; 0.3% of the total; from one tool of the HSH phase with 3.6% ubiquity) resemble beans, such as Vicia spp. and Vigna spp. Inner Mongolia has ten wild species of Vicia, including Vicia sativa L, or yewandou in Chinese (Ma, 1977). Yewandou was recorded as a famine food in an ancient text of the 15th century (Zhu, 1406). Type X starch grains (n = 8; 1% of the total; from four tools of all phases with 14.3% ubiquity) are similar to several oak species (Quercus spp.) in our reference data, such as Quercus viriabilis which is widely distributed in China (Wu and Raven, 1999). Inner Mongolia today has two species of Quercus, Q. liaotungensis and Q. mongolica (Ma, 1985b).

body_evidence.quote: In order to study the tool functions, usewear patterns and residues recovered on the four tool types are described below. Table 6 provides the detailed usewear traces observed on each tool. Slabs (n = 4) are present in all phases and each is heavily worn. All slabs exhibit polish of various levels, ranging from low to high. Striations are present on two tools (GS1 and GS10); some are fine and short, similar to grinding plants, including fiber-rich tubers, while others are long furrows, likely caused by processing hard materials, such as stone (Fig. 7: 1, 2). A small number of starch grains were recovered, including snake gourd root and other USOs, millet, and acorn. Long plant fiber bundles are found on GS11 (Fig. 6), suggesting that slabs were also used for processing non-starchy plants, probably for fiber use. No phytoliths were observed in slab residues. In general, these slabs were used for processing different objects, including various plants and non-plant materials. No evidence suggests that the function of this tool type changed from XLW to HSH period. Mortar-slabs (n = 3) are found only in the XLW phase. The surface depressions exhibit macro-pecking marks, micro-pitting, polish on high plateaus, and striations of different forms. The flat surfaces of the tools were also used, indicated by different levels of polish and stria- tions. The crystals often show rounded edges (Fig. 7: 3, 4). All these characteristics are consistent with processing soft materials including plants in our reference data. The depression and flat surface are likely to have been used as mortar

body_evidence.quote: Results A total of 541 starch grains were recovered from the funnels and pottery sherds (Table 1). Of these grains, 488 starch grains (90.2% of the total) were identifiable to various taxonomic levels com- pared with our reference data. The starch assemblage mainly consists of millet, Triticeae, and Job’s tears, with a smaller contri- bution from tubers that include snake gourd root (Trichosanthes kirilowii), yam (Dioscorea sp.), and lily (Lilium sp.) (Fig. 3 A–F). A high percentage of starch grains (n = 166, 30.7%) exhibit signs of damage, and among them two types of damage closely resemble that produced by beer brewing. First, some grains show pits and channels on their surface, ranging from being slightly pitted to completely hollow (Fig. 4A). Second, a large number of starch grains are swollen, folded, and distorted (Fig. 4B); some still retain their individual boundaries, but many merge into one another. These two damage patterns precisely match the morphological changes developed during malting and mashing, as we observed in our brewing experiments and that reported in published literature (Fig. 4 C and D, Fig. S3, and SI Materials and Methods) (19–22). During malting, enzymes in sprouting cereals break down starch to dextrins and simple sugars, creating typical surface pits and interior channels in the grains (19). Furthermore, mashing involves heating of the malt in water for a period, which causes gelatinization, swelling, folding, and distortion of starch grains (19). Thus, the damaged state of the starch grains in our archeological sample provides strong evidence

Phytolith data indicate the presence of cereal husks (Table 2). Phytoliths identified to the Panicoideae grass subfamily pre- dominate the assemblage. Seven vessels revealed η-shaped long cells that are consistent with phytoliths formed in epidermal husk tissues of broomcorn millet (Fig. 3J) (15). Cross-shaped phytoliths showing a considerable variation in form and size, comparable with the crosses produced by Job’s tears in our modern references, were observed (Fig. 3H). Phytolith forms produced in Pooideae were also identified. In particular, articulated dendritic phytoliths con- sistent in pattern and shape with those produced in the husks of Triticeae species were observed (Fig. 3K). Our morphometric analysis of the articulated dendritics indicates their most probable origin to be from the inflorescence bracts of barley (Hordeum vul- gare). body_evidence.quote: A total of 1055 starch granules were recovered from 16 stone tools and one ceramic cooking pot (Table 3). Many of them (N 1⁄4 209; 19.81% of the total) show characteristics of damage, indicated by broken edges, rough surface, deep fissures, pro- nounced lamellae, and/or a dark area in the center of the extinction cross. Those features have been found on ancient starch from grinding stones in our previous studies and other researchers report similarly damaged starch grains that relate to tool function (e.g., Babot, 2003; Haslam, 2004; Liu et al., 2013a). The starch granules can be classified into eight types (Fig. 3), corresponding to particular plant taxa as compared with our reference data, on the basis of morphology (Fig. 4) and size (Fig. 5). The main character- istics of starch types are described in detail in Table 4.

Type I starch granules (N 1⁄4 429; 40.66% of the total), present on all grinding stones examined, are the most numerous granules in the assemblage. These are characterized by a very large grain size (5.85e79.94 mm) with various shapes, including elongate, trian- gular, oval and spherical, usually with an extremely eccentric hi- lum. Type 1 starch morphotypes can be found in Lilium sp. bulb, but some large, triangular-shaped grains also resemble Dioscorea pol- ystachya Turcz. yam. Both wild and cultivated lilies and yams are growing in north China. In Inner Mongolia today, only cultivated D. polystachya grows in the study area, but five wild species of Lil- ium are widely distributed (Ma, 1985), and at least two species (Lilium concolor Salisb. var. pulchellum (Fisch.) Baker and Lilium pumilum DC) are found in the Daihai area (Ma, 1985; Xiao et al., 2004). Type I starch grains are particularly similar to L. pumilum from northern Shaanxi and a wild D. polystachya from Henan in our reference collection. We therefore identify them as Lilium sp. and/ or D. polystachya (lily/yam). Type II starch granules (N 1⁄4 131; 12.42% of the total) were found on 13 tools examined. They are medium-sized grains (9.52e36.65 mm) with three basic forms: spherical, slightly oval, and bell-shaped. Type II starch grains are most comparable in morphology and size with the root of snake gourd (Trichosanthes kirilowii Maxim.). Today cultivated snake gourd is distributed in the study area (Ma, 1980). Type III starch granules (N 1⁄4 264; 25.02% of the total) were found on 14 tools. They are medium in siz

type of phytolith is classified as a Variant 1 cross in the medium size range in Piperno's (1984) classification of crosses produced in maize and various other grasses. A comparative study of grasses needs to be done for this region, however, other genera of grasses studied by Piperno and others (Piperno, 1988; Pearsall and Piperno, 1990; Piperno and Pearsall, 1998; Iriarte, 2003) that produce me- dium sized Variant 1 crosses do not occur in this study area, with the exception of cultivated Setaria sp. Our comparative specimens of C. lacryma-jobi show this cultivated taxa also produces Variant 1 crosses as well as considerable variation in lobate forms and crosses as previously observed by Dinan (1990). In our specimens of both cultivated and wild forms of Job's tears, Variant 1-type crosses are common in leaf and involucre tissues in the medium (11.45e15.98 mm) to large (16.03e20.56 mm) size range. Although cross shaped phytoliths appear to be highly variable in Job's tears, Lu and Liu (2003) report cross shaped forms referred to as Type E2 that occur only in this species. The cross-shaped phytolith from WMS-GS1 conforms to Lu and Liu's type E2 produced in C. lacryma- jobi. As it is associated with starch grains of Job's tears in residues, the WMS cross-shaped phytolith in this assemblage most likely represents this species. The cross-shaped phytolith recovered from YZG also corresponds to starches of Job's tears or perhaps Setaria spp. Raphides and fibers also were noted in the analysis and their abundance recorded (Fig. 6). Phytolith counts were low overall with samples having be- tween 0 and 12 individual plant silica forms or elements identified (Table 5; Fig. 6). Silicified tracheary elements are the most abun- dant phytolith type in this assemblage. Generally, tracheary ele- ments do not have diagnostic taxonomic value. These forms are silicified vascular tissue (Piperno, 2006) that may be produced in a number of different plant families, however they may also silicify in underground storage organs such as those produced by Typha sp. (Guo et al., 2012) and their presence in residue on tools used for processing such organs is likely. Hair cells are the second most common phytolith types in the assemblage. Hair cell appendages silicify in a large number of non-grass eudicot plant families (Kealhofer and Piperno, 1998; Piperno, 2006). None of the hair cell types in this assemblage is identified to taxa, but they likely represent non-grass plant tissues processed with these tools, perhaps Lilium sp. that was identified by starch grains. The hair cells are not consistent with those produced in the Cucurbitaceae, such as snake gourd that was also identified in the starch assemblage. Other silicified epidermal elements from eudicots are also present. One diagnostic element, an opaque perforated sheet produced in the Asteraceae family (Bozarth, 1992), was identified.

Other phytolith types produced in various grasses are repre- sented in small number in the assemblage. Phytoliths identified to the Poaceae family include a bulliform, papilla, prickle cell, and articulated epidermal cells with stomata. One phytolith, a rondel form produced in Pooideae is present. In addition, silicified husk tissues identified to the grass tribe Triticeae of the Pooideae subfamily are also present. Grasses in the Triticeae tribe are common in temperate and warm-temperate regions (Zhengyi et al., 2006) and include cultivated wheat (Triticum spp.) and barley (H. vulgare L.). In this assemblage, wave-shaped long-cells of silicified epidermal tissue from husks (Fig. 6) are consistent in pattern and shape with those produced in wheat or barley

(Kaplan et al., 1992; Rosen, 1992, 1993), but may also be produced in wild Triticeae. Other characteristic phytoliths from wheat and barley, such as pitted papillae, are not present (Tubb et al., 1993; Ball et al., 1999). At this point, a tribe-level identification of the husk phytoliths in this group is appropriate. Triticeae phytoliths are consistent with starch grains from these grasses occurring in the tool residues. Panicoidea grass subfamily type phytoliths, crenate, bilobate and cross forms (Piperno and Pearsall,1998), were also identified in the assemblage (Fig. 6). body_evidence.quote: Type A (Fig. 3: a, a0, b, b0, c, c0) can be divided into two groups. Group AI is polyhedral or round polyhedral shape with centric hi- lum closed, lamellae invisible and the extinction cross is shaped as “X”. Group AII is a kind of compound starch grain which is typical morphological characteristic of Oryzeae Tribe (Wei et al., 2008a, b, c) (Fig. 4: a, a0, b, b0). In rice endosperm cells, well developed starch grains are polyhedral with compact arrangement in amyloplast, and these starch grains kept the outline of amyloplast after amyloplast envelope degraded. Poorly developed starch grains are round polyhedral with loose arrangement in amyloplast, and these starch grains could not keep the outline of amyloplast after amyloplast envelope degraded (Wei et al., 2008a, b, c). Starch of Type AI and AII are derived from these two cases. In the result of micro measurement, the size of these starches (3.58e8.43 mm) is in ranging of Oryza sativa and Oryz. rufipogon Griff., the mean value of the grain size was slightly higher than that of the modern rice (Fig. 5: a). Evidence of spikelet and phytolith indicates that the domestication of rice had began from early Neolithic in the Xiao- huangshan site (Zheng, 2009; Wu et al., 2014). We conclude that Type A starch grains may be from the seeds of Oryza sp.. Type B (Fig. 3: d, d0, e, e0, f, f0) are a lenticular or discoid shape, with flat surface and centric hilum, lamellae is visible on large grains, and the extinction cross is shaped as either “x” and “þ”. Under the microscope, a lot of small starch grains can be observed attaching wit

It is concluded that starch of Type B may come from a wild species of Triticeae Tribe. Type C (Fig. 3: g, g0, h, h0) are spherical or oval-spherical in shape, more or less polyhedral with two or three flat facets, centric hilum that normally have T- or linear-shaped fissures, Z-shaped arm on the extinction cross is the typical morphological characteristic of these starch grains. Compared to modern references, starch grains of Type C reveal a great similarity to Coix lacryma-jobi (Liu et al., 2014a, b) (Fig. 4: d, d0), which also shows considerable over- lapping in size (Fig. 5: c). Starch grains of Job's tears are also found in the Shangshan site (11,400e8600 BP) (Liu et al., 2010) and the Kuahuqiao site (8000e7000 BP) (Yang and Jiang, 2010), which dates covered the Xiaohuangshan period. It is indicated that Type C starch grains may come from Job's tears. Starch grains of Type D are extremely eccentric hilum and well- defined lamellae, which are generally considered from under- ground storage organs of geophytes. The major difference among these three types is the shape of grains. N 1⁄4 1). The combination of DI and DII is the typical characteristics of starch grains from the root of Nelumbo nucifera (4.38e65.66 mm, N 1⁄4 144) (Wan et al., 2011) (Fig. 4: e, e0). These starch grains have been found in early Shangshan phase (Liu et al., 2010), so it is reasonable to conclude that Type DIII starches orig- inate from the Chinese yam. Starch of Vigna spp. has been found from charred residues adhering to pottery sherds at Kua- huqiao (Yang and Jiang, 2010). Due to the limited number of starch grains, Type E may come from the species of Phaseoleae, among which Vigna spp. presents the best possibilities.

Type F (Fig. 3: o, o0) starch grain is triangular ovate or water drop-shaped, centric hilum and the extinction cross is shaped as “x” and “þ”. This morphotype resembles starch from fruits of Fagaceae plants (Yang et al., 2009a, b) (Fig. 4: h, h0). To deflocculate the clay particles in solution and ease dispersion, a 5% solution of Calgon was added to each sample; the sample was then rinsed twice with ultrapure water. Finally, starch grains were isolated using the CsCl solution described above, and the recov- ered residue was mounted on a slide for analysis under the microscope. Each slide was scanned under a Zeiss microscope (Axio Scope A1). One slide was scanned in its entirety at 200  for each sample. Starch was identified by the presence of an extinction cross under cross-polarized light; only bodies with clear extinction crosses were accepted as starch grains in this analysis. Starch grains were photographed at 400  in cross-polarized, transmitted light and measured using the UV-G550 software (Beijing United Vision Technology Company, Beijing, China). When a starch grain was found, it was rotated using pressure from a probe pressed against the cover slide, and its three-dimensional morphology was drawn. For identification, the recovered starch grains were compared with a modern reference collection of plants that are common in the study area and in other areas of China (Yang et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010a, Li et al., 2010b; Yang and Jiang, 2010; Yang et al.,2012a; Yang et al.,2012b; Wan et al., 2012; Li et al.,2013). body_evidence.quote: swelling in shape, folded surface, pronounced lamellae, and/or a dark central area on the extinction cross (Fig. 6A, B). In conclusion, morphological features and statistical data (23.51 ± 6.26 mm, N 1⁄4 200) of this type of starch grain point to the Triticeae, most probably from T. aestivum, H. vulgare, or H. vulgare var. coeleste (Piperno et al., 2004; Henry and Piperno, 2008; Henry et al., 2009; Yang and Perry, 2013). A more precise identification is necessary by following phytolith and bran analyses.

The contents of phytoliths are extremely rare. Only dendritic and papilla phytolith from the inflorescence of Triticeae were found (Fig. 6C, D). Ball et al. (1996, 1999) and Tubb et al. (1993) have developed several methodologies to distinguish the phytolith from different species of Triticeae. Nevertheless, the number of extracted phytoliths was scarce and their poor preservation state prevented further identification.

Body-text clarification (editorial addition from the cited PDF):
a–b: Damaged starch whose morphology was lost through processing and/or cooking; botanical origin unresolved. (PDF p. 4).
c–f: Millet-type starch; foxtail and broomcorn millet were not separated to species. (PDF p. 4).
g–j: Underground storage organ (USO) starch. Types II–IV collectively share traits with snake gourds (Trichosanthes), lotus (Nelumbo) and aroids (Typhonium); these genera are not assigned one-to-one to the three types. (PDF p. 5).
k–m: USO starch; the shared comparison for Types II–IV does not resolve this type to a genus. (PDF p. 5).
n–o: USO starch; the shared comparison for Types II–IV does not resolve this type to a genus. (PDF p. 5).
p–r: Starch similar to several oaks (Quercus) species; no species-level diagnosis. (PDF p. 5).
s–t: Unidentified starch; no match in the available modern references. (PDF p. 5).

In this study, we recovered microfossils of starch and phytolith from dental calculus. Starch grains are an end-product of carbon fixation by photosynthesis and are a major energy source for humans. The formation of an individual starch grain begins at a central point called the hilum, continues with the formation of alternating layers called lamellae, and finally results in a starch grain with a semi-crystalline structure with a regular shape and a polarization cross under cross-polarized light (Leonard et al., 2015). Because of differences in the hilum, lamellae, shape, polarization cross, fissure and size, starch grain morphologies are often taxo- nomically distinct (Piperno and Dillehay, 2008). Phytoliths are microscopic non-crystalline silica bodies formed between and in plant cells after the precipitation of soluble silica from ground water in plant tissues (Leonard et al., 2015). Diagnostic features include shape, ornamentation and size (Wang and Lu, 1993). Phy- toliths are mainly concentrated in husks, rinds, leaves, bark, and fruits (Leonard et al., 2015), and therefore they can be potentially ingested by humans. In the process of ingestion, food particles (including starch grains and phytoliths) may become incorporated into dental calculus. Therefore, by recovering plant microfossils from dental calculus, we can obtain a direct record of the plant foods ingested by humans. body_evidence.quote: The results of statistical analysis of the phytoliths extracted from fossil dental calculus are listed in Table 3 and examples of the phytoliths are illustrated in Fig. 3. We recovered a total of 619 phytoliths, of which 14 are unidentified. The main phytolith types are: double peaked, bilobate, elongate smooth, acicular, rectangle, bulliform (fan-shaped) and square-shaped. 201 are from rice (Oryza spp.), some of which are large and completely-silicified hair cell phytoliths characterized by double ‘peaks’ (Fig. 3a), which are produced by rice glumes. Some of them are dumbbell-shaped with

scooped ends, with a paralleled arrangement (Fig. 3b) in leaf tissue. Others are bulliform phytoliths (Fig. 3c) of Oryza which are char- acterized by numerous small, shallow scale-like decorations on the half-rounded side, which are produced by rice leaf tissue. It is noteworthy that double-peaked phytoliths from the glume of rice grains are dominant. In addition, we recovered four globular echinate phytoliths produced by palms (Arecaceae) (Fig. 3d).

body_evidence.quote: We chose 17 Old World plants covering A-, B-, and C-type starches, including both wild and domesticated species (Table 1). Prior to the experiments, the native starches of the raw plants were examined to have a baseline against which to compare changes due to beer making (Fig. 2). The experiments employed three brewing methods. Method A applied to all Triticeae plants and millets, during which each plant went through three main stages of malting, mashing, and fermentation, producing single-ingredient brews (Fig. 2 Box a). Method B used barley as the main ingredient and followed the same procedure as Method A, with the only difference that a non-cereal plant was added to each set of barley to produce a mixed beer (Fig. 2 Box b). Method C applied to rice, which was steamed and then mixed with a starter (honey or jiuqu fer- mentation starter) to initiate saccharification and fermentation (Fig. 2 Box c). To compare the damage to starch resulting from beer brewing with the damage from other food processing techniques, we conducted additional cooking experiments on selected plants (Fig. 2 Box d). De- tailed information about the experimental procedures is shown in Fig. 1 and Table 2. After the experiments, a part of each sample was taken by scraping offa portion of solid substances. body_evidence.quote: therefore we highlight one species from each group to demonstrate the results. The damage to Triticeae starch by sprouting is classified into four types, representing several continuous phases of enzymatic action. The first type shows random pits on the granule surface (Fig. 3a), a direct result of initial starch hydrolysis by enzymes (Claver et al., 2010). During germination, the enzymatic attack of a lenticular granule starts at the equatorial groove, as well as on random spots elsewhere on the surface (Dronzek et al., 1972; Galliard and Bowler, 1987). Using a light microscope, it is hard to observe the pits on the groove area, but the ones on the flat surface are readily visible. Following the initial attack, enzymes will hydrolyze one or more paths, penetrating to the center of the granule, and subsequently radiating outwards to the broader front. Some areas are more susceptible to enzymatic attack and thus are di- gested first, a character that leads to the formation of three other identifiable damage forms. One is the appearance of missing areas in the shape of concentric rings (partial or whole), a result of the erosion

the granule looks similar to a native starch, but under polarized light it loses its birefringence in the hilum area or appears entirely dark (Fig. 3d). Based on previous research (e.g., Dronzek et al., 1972 Fig. 5; Evers and McDermott, 1970 Fig. 7), we suggest that this damage type indicates that the granule has become an empty shell, with its interior

completely digested away but the surface mostly intact. Similar to Triticeae, sprouted millet starch exhibits distinct damage features. As Fig. 3e and f show, the erosion of both spherical and polygonal granules starts as discrete holes randomly distributed over the surface or as a hole at the hilum. As enzymatic hydrolysis proceeds, the holes enlarge and tend to join, creating radiating fissures and causing complete fragmentation of some granules (Fig. 3g), a feature only occasionally visible on Triticeae starch as observed in previous studies (Lineback and Ponpipom, 1977; Malleshi et al., 1986). Compared to A-type starch, C-type starch is more resistant to en- zyme activity. The starch granules of lentils mostly appear intact after germination (Table 3), but in the occasional cases where degradation is visible, the pattern appears consistent with the process of endocorro- sion. Enzymatic attack expands from the interior of the granule, creating a central cavity while the external shape remains mostly intact. For Triticeae starches, the swelling is mainly a radial expansion in the xy plane (Bowler et al., 1980). Thus the fermented granules appear enlarged and flattened without significant tangential expansion or folding. For other A-type starches, including millets, rice, and Cyperus roots, fermented granules swell by 3-dimensional radial expansion and pro- duce, essentially, a larger version of the original granules (Fig. 4c, d, g) (Bowler et al., 1980; Galliard and Bowler, 1987). This mode of swelling gives the fermented granule a donut-shaped appearance—the periph- eral region seems “pumped” by swelling, and the central area is stret- ched and mostly digested by enzymes (Fig. 4c, d, e, g). Mashing and fermentation cause similar morphological changes to Fabaceae starches, which belong to C-type, but to a significantly lesser extent. As Fig. 4g shows, the damaged lentil granule still preserves its

form after prolonged enzymatic digestion. Compared to sprouted granules, fermented granules show enlarged central cavities, radial fissures, and more pronounced lamellae. This diagnostic damage type, characterized by a spongy-looking appearance with a depressed central area, is comparable with fermented A-type starch and consistent with the results of previous studies (Rosenthal and Nakamura, 1972; Sotomayor et al., 1999). However, another C-type starch, Dioscorea polystachya (Wang et al., 2011), does not exhibit typical characteristics of endocorrosion in our experiment. Instead, most modified starches only show eroded sections and disappearing extinction crosses (Fig. 4i). More experiments need to be conducted to confirm this observation in the future. Fermented lily bulb starches show high resistance to enzymatic hydrolysis, with < 10% granules exhibiting only minor surface erosion, consistent with the process of exocorrosion. The damage pattern observed in fermented A- and C-type starches, as identified in the previous section, is apparently different from those resulting from simple physical processes such as pounding and grinding (Babot, 2003; Henry et al., 2009). We conducted two cooking experi- ments that eliminated the effect of enzymatic hydrolysis. The first ex- periment involved grinding and boiling the seeds, a method that could have been used by ancient people to make porridge. The second ex- periment was heating ungerminated, crushed seeds in water at mashing temperature (65 °C), a process that could be initiated accidentally and potentially produce starch modifications similar with those from beer making. In addition, a sample from steamed rice was taken during the brewing process for starch analysis. As our results show, boiling ground seeds causes severe damage to both A- and C-type starches, clearly different from the damage from beer making (Fig. 5). When ground barley is boiled, even for 1 min, its starches exhibit clear distortion, significant swelling, folding, and loss of extinction cross (Fig. 5a). Boiled barley starches are different from fermented ones in two aspects: 1) boiled barley starches develop folding from the centers (Fig. 5a), a feature rarely occurred in fermented barley; and 2) the average granule size of boiled barley is much larger than that of fermented barley (see Fig. 6 for a size comparison). of enzymatic hydrolysis and gelatinization, which together indicate a multi-stage brewing process reflecting a deliberate human behavior. If the ancient beer making generally followed Method A or Method B, as discussed above, there would be starch granules showing evidence of sprouting, mashing, and fermentation. Fig. 7 Box A illustrates an ex- ample of starch types present from the barley beer produced in our experiment. There are 1) starches showing random pits (Fig. 7a), missing lamellae (Fig. 7b), central holes (Fig. 7c), or completely hol- lowed interior (Fig. 7c), all of which are features of enzymatic hydro- lysis; 2) pizza crust-shaped granules (Fig. 7e), an unique damage type

resulting from mashing and fermentation; 3) gelatinized granules showing even expansion, without evidence of enzymatic attack (Fig. 7f), 4) undamaged granules resembling native starches (Fig. 7g); and 5) damaged starch granules from other plants, in the case that the final product is a mixed brew. Similar criteria can be applied for the identification of millet beer. If the ancient brewing process followed Method C, there would be starch granules resembling steamed and fermented rice, as well as intact ones (Fig. 7 Box B). The starch as- semblage generally includes: 1) granules showing central pitting and gelatinization (i.e. donut-shaped), which is indicative of fermentation (Fig. 7h); 2) granules only show swelling and distortion without missing parts, resembling the modifications from steaming (Fig. 7i); and 3) undamaged granules (Fig. 7j). Regardless of all variations, the “pizza crust-shaped” and “donut-shaped” granules represent the two most di- agnostic types of damage. In addition to damaged starches, other forms of remains are likely to be present in beer-brewing residues. Phytoliths, especially those from cereal husks, tend to preserve alongside with starches because brewing usually involves using whole grains to produce active enzymes (e.g., Fig. 7h, showing barley husk phytolith). Another type of remain is calcium oxalate, which is a byproduct that precipitates from beer brewing, also known as beer stone (Michel et al., 1992; Xie et al., 2011). body_evidence.quote: 3.2.1. Starch types A total of 1307 starch grains were recorded, and among them 767 (58.7% of the total) can be classified into two types based on their morphology and size (Table 1; for detailed starch counts see Table S2, and for starch sizes see Table S3). We found that the starch types from experimental tools match well with those from the corresponding plant stems/leaves, confirming their common origins. Therefore, we include the starches from both sources into discussion here. Type I starch grains (n = 523; 40% of the total) are polygonal or sub-round in form, often facetted; the hilum is centric or slightly ec- centric; the fissure is “V”, “Y”, or linear in shape, or radiating outward; extinction crosses are often nearly “+” shaped, but many are slightly curved or with zig-zag arms (due to the facetted shape). Sizes vary

considerably, ranging from 3.75–25.28 μm. Type I starch grains in general resemble those found in Panicoideae seeds (Yang et al., 2011). However, their size range is much greater than those from the seeds of wild and domesticated millets, but similar to those from the seeds of Job's tears. The zig-zag arm on the extinction cross and an eccentric hilum have been observed as diagnostic features in seed starch of Job's tears in previous studies (Liu et al., 2014). Type I starch grains are the most predominant type, and present in all the samples from tools and plants examined in the Panicoideae, Pooideae, and cattail assemblages (Figs. 5 and 8:3,5). Type II starch grains (n = 236; 18.1% of the total starch counts) are round or oval in the 2D form and lenticular in the 3D form, the hilum is centric, the extinction cross is “+” or “×” shaped, and lamellae are

visible on large grains. The size range is large, measuring from 9.71–38.42 μm. Type II starch resembles those from seeds of Triticeae (such as the genera of Triticum, Hordeum, Agropyron, Leymus, etc.) (Yang and Perry, 2013) and brome grass. They are present in all assemblages examined except for wild oats and reeds (Figs. 6 and 8:4,6). UNCL (Unclassified): There are 546 starch grains (41.8% of the total) not classified into types. They are extremely various in form and size (3.03–51.75 μm), and many do not exhibit diagnostic character- istics used for identifying taxa based on our reference data. Some are small, likely representing the transient starch, and some may be derived from the general surrounding environment, as airborne starch grains can travel in outdoor conditions (D'Amato et al., 2007; Dozier, 2016). UNCL starches, therefore, are not analyzed further in this study. We also compared the starches in stems/leaves with those in seeds from the same plants (Fig. S1). In the following discussion we focus on Type I and II starches in three taxonomic groups in our samples: Panicoideae, Pooideae, and reed-cattail (see S1 Text B for detailed de- scription).

3.2.2. The Panicoideae group The Panicoideae group includes samples from green foxtail, foxtail millet, broomcorn millet, barnyard grass, and Job's tears. Five tools were used to cut these plants. We analyzed tools and the plants cut with these tools, as well as plants collected from other regions for compar- ison. In all samples examined we found Type I and Type II starches. In Panicoideae stem/leaf samples collected in a half-green or nearly dry conditions, Type I starch is more numerous than Type II. However, a relatively high percentage of Type II was found in the green foxtail

body_evidence.quote: 3.2.4. The reed-cattail group We extracted residues from two tools used for cutting reeds and one for cutting cattails, as well as from cattail leaves collected in Shenmu. The reed-cutting tools revealed numerous starch grains, mostly small, round, sub-round, or semi-facetted in form, all identified as UNCL (Fig. 8; Table S3). The cattail-cutting tool and cattail leaves revealed Type I and Type II starches. The starch grains from stems/leaves are very different from those in the rhizomes, as the latter is much smaller in size. One thing in common among the tool, leaves and rhizomes is that they all contain abundant raphides (Fig. 8; Tables S2 and S3).

3.2.1. Starch types A total of 1307 starch grains were recorded, and among them 767 (58.7% of the total) can be classified into two types based on their morphology and size (Table 1; for detailed starch counts see Table S2, and for starch sizes see Table S3). We found that the starch types from experimental tools match well with those from the corresponding plant stems/leaves, confirming their common origins. Therefore, we include the starches from both sources into discussion here. Type I starch grains (n = 523; 40% of the total) are polygonal or sub-round in form, often facetted; the hilum is centric or slightly ec- centric; the fissure is “V”, “Y”, or linear in shape, or radiating outward; extinction crosses are often nearly “+” shaped, but many are slightly curved or with zig-zag arms (due to the facetted shape). Sizes vary

considerably, ranging from 3.75–25.28 μm. Type I starch grains in general resemble those found in Panicoideae seeds (Yang et al., 2011). However, their size range is much greater than those from the seeds of wild and domesticated millets, but similar to those from the seeds of Job's tears. The zig-zag arm on the extinction cross and an eccentric hilum have been observed as diagnostic features in seed starch of Job's tears in previous studies (Liu et al., 2014). Type I starch grains are the most predominant type, and present in all the samples from tools and plants examined in the Panicoideae, Pooideae, and cattail assemblages (Figs. 5 and 8:3,5). Type II starch grains (n = 236; 18.1% of the total starch counts) are round or oval in the 2D form and lenticular in the 3D form, the hilum is centric, the extinction cross is “+” or “×” shaped, and lamellae are

visible on large grains. The size range is large, measuring from 9.71–38.42 μm. Type II starch resembles those from seeds of Triticeae (such as the genera of Triticum, Hordeum, Agropyron, Leymus, etc.) (Yang and Perry, 2013) and brome grass. They are present in all assemblages examined except for wild oats and reeds (Figs. 6 and 8:4,6). UNCL (Unclassified): There are 546 starch grains (41.8% of the total) not classified into types. They are extremely various in form and size (3.03–51.75 μm), and many do not exhibit diagnostic character- istics used for identifying taxa based on our reference data. Some are small, likely representing the transient starch, and some may be derived from the general surrounding environment, as airborne starch grains can travel in outdoor conditions (D'Amato et al., 2007; Dozier, 2016). UNCL starches, therefore, are not analyzed further in this study. We also compared the starches in stems/leaves with those in seeds from the same plants (Fig. S1). In the following discussion we focus on Type I and II starches in three taxonomic groups in our samples: Panicoideae, Pooideae, and reed-cattail (see S1 Text B for detailed de- scription).

body_evidence.quote: No starch grains were recovered from the eight soil samples from the field and the surrounding area covered by the natural secondary vegetation near the wheat field. For the modern wheat seed samples, we recorded morphological data for 126 starch grains including 103 large Type A (>10 μm; mean, 20.5 ± 4.3 μm; range, 11.0–34.4 μm) and 23 small Type B (mean, 7.6 ± 1.2 μm; range, 5.6–9.7 μm)within the bimodal distribution. The large, diagnostic Type A starch grains are characterized by a lenticular shape with a centric hilum. Some possessed lamellae and craters on the surface. The starch grains were olivary in shape and the equatorial groove appeared as a longitudinal dent when the grains were rotated (Figure 2a–c). These observations are consistent with the large body of literature on wheat starch grains [17,36]. All starch grains extracted from the seeds of the purslane, plantain, dandelion, grey amaranth, and goosegrass seed samples growing near the wheat field measured <5 μm in size. The morphological characteristics on the surfaces of starches <5 μm were unclear even at 400× magnification, and this size class of starch is always excluded from our archaeobotanical analyses. Starches from green bristlegrass have grains that measure >5 μm, with a mean length of 6.8 ± 1.4 μm (n = 143; range, 5.1–9.2 μm). Our observations demonstrate that green bristlegrass grains have a polyhedral or semi-round shape, centric hilum, and rough edges, with occasional transverse fissures (Figure 2d). The consistently small size, however, eliminates them from potential inclusion within a starch a

Like in the samples from the modern wheat fields, no starch grains were recovered from the four soil samples from the maize field and the surrounding area covered by natural secondary vegetation. The starch grains of the modern maize seeds we studied possessed both irregular and spherical shapes (Figure 2e). The irregular grains were characterized by rough edges and wrinkled surfaces, while the spherical grains were smooth. The mean maximum length of the starch grains was 13.8 ± 1.4 μm, ranging from 8.4 to 21.3 μm (n = 123). These observations are consistent with the large body of literature that addresses maize starch grain morphology [37].

Starch grains extracted from the wormwood seeds were all <5 μm and their surface morphological characteristics were unclear at 400× magnification. Green bristlegrass starch grains exhibited a mean maximum length of 6.4 ± 1.3 μm (n = 132; range, 5.3–9.1 μm), and their morphological characteristics (Figure 2f) were like those noted in the green bristlegrass from Shandong Province.

Among the 28 sedimentary samples from the cultural layer, its overlying layer, and its underlayer, only one starch grain was recovered, and it was from the cultural sediment (No. NZT6, n = 1; Table 2). The grain is 19.4 μm in maximum length, exhibits a polygonal shape, a centric hilum, and rough edges (Figure 2g), but could not be identified because of surface damage on one side.

body_evidence.quote: Of the 42 tools examined, 1114 starch grains were recovered from 39 tools (397 from grinding stones and 717 from cutting tools). We recorded starch counts and ubiquity measures (percentage presence) (Pearsall 1989: 212–17) to indicate relative abundances of plant taxa (Table S1). Recovered starch grains can be classified into six types, some of which correspond to data from a modern reference collection comprising more than 120 species from 23 families (Figures 4 & S1, Table S2). Type I starch grains (n = 220; 19.7 per cent of the total), which are lenticular in form, were found on 35 tools (ubiquity 89.7 per cent). On grinding stones, they are probably derived from seeds of Triticeae grass, such as Agropyron, Leymus and Roegneria. As the lenticular grains have also been found in the stems and leaves of both Triticeae and Panicoideae grasses, the presence of this starch on cutting tools may have come from stems or leaves. Type II starch grains (n = 674; 60.5 per cent), polygonal or sub-round in form, were found on 31 tools (ubiquity 79.5 per cent). They resemble those found in Panicoideae seeds, including green foxtail, barnyard grass and Job’s tears. Type II grains on grinding

stones may have derived from the seeds of Panicoideae. Type II starch grains also resemble the polygonal type found in stems/leaves of Panicoideae and some Triticeae grasses. Type III starch grains (n = 58; 5.2 per cent) were found on seven tools (ubiquity 18 per cent). They best match green foxtail and barnyard grass in morphology and size.

Type IV starch grains (n = 4; 0.4 per cent) were found on one tool (ubiquity 2.6 per cent). They resemble the starch from Lilium bulbs, with the best match to L. tigrinum and L. pumilum. Type V starch grains (n = 10; 0.9 per cent) were found on 10 tools (ubiquity 25.6 per cent) and resemble the yam Dioscorea polystachya. Type VI starch grains (n = 10; 0.9 per cent) were found on six tools (ubiquity 15.4 per cent), and resemble the root of snake gourd, Trichosanthes kirilowii. Starch grains (n = 136; 12.2 per cent) from 31 tools (ubiquity 82.1 per cent) lacked diagnostic features comparable to taxa in our reference collection; these are classified as UNID (unidentified). In summary, types I–III, representing wild cereals, dominate the entire starch assemblage (85.6 per cent), with high ubiquity (94.9 per cent), while tubers and bulbs (types IV–VI) account for 2.2 per cent of the total starch, with low ubiquity (28.2 per cent). All these plants have been identified in micro- or macro-botanical remains from Upper Palaeolithic sites at Shizitan and Shuidonggou (in Ningxia) on the Loess plateau (Liu et al. 2011, 2013; Bestel et al. 2014; Guan et al. 2014).

On flake SF5, some highly polished areas near the edge are associated with fine, multi- diagonal striations, resembling cutting plants, and motions of transverse cutting and vertical scraping or splitting (Figure 6.11). All flakes revealed starches, including types I and II, yam and snake gourd root. Three flakes (SF4–6) yielded abundant starch grains (>100 each).
