body_evidence.quote: A total of 761 starch granules was found in the 10 PLG samples (n = 602) and two SQ samples (n = 159), of which 651 (85.5 %) were clas sified into six types, identifiable taxonomically (Fig. 2) when compared with our modern reference samples (Fig. 3). Some starch grains (n = 110; 14.5 %), lacking diagnostic characteristics or being severely damaged, were classified as unidentifiable (UNID). Most starch granules show damage characteristics (n = 735; 96.6 % of the total) and can be divided into three types: damage caused by enzymatic digestion (n = 126; 16.6 % of the total), gelatinization caused by fermentation (n = 556; 73.1 % of the total), and gelatinization due to cooking (n = 53; 7.0 % of the total) (Table S4). The morphological alterations due to enzy matic digestion include random pitting, deep channels, broken edges, and central depression (Fig. 2:2,4, compared with Fig. 3:2–4). Gelati nization caused by brewing process is characterized by moderate swelling with a hollowed center, often showing as a glossy periphery with a dark center (Fig. 2:8,11, compared with Fig. 3:9,12). The starch damage caused by boiling and steaming shows rather evenly expanded surfaces, and starch grains tend to fuse into large masses (Fig. 2: 9,10, compared with Fig. 3:10,11). These alterations are consistent with re ported results from experimental fermentation and cooking (Henry et al., 2009, Wang et al., 2017). We provide a detailed description of each starch type, as follows, along with starch counts, morphological features, and measurements, which are documented in Tables S4 and S5. Ty

the Triticeae tribe, such as genera Elymus, Hordeum and Agropyron (Fig. 3:6), widely distributed in north China (Wu et al., 2006). Some of the Type IV starches are apparently gelatinized due to fermentation and cooking (Fig. 2:8,9), consistent with those in our reference samples (Fig. 3:9,11). It is not possible to further determine the taxonomy of the Type IV starch granules. Type V: root of foxnut (Euryale ferox), found on nine PLG samples (n = 219; 28.8 % of the total counts; 64.3 % of the ubiquity). The large grains containing numerous small compound granules, which show illumination in polarized view, but no extinction crosses are visible, likely due to fermentation (Fig. 2:6, compared with Fig. 3:7). This plant grows in lakes and ponds, and is widely distributed in China (Wu and Raven, 2001). Type VI: yam (Dioscorea polystachya), found in one SQ sample (n = 1; 0.1 % of the total counts; 7.1 % of the ubiquity) (Fig. 2:7, compared with Fig. 3:8). This tuber is distributed widely over north China, and has been identified in Paleolithic and early Neolithic sites in the middle Yellow River region (Liu et al., 2018, Liu et al., 2019). Out of the six starch types identified, rice exhibits the highest num ber and ubiquity, followed by foxnut, Panicoideae, Triticeae, Job’s tears, and yam. Foxnut was exclusively found in PLG vessels, while Job’s tears and yam were only present in SQ vessels. The remaining plants were identified at both sites (Table S4). body_evidence.quote: A total of 761 starch granules was found in the 10 PLG samples (n = 602) and two SQ samples (n = 159), of which 651 (85.5 %) were clas sified into six types, identifiable taxonomically (Fig. 2) when compared with our modern reference samples (Fig. 3). Some starch grains (n = 110; 14.5 %), lacking diagnostic characteristics or being severely damaged, were classified as unidentifiable (UNID). Most starch granules show damage characteristics (n = 735; 96.6 % of the total) and can be divided into three types: damage caused by enzymatic digestion (n = 126; 16.6 % of the total), gelatinization caused by fermentation (n = 556; 73.1 % of the total), and gelatinization due to cooking (n = 53; 7.0 % of the total) (Table S4). The morphological alterations due to enzy matic digestion include random pitting, deep channels, broken edges, and central depression (Fig. 2:2,4, compared with Fig. 3:2–4). Gelati nization caused by brewing process is characterized by moderate swelling with a hollowed center, often showing as a glossy periphery with a dark center (Fig. 2:8,11, compared with Fig. 3:9,12). The starch damage caused by boiling and steaming shows rather evenly expanded surfaces, and starch grains tend to fuse into large masses (Fig. 2: 9,10, compared with Fig. 3:10,11). These alterations are consistent with re ported results from experimental fermentation and cooking (Henry et al., 2009, Wang et al., 2017). We provide a detailed description of each starch type, as follows, along with starch counts, morphological features, and measurements, which are documented in Tables S4 and S5. Ty

the Triticeae tribe, such as genera Elymus, Hordeum and Agropyron (Fig. 3:6), widely distributed in north China (Wu et al., 2006). Some of the Type IV starches are apparently gelatinized due to fermentation and cooking (Fig. 2:8,9), consistent with those in our reference samples (Fig. 3:9,11). It is not possible to further determine the taxonomy of the Type IV starch granules. Type V: root of foxnut (Euryale ferox), found on nine PLG samples (n = 219; 28.8 % of the total counts; 64.3 % of the ubiquity). The large grains containing numerous small compound granules, which show illumination in polarized view, but no extinction crosses are visible, likely due to fermentation (Fig. 2:6, compared with Fig. 3:7). This plant grows in lakes and ponds, and is widely distributed in China (Wu and Raven, 2001). body_evidence.quote: A total of 337 phytoliths was found in nine vessels, mostly in a globular jar (PLG-GLB1) and the strainer (PLG-STRA) (n = 109, 107, respectively). The morphotypes are mainly associated with Poaceae, including husk cells from Paniceae and Pooideae grasses, bilobate, polylobate, cross, rondel, bulliform, and elongates. Paniceae husk phy toliths were found only in the strainer (n = 11), including η-Type from broomcorn millet (n = 2). Elongate dendriform phytoliths, possibly coming from Triticeae husks, were also recovered from the strainer (n = 4). Double-peaked phytoliths from rice husk were found in PLG-GLB1 and PLG-STRA (n = 6 and 7, respectively). Considerable numbers of elongate phytoliths, mainly from unidentifiable stems and leaves, were also recovered from PLG-GLB1 and PLG-STRA (n = 24 and 25, respec tively). Tracheid and epidermal tissues were found in five vessels (n = 30). As a point of comparison, the stone roller (Control2) exhibited a substantial presence of phytoliths (n = 182) with diverse morphotypes. These included husk cells that could be identified as Paniceae (n = 25), η-Type phytoliths from broomcorn millet (n = 7), and double-peaked phytoliths from rice (n = 7). These findings suggest that the stone rol ler likely had a function related to plant processing (Fig. 4; Table S6). With the exception of PLG-GLB1 and PLG-STRA, most pottery vessels displayed limited or no presence of phytoliths, indicating that they likely contained well-processed food materials. body_evidence.quote: In total, 87 individual starch grains were discovered in hare dental residue (Fig. 3, a-f; Table 1). 32 starch grains proved unmeasurable or unidentifiable due to deformation and damage. Two typologies (I and II) for starch grains were positively identified and assigned to two human- related plant groups: Triticeae and Paniceae (millets and their wild relatives, e.g. Setaria italica, Panicum miliaceum, and Setaria viridis). The morphological attributes of these seedy starch grains have been amply described in the literature (Yang et al., 2005; Ge et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2012a; Yang et al., 2012b; Yang and Perry, 2013). In addition to starch grains, nine plant fragments were found in hare dental calculus, some of which derived from the hardwood cells (Wheeler et al., 1989), but we were unable to identify these to the genus/family level (Fig. 3, g-i). Type I. starch grains (n = 11, 3.44–30.57 μm) are round in 2D profile and lenticular in 3D profile, with clear lamellae and straight, distinct extinction crosses (Fig. 3, a). When the starch is flipped by tapping the slide, a long “-” shaped fissure appears. This grain was damaged, with only 2/3 of the body preserved, while fissures on the edges could also be observed (Fig. 3, b). This damage could be the result of plant processing

or mastication by the Tolai hare. This type of grain matches strongly to traits of starch grains from Triticeae plant seeds (Piperno et al., 2004; Yang and Perry, 2013). Triticeae plants include both local wild grasses, such as Agropyron, and domesticated plants, including a range of wheat plants. Because there is no archaeological evidence for domesticated wheat in this area (Sheng et al., 2017), it is believed that the starch grains for Type I are most likely derived from wild grasses. Given that only 11 grains were assigned this category, a more fine-grained identi fication was beyond us at this present time. Type II. starch grains (n = 44, 3.45–21.88 μm) are mostly polyhedral, with a small number of round or oval examples (Fig. 3, c-f). The extinction arm was cross-vertical in polarized light, the lamellar is not visible, and the centered hilum showed depressed and clear linear- shaped fissures. Available references (Yang et al., 2005; Ge et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2010) and our modern specimen database indicate that these morphological attributes represent close similarities to starch grains from the Panicoideae plants, especially the millets and their wild relatives from the Paniceae plants. Statistics on characteristics of starch

grains in modern plants suggest that starch grains from wild millets within the genus Setaria are characterized by wrinkled surfaces and rough edges, and the mean size is typically < 11 μm; and the starch grain with a diameter > 14 μm is a certain trait of foxtail millet (Yang et al., 2012a; Yang et al., 2012b). Based on the dichotomous key learned from previous works and the morphology of these 44 type II starches, 17 grains could be identified as foxtail millet starches (Fig. 3, c-d). The remaining starches show some characteristics of Setaria viridis or wild Setaria grasses, such as wrinkled surfaces (Fig. 3, e); and others might derive from Panicum milliaceum or Panicum bisulcatum, as the surface is smooth, without fissures, and < 11 μm in diameter (Fig. 3, f). However, due to our limited comparison database and knowledge, it remains possible that other Paniceae plants would have produced similar starch grains. A more wide-ranging comparison should be conducted in the future.

body_evidence.quote: 185 starch grains were uncovered from 56 human dental calculus (Table S2, S3). A total of 137 starch grains had been identified and were mainly classified into six types based on the reliable diagnostic attri butes mentioned above (Table 2). Type 1 starch grains (n = 46) are polygonal or nearly round. In addition, they have centric hilum, no lamellae with clear and straight extinction cross under polarized microscope (Fig. 3, a-f). Moreover, some starch grains had fissures with Y-shaped or transverse linear at the hilum. The size of type 1 starch grains ranges from 4.37 μm to 15.28 μm with an average of 9.99 μm. Based on previously studies, polygonal grains were often from the grass family Poaceae (Yang, Wan, et al., 2012; Yang, Zhang, et al., 2012; Tao, 2012). The size of starch grains from rice are smaller than type 1 grains while the common millet (5.96 to 10.99 μm) is similar with type 1. Furthermore, most of starch grains from common millet have no fissure (Figure S1). The size of starch grains from foxtail millet is 6.23–19.35 μm, and some of them have visible fissures (Figure S1). Starch grains from sorghum are bigger with distinct lamellae while Job’s-tear always have a Z-shaped arm on the extinction cross, partic ularly on larger grains (Yang, Wan, et al., 2012; Yang, Zhang, et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2014). Nine grains with larger sized (greater than12 μm

diameter) and visible fissures indicates great similarity to foxtail millet, and the other smaller grains were identified as common millet (P. miliaceum) or foxtail millet (S. italica). Type 2 starch grains (n = 75) are lenticular/discoidal or spherical in shape and have centric hilum (Fig. 3, g–l). Some grains with large size have visible lamellae. 32 of 75 grains have intact morphology while other grains are varying degrees of damage. The size of those 32 grains have wide range from 3.1 μm to 18.82 μm with a mean value of 8.85 μm. Cereal starches from family of the tribe Triticeae show characteristic of bimodal size distribution of large and small granules (Hardy et al., 2012; Lindeboom, Chang and Tyler, 2004). Triticeae are discernible from those of other tribes by their distinctive lenticular or discoid morphol ogies. They also have an olivary side view and pressure craters on the surfaces of grains that appear as small depressions (Yang and Perry, 2013). Therefore, type 2 starch grains show best matches to the tribe Triticeae. The tribe Triticeae in China includes Triticum, Hordeum, Agropyron, Aegilops, Elymus and Leymus. Considering starch grains from Elymus, Leymus and Aegilops without lamellae, visible lamellae appear on some starch grains extracted from Podi human dental calculus (Fig. 3, k-l). We infer that these starch grains were not from the above three genera. Moreover, starch grains extracted from dental calculus of Podi humans were different from the starch grains of Agropyron with diagnostic four to six well-defined concentric and equidistant lamellae. According to Guo and Jin (2019), wheat was more common found in archaeological sites during the Bronze Age in North ern China. Therefore, we argue that type 2 starch grains probably derived from common wheat (Triticum aestivum). Type 3 starch grains (n = 12) are polygonal and have no lamellae with clear and curving extinction cross. Few starch grains had fissure with transverse linear at the hilum (Fig. 3, m-r). The size of type 3 grains ranges from 8.06 μm to 13.69 μm with a mean value of 10.09 μm. The size of type 3 grains overlapped with those of foxtail millet (Setaria italica), common millet (Panicum miliaceum), sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) and Job’s-tear (Coix lacryma-jobi). We inferred type 4 grains likely derived from root and tuber plants. Type 5 starch grain (n = 1) is triangle with round corners with a diameter of 8.57 μm (Fig. 3, u-v). body_evidence.quote: >83 starch grains were recovered from 24 subsamples of the twelve perforated shells, and they can be divided into 5 categories (Supple mentary Table). Type A - the Fagaceae: The common features of type A grains (n = 4) were their various ovate shapes. Some type A grains were aggregated together in a cluster. When the grains were rotated, they still retained their ovate shapes. The properties of type A starches were consistent with the morphological characteristics of Fagaceae, therefore, we identified the type A grains as a type of Fagaceae. Based on the differ ences in the size of their diameters, surface morphologies, and fissure types, the type A grains could be divided into two subtypes: type A1 grains (Fig. 4i, j) with lengths 15.4 μm and 18.7 μm, which are consistent with the features of the grains of Cyclobalanopsis aggregated together; type A2 grains (Fig. 4k, l) with a smooth surface, regular oval shape, and smaller particle sizes (diameter lengths of 11.0 μm and 14.7 μm), which are consistent with the features of the disarticulated grains of Cyclobalanopsis. Type B - the Poaceae: Thirty-nine starch grains were polyhedral in shape with a centric hilum and lacked the presence of lamellae; most grains also had deeply crossed or winged fissures. Their size range and mean diameter were 7.3–25.9 μm and 15.8 ± 2.4 μm, respectively. Modern reference collections show that starch grains from the pith of Sorghum, Zea, Setaria, Panicum, and Coix are similar to the type B starch grains, as characterized by their pressure facets. In general, it is un derstood that the genera So

starch grains into three groups: type B1 starch grains, those of wild millets from genera of Setaria and Panicum, which are small particles (n = 19; range, 7.3–9.7 μm; mean size, 8.7 ± 1.8 μm) with wrinkled sur faces and rough edges (Fig. 4m, n); type B2 starch grains, those from Coix, which are polyhedral in shape with a smooth surface, a zig-zag arm on the extinction cross, and an eccentric hilum (n = 13, 20–25.9 μm, 24.5 ± 3.1 μm; Fig. 4o, p); the remaining 7 starch grains (type B3 starch grains, n = 7, 8.5 ~ 19.9 μm, 18.9 ± 2.7 μm; Fig. 4q, r), which may contain grains from ordinary seeds, stems of millets, and Coix plants (Fig. 4s, t). In summary, the type B starch grains are derived from grasses in the Panicoideae, probably genera from Setaria, Panicum and Coix plants, including some starches from stems of the three genera. Type C - geophytes: nineteen starches were characterized by a larger granule size, an eccentric hilum, irregular triangular or oval shape, and bent extinction crosses (range, 9.0–26.5 μm; mean size, 16.2 ± 4.8 μm). These starches show strong similarities in morphology and size with those of the roots and tubers in our modern samples (Wang et al., 2018). Based on the morphological characteristics of type C starch grains, they were categorized as polyhedral type C1 starch grains (Fig. 4u, v) with a slightly eccentric hilum, vertical or slightly bent extinction crosses, lamellae, and fissuring, which occasionally appears on the large grains (n = 11; range, 9.0–22.5 μm; mean size, 15.7 ± 5.2 μm), oval type C2 starch grains (Fig. 4w, x) with an irregula

Based on the thin and long lateral and oblique striations left on the surfaces of the twelve perforated shells from the Xianrendong and Dia otonghuan sites (Fig. 4c-h), it appears that the main direction of motion during use was parallel to the edge or in a direction that presents a consistent angle with the edge. It is of note that all of the shells analyzed had scars caused by stress cracking during use (Fig. 1B1-12). These usage traces are consistent with the wear patterns from cutting, mowing, scraping, slicing, planting, and digging observed in previous simulation experiments (Liu et al., 2017; Barton and White, 1993; Shen and Chen, 2001). On the basis of this it appears that the perforated shells analyzed in this study were likely used for cutting, digging, and scraping. Further, we observed that each shell was perforated with holes in varied sizes (Fig. 4a, b). Using methods of typology and ethno-archaeology, scholars have hypothesized that the drilled holes on the shell may have been used to tie the tool with strings of different thicknesses or embed it in wood implements of different sizes, which would be convenient to grasp and use (Wang, 1987). If the shells were used to harvest crops as tools, the edges would be in contact with the stems and leaves of the crops. First, starches and phy toliths from stems and leaves could be left on the surface of tools; sec ond, the numbers of starch grains and phytoliths should be greater than what was collected from the unused tools in a previous study (Liu et al., 2017; Yang and Perry, 2013). In this study, six phytoliths and

and they were all from stems and leaves of the Poaceae. One smooth elongate (Fig. 4I) and one acicular hair cell (Fig. 4J) were recovered from residues on the shell 99WX-1746 E10N12 Z:2A3from the Xian rendong site. Four phytoliths were recovered from three perforated shells in the Diaotonghuan site, including one bilobate of the Pan icoideae from shell 93WW-2265 W3S1 Z:L (Fig. 4K), one long-saddle of the Bambusoideae from 95WW-3452 W3N0 Z:H (Fig. 4L), and two squares from 95WW-3353 W2S3 Z:G and 95WW-3452 W3N0 Z:H (Fig. 4M). No starches or phytoliths were extracted from the dust samples taken from the storeroom in which the twelve shells were stored. This in dicates that the phytoliths detected on the shells were likely archaeo logical and probably not modern museum contaminants.

body_evidence.quote: A total of 104 starch granules were recorded, of which 98 (94.2% of the total) can be identified as four types corresponding to certain taxonomy. The great majority of the granules (n = 97; 93.3% of the total) show various forms of damage. By comparing with our ref- erence data, these damaged starch granules can be classified into three categories: (1) enzymatic digestion, (2) fermentation and cooking, and (3) gelatinization through high heat cooking (steam- ing or boiling). In addition, some starch granules (n = 6; 5.8% in total) are too damaged to be identified or, by lacking any diagnos- tic features, are classified as unidentifiable (UNID) (Table 1). Type I, rice (Oryza sp.): appearing in a compound form con- sisting of multiple small granules, found in JAR and PLATE. Most individual granules are blurry, but when visible, they are polygonal in shape. Some of the granules are birefringent, but no extinction cross is visible. These forms match rice starch in fer- mented conditions based on our modern reference data (Figure 2: 1, 2 compared with 7, 8). A total of 24 rice compounds were recorded, and 91 granules (2.63–6.14 μm) were measured. We count the percentage of Type I starch based on visible individual granules, which give the most numerous counts in the assemblage (87.5% of the total). Type II, Job’s tears (Coix lacryma-jobi; n = 4; 3.8% of the total): appeared in JAR and PLATE. The shape is polygonal or near-circular, hilum is centric or slightly eccentric, fissures are often present, and the size range is 11.37–16.09 μm. These gran- ules most resemble Job’s tears

Starch granules of rice, Job’s tears, Fagaceae acorn, and lily bulb have been previously found on grinding stones and pottery vessels at several Shangshan culture sites, including Xiaohuang- shan (Liu et al., 2010; Wang and Jiang, 2022; Yao et al., 2016). These plants, mostly perhaps wild, may have been used as staples. Several observations in the starch assemblage are also noted: (1) Most starch granules in JAR and PLATE are damaged by fermen- tation or cooking, suggesting the two vessels once contained fer- mented beverages and cooked foodstuffs, respectively; (2) JAR, a vessel type for liquid storage, revealed the highest number of starch granules and most diverse starch types among three vessels, indicating that fermented beverages were made of rice, Job’s tears, lily, and acorns; and (3) BASIN yielded only one unidentifiable starch granule without sign of fermentation/cooking damage, thus, this vessel probably had functions other than food fermentation. Only one starch granule, resembling Type II starch (Job’s tears) was recovered from the perforated stone.

body_evidence.quote: Starch grains from aroids and yams accounted for around 34 per cent of the total findings (Type I & II, n > 170) (Figure 8). Numerous small grains (Type Ia) on a stone pounder from Liyupo resemble both wild and domesticate taro starch grains (Figure 6A–C). Furthermore, eight clusters (compound grains) comparable with taro were also identified from all examined samples (Figure 6A’–C’). Eighty-five starch grains exhibit a large size and a multifaceted morphology (Type Ib, Figure 7A–A’) consistent with other aroid plants outside the Colocasia genus, including kon- jac (Amorphophallus konjac) (Figure 7J–J’). Raphides—needle-shaped calcium oxalate crystals —are commonly produced in aroid plants, but none were observed in our samples. This lack of observation can be attributed to the complexities of preservation at archaeological sites, varied raphide content in aroid species and probable raphide destruction during food process- ing. Fifteen per cent of the grains are from Dioscorea (Type II, n = 77, Figure 8), including 65 small polygonal granules (Type IIa) that compare well with lesser yam (Dioscorea esculenta) (Figure 7B–J’, K–K’). Twelve starch grains of Type IIb have triangular ovoid shapes and lar- ger sizes that relate them to the greater, or purple, yam (Dioscorea alata) (Figure 7C–C’, L–L’). Thirty-seven per cent of the starch grains exhibit the typical features of panicoid grasses (Type III, n = 187, Figure 8). Forty-eight (Type IIIa) probably come from wild grasses such as green foxtail (Setaria viridis) (Figure 7D-D’, M–M’; Table S2). The other 139 specimens (Type II

Fourteen per cent of the starch grains (Type IV, n = 52) can be identified as from Casta- nopsis (Figure 7G–G’, P–P’) and Quercus tree nuts (Figure 7H–H’, Q–Q’) from the family Fagaceae. One per cent are from piths of the Arenga palm (Arenga sp.) (Type V, n = 6, Figure 7I–I’, R–R’).

Our results show that early populations in southern China exploited panicoid grasses, as also observed at Niulandong (c. 12 000 BP), Zengpiyan (c. 12 500–7600 BP) and Baozitou (c. 8000–7000 BP). Starch grains from grasses account for a large proportion of the micro- remains so far identified at these sites (Institute of Archaeology, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences et al. 2003; Wan 2012; Li 2016). We recovered 139 starch grains (Type IIIb) that resemble those from the Job’s tears plant (Figure 7E–E’, F–F’, N–N’, O–O’). Despite widespread documentation of starch grains from this plant at archaeological sites in both southern and northern China (Yang 2017; Liu et al. 2019), their starch identification is controversial due to the scarcity of associated macro-remains of the plant. The lack of macro-remains of Job’s tears at Huiyaotian (Deng et al. 2019) means that we cannot confidently claim that the 139 micro-remains of starch grains reported here are from it. This plant is, however, a widespread and potentially early crop in Mainland Southeast Asia that grows easily in ditches and watercourses (Fuller & Cas- tillo 2021). Overall, the role of Job’s tears in ancient economies needs further investigation. Starch grains from aroids and yams accounted for around 34 per cent of the total ﬁndings
(Type I & II, n > 170) (Figure 8). Numerous small grains (Type Ia) on a stone pounder from
Liyupo resemble both wild and domesticate taro starch grains (Figure 6A–C). Furthermore,
eight clusters (compound grains) comparable with taro were also identiﬁed from all examined
samples (Figure 6A’–C’).
Eighty-ﬁve starch grains exhibit a large size and a multifaceted morphology (Type Ib,
Figure 7A–A’) consistent with other aroid plants outside the Colocasia genus, including kon-
jac (Amorphophallus konjac) (Figure 7J–J’). Raphides—needle-shaped calcium oxalate crystals
—are commonly produced in aroid plants, but none were observed in our samples. This lack
of observation can be attributed to the complexities of preservation at archaeological sites,
varied raphide content in aroid species and probable raphide destruction during food process-
ing. Fifteen per cent of the grains are from Dioscorea (Type II, n = 77, Figure 8), including 65
small polygonal granules (Type IIa) that compare well with lesser yam (Dioscorea esculenta)
(Figure 7B–J’, K–K’). Twelve starch grains of Type IIb have triangular ovoid shapes and lar-
ger sizes that relate them to the greater, or purple, yam (Dioscorea alata) (Figure 7C–C’, L–L’).
Thirty-seven per cent of the starch grains exhibit the typical features of panicoid grasses
(Type III, n = 187, Figure 8). Forty-eight (Type IIIa) probably come from wild grasses such
as green foxtail (Setaria viridis) (Figure 7D-D’, M–M’; Table S2). The other 139 specimens
(Type IIIb) resemble Job’s tears (Coix lacryma-jobi) (Figure 7E–E’, F–F’, N–N’, O–O’).

body_evidence.quote: (Figure 3b), β-type (barnyard grass inflorescence) (Figure 3c), double peak (rice husk) (Figure 3i) and Oryza-type bulliform (rice leaf) (Figure 3h). Other diagnostic types include opaque perforated platelet (cf. Asteraceae inflorescence) (Figure 3e) and dendritic long cell (cf. Triticeae inflorescence) (Figure 3d). Starch granules are less numerous than phytoliths, but they indicate the consumption of USOs (Figure 4c), whose granules are characterised by extremely eccentric hilum and bright extinction crosses. Other identified starch granules include millet (Figure 4a), Triticeae (cf. wheat) (Figure 4b) and rice (Figure 4d), thus consistent with phytolith data (see Table S2 for starch identification criteria).

Thirty-eight starch granules exhibit evidence of damage, characterised by pitting, cracking and swelling (Figure 4e–h). Some of the pitted and/or cracked granules are likely the result of chewing or bacteria degradation during food consumption, but 13 show gelatinisation dam- age consistent with that caused by cooking (Henry et al. 2009; Wang et al. 2017). The pres- ence of cooked starches provides strong evidence that pigs and dogs were provisioned with or scavenged kitchen scraps.

body_evidence.quote: (1) Type I, INTERDIGITATING Ω type phytoliths from the S. italica husk (Figure 4j); (2) Type II, INTERDIGITATING η type phytoliths, originating from the P. miliaceum husk (Figure 4a,b,e,g,i); (3) Type III, illustrating the characteristic of a phytolith combination of Triticeae, including the PAPILLATE phytoliths, TRICHOME BASE phytolith, and DENDRITIC phytoliths (Figure 4c,d,f,h); (4) Type IV, exhibiting ELONGATE ENTIRE and ELONGATE ECHINATE phytoliths, commonly viewed in plants of the Poaceae family (Figure 4k,l); (5) Type V, BILOBATE phytoliths (Figure 4n); (6) Type VI, ACUTE phytoliths (Figure 4o); (7) Type VII, BULLIFORM FLABELLATE PELTATE phy- toliths from reeds (Figure 4m). According to the results, INTERDIGITATING η-type from broomcorn millet husk was most abundant in Samples HW1, HW3, HW4, and HW5, and DENDRITIC from Triticeae were also identified in Samples HW3 and HW4. In addition, in Sample HW5, very minute traces of INTERDIGITATING Ω-type phytoliths fragments from foxtail millet husk were viewed. In sample HW2, only the DENDRITIC from Triticeae phytoliths were identified. Thus, combined with the archaeobotanical records of the Wupu Cemetery, it can be inferred that broomcorn millet com- posed the major portion of Samples HW1 and HW5, with a mixture of flour of broomcorn mil- let, wheat, and barley in Samples HW3 and HW4. Wheat and barley were predominantly found in Sample HW2.

body_evidence.quote: A total of 322 starch granules were recorded. Among them, 299 (92.9%) could be classified into four types identifiable to certain taxa. Almost all granules appeared damaged, showing blurry extinction crosses, broken edges, deep channels or fissures, pitting on the surface, a depression in the center, or gelatinization (Figure 2). These features are consistent with those affected by enzymatic digestion and cooking, commonly found in fermented and cooked foods in experimental studies (Figure S3) [26,27,29]. The taxa of 23 granules (13.5%) were unidentifiable (UNID) due to a lack of diagnostic features or severe damage (Figure 2I,J,M; Table S3). The type I granules (n = 19; 5.9% of the total) were slightly polygonal in shape, mea- suring 7.06–27.04 μm in maximum length. The hila were centric, and the extinction crosses were “+” shaped. These characteristics resembled those of the Panicoideae subfamily, including broomcorn millet (Panicum miliaceum), foxtail millet (Setaria italica), and Job’s tears (Coix lacryma-jobi), all domesticated in China [32]. One relatively large granule with a zig-zag-shaped arm was typically consistent with Job’s tears (Figure 2A,B compared with Figure S3A,B), based on previous studies [33]. When the starch morphology and size ranges were compared, type I fell into the combined size range of broomcorn millet, foxtail millet, and two variants of domesticated Job’s tears (C. lacryma-jobi var. ma-yuen and C. lacryma-jobi var. lacryma-jobi) (Figure S4A).

starch in our modern reference (Figure 2C compared with Figure S3C). Vicia wild pea is native to China; there are 17 species of Vicia growing in Shaanxi, one of which, V. gigantea Bge [34], was referred to as wei in ancient texts and used for food in the Zhou dynasty [35]. Domesticated pea (P. sativum), a Near Eastern crop, was introduced to China probably around the Eastern Zhou dynasty, as inferred from the presence of a charred seed at the Dongyang site in Huaxian, Shaanxi [36]. Starch granules from wild and domesticated peas are morphologically similar; thus, it is not possible to make further taxonomical identifications of type II starch. The type III granules (n = 242; 75.2%) were consistent with Triticeae, with a size range of 4.36–33.33 μm. The hila were centric, and the extinction crosses were “+”-shaped. Triticeae starch granules exhibit a bimodal size distribution, consisting of large granules, lenticular in 3D (A-type; >10 μm), and small, almost spherical, granules (B-type; <10 μm). The type III granules exhibited various damaged features, such as pitting, central depres- sions, concentric channels, and gelatinization, resembling those found in fermented wheat (Triticum sp.) and barley (Hordeum sp.) starch in our brewing experiments (Figure 2D,E,L compared with Figure S3D,K,L). Wheat and barley were introduced to China by the second millennium BC and gradually became widespread thereafter [37]. The type IV granules resembled rice (Oryza sp.). body_evidence.quote: The most numerous microparticles recorded are yeast cells (n = 689), which can be classified into three groups: (1) oval or round (n = 616; 2.9–10.83 μm in length); (2) elongated– oval (n = 31; 3.32–9.88 μm in length); and (3) irregular rod-shaped (n = 42; 3.06–14.71 μm in length). Many cells exhibit characteristics of a budding process, such as a small protu- berance on the parent cell, a smaller cell attaching to the bigger parent cell, or two cells of similar size connecting to one another (Figure 3A–E; Table S3). Budding is a typical feature of many yeasts, as they reproduce asexually by the asymmetric division process [30]. In our brewing experiments, yeast cells became more dominant in the microbial assemblage

were compared, the Qin round–oval and elongated–oval cells appeared smaller than the Shimao wild S. cerevisiae and P. kudriavzevii, respectively, but similar to their corresponding cultured cells (Figure S4B). Several rod-shaped yeast cells show a budding process, similar to unidentified yeast in a daqu sample from a Chinese distiller (Figure 3H compared with Figure 4E). The Qin rod-shaped cells exhibited a wide size range, overlapping with both wild and cultured P. kudriavzevii as well as with the rod-shaped yeast from the daqu (Figure S4B). Apparently, the Qin yeast community consists of various species, not limited to S. cerevisiae and P. kudriazevii, but some are currently unidentifiable. S. cerevisiae, due to its high ability to ferment sugars to ethanol, is the most commonly used yeast for alcohol fermentation [41]. In Chinese qu starters, S. cerevisiae, Pichia sp., and many other genera (e.g., Hanseniaspora, Hansenula, and Candida) have been identified [9,42]. These yeasts contribute to the fermentation process in different ways. S. cerevisiae, for example, played a dominant role during the early stages of the fermentation process [43]. P. kudriavzevii produced about 35% and 200% more ethanol than S. cerevisiae at high tem- peratures of 40 and 45 ◦C, respectively [44], but also contributed to the negative effect of film-formation in fermented food [45].

Numerous fungal elements were recorded (n = 536), including hyphae (n = 20), mycelia (n = 9), fungal spores in germination (n = 3), conidial clusters resembling Aspergillus (n = 472), and cleistothecia likely from Monascus (n = 2) (Table S3). The hyphae and mycelia appeared either transparent or brown in color and were mostly septate (Figure 3L–N,P,Q). Some small spores were seemingly in a state of germination (Figure 3K). Many small, dark-colored spore clusters, in some cases connecting to hyphae or mycelia, were present (Figure 3M,N,P,Q). These mold particles resembled those of Aspergillus, particularly A. niger and A. oryzae (Figure 4G–L). These two species were very similar in our reference data, but the former produced smaller and darker conidia than the latter (Figure 4G–L,N). In the Qin liquid, the spores in those dark-colored spore clusters measured 0.96–2.79 μm, resembling those in A. niger, while two larger conidia during germination were transparent and measured 6.14 μm and 6.74 μm, falling within the range of A. oryzae (Table S4). Addi- tionally, two cleistothecia were present, appearing red in color and containing numerous oval ascospores, which are typical characteristics of Monascus (Figure 3O, compared with Figure 4N,P). In our experimental brewing of millet beer, mycelia associated with starches were present in the beverage after the fermentation process was completed, a situation resembling that of the Qin liquid (Figure 4M) [27]. When a single starch granule abscises from the assemblage (vibrating may accelerate the abscission), small facets are observable under DIC filters (Fig. 3). Their mean lengths are considerably longer than those of starch granules from modern wild rice, but similar to those from modern cultivated rice (Fig. 4). The starch granules from cultivated rice at the Xiaohuangshan site (early phase, c. 9000–8500 cal. BP) were reported to be mostly recovered from potsherds, whereas those of wild plant species were mainly recovered from grinding slabs (Yao et al. 2016). This suggests that grinding slabs were likely not used for processing rice, or that specialized processing techniques may have obscured initial informa- tion. Simulation experiments indicate that dry-grinding can significantly alter starch morphology, including loss of extinction crosses, compli- cating detection and identification (Li et al. 2020). The dry-grinding procedure may have contributed to the absence of rice starch on Xiao- huangshan slabs. However, the presence of embedded rice grains in Hemudu foodcrusts suggests that rice was consumed whole after dehusking, rather than being ground into flour. body_evidence.quote: 4.1.2. The Triticeae tribe Two granules of wheat starch were retrieved, with maximum lengths of 27.37 and 26.73 μm, respectively. Both granules are nearly round in shape and may turn lenticular after tapping the cover slides using a pipette tip (Fig. 5: a, b). The two granules’ hila are centrally located. The arms of the extinction crosses are slender near the hilum and gradually widen toward the edge. Because there are many morphological overlaps in starch among several genera in the Triticeae tribe, it is difficult to assign them to a specific genera or species (Liu et al. 2011, Yao et al. 2016). The widespread use of wheat and barley starch in modern industry and daily life raises the possibility of airborne contamination in ancient starch research (Crowther et al. 2014). The domesticated species of Triticeae (mainly wheat and barley) originated in West Asia and were first spread to China around 2000 BCE (Liu et al., 2018b, Long et al. 2018, Chen et al. 2020). Although there is no clear evidence that wild species of the wheat tribe were collected for food in prehistoric China, given the vast distribution of wild Triticeae species, it seems likely that they were the objects of human collection in Neolithic China. Our lab- oratory work conformed to strict guidelines for avoiding and identifying contamination, and no Triticeae starch was found in the control group. Numerous Triticeae starch granules were discovered on pottery sherds and stone slabs from Xiaohuangshan (Yao et al., 2016). These findings suggest the presence of wild wheat species. body_evidence.quote: 4.1.4. The Papilionoideae subfamily A single, kidney-shaped starch granule from legumes was recovered, measuring 25.48 μm in length (Fig. 7: a-c). It features a central hilum with irregular fissures and a clear extinction cross forming a thick “x”. The length is comparable to that of modern cowpea (Vigna unguiculata, 5.1–28.56 μm). However, due to its morphological resemblance to some wild species in the Vicieae tribe (e.g., Vicia spp., see Hart 2014, Liu et al. 2016b), it cannot be definitively assigned to any specific genus or tribe. Notably, Yao et al. (2016) described Vigna starch granules from a slab and a potsherd, which were believed to be more similar to those of mung beans. Yang and Jiang (2010) also reported Vigna starch from Kuahu- qiao foodcrusts, identifying it as more similar to cowpea. The starch

granules observed in this study lack the long-merged extinction arms around the hilum that distinguish mung bean starch (see Fig. 4. g, g’ in Yao et al. 2016), but resemble the cowpea granules we collected (Fig. 7: d, e). Unidentified Fabaceae seeds recovered from the Tianluoshan site were identified as belonging to Cladrastis sp., Dalbergia sp., or Ormosia sp. (Fuller et al. 2011). body_evidence.quote: 4.1.5. Lilium sp This starch granule is a rounded rectangle, measuring 39.68 μm in length (Fig. 8). The hilum is located at approximately the 1/6 point along one of the rectangle’s diagonals (Fig. 8: 1b). Four straight extinction arms connect the hilum to the four corners. Fine lamellas are visible on the smooth surface. Its morphological features align with those of Asiatic lily bulbs (Lilium asiatic), which range from 5.75 to 65.62 μm in length. Yao et al. (2016) reported tuber starch from pottery sherds and stone slabs at Xiaohuangshan, including Nelumbo sp. and Dioscorea sp. This study is the first to report archaeological lily starch in the Ningbo-Shaoxing plain. The lily bulb has been traditionally used as both a vegetable and a medicine due to its high starch content and other health-promoting components (Li et al. 2019). Because of their high- water content, lily bulbs are difficult to preserve, yet the starch re- mains provide invaluable evidence of the Hemudu ancient people’s prehistoric use of lilies. Wang and Jiang (2022) recovered lily starch from Shangshan’s (c. 11000–8600 BP) grinding stones and potsherds, potentially the earliest in China. Pollen from the Liliaceae family was found in early Yangshao culture strata (c. 6800–6400 BP) at the Dadi- wan site in Gansu province (Huang, 1991), where lilium starch residues were discovered on shell knives (c. 6500–5900 BP) (Yang et al. 2019). Liliaceae starch was also discovered on the surfaces of stone knives and sickles from the Longshan (c. 5000–4000) to Erlitou (c. 4000–3500 BP) phases at the Huizui site in Yanshi

body_evidence.quote: 4.1.6. Unidentified and damaged starch granules Some tiny, round starch granules were not identified as they may originate from various genera or species (Fig. 9: 1a, 1b). Others were left

unidentified due to damage, but they may have cultural significance. These granules exhibit an expanded extinction region under polarized light and a flattened depression around the hilum (Fig. 9: 2, 3a, 3b). In the larger granules, the lamellae also became more visible around the hilum (Fig. 9: 3a). These characteristics align with features of starch damaged by heating (Henry et al. 2009, Ge et al. 2010, Crowther 2012). The cooking process can damage starch structures through gelatini- zation, which depends on temperature and humidity (Crowther 2012). High water content and elevated temperatures can lead to complete gelatinization. This process alters the morphological characteristics of starch granules, which consist of alternately ordered layers of amor- phous and semi-crystalline polymers with varying stability (Martin and Smith 1995). Common rice cooking methods, involving mixing rice grains with water and heating, typically result in starch gelatinization. Gelatinization requires time, and the duration of heating can affect the degree of gelatinization and visible morphological changes in starch. As gelatinization progresses, starch granules may swell, distort, and even- tually lose structural integrity, transforming into a glue-like amorphous substance (Henry et al. 2009, Ge et al. 2010). This process causes the extinction features to fade, indicating crystal structure disintegration. body_evidence.quote: Of all the starch grains, 250 were classified into types I–VI based on their morphology, size, and extinction cross characteristics. The remaining 37 grains lacked identifiable features and were classified as unidentified. Notably, some grains were unmeasurable owing to overlap within clusters, making them difficult to observe entirely after rotation; however, they were still included in the analysis. Type I starch grains (n = 164; 65.6 % of the total; from 17 tools with 58.6 % ubiquity) closely resemble those found in Panicoideae, particu larly foxtail millet (Setaria italica) and broomcorn millet (Panicum mil iaceum) (Figs. 3a; 4a). These grains were identified based on their morphological characteristics and sizes, ranging from 4.61 to 19.5 μm. The overlap in starch characteristics between foxtail millet and broomcorn millet is relatively high, making it difficult to distinguish between them. This type of starch is also found in the stem/leaf of Panicoideae (Liu et al., 2017). Therefore, Type I is associated with millets (S. italica and P. miliaceum) starch, which likely originated from seeds and stems/leaves. Type II starch grains (n = 23; 9.2 % of the total; from 13 tools with 41.4 % ubiquity) are polyhedral with a centric hilum and normally have T- or linear-shaped fissures. Their extinction cross is “+” shaped with a bent end (Fig. 3b). These starch grains closely resemble those from Job’s tears (Coix lacryma-jobi) (Fig. 4b), based on their size (10.1–26.5 μm)

and morphological characteristics. Type III starch grains (n = 31; 12.4 % of the total; from 16 tools with 55.2 % ubiquity) are more typical of the Triticeae tribe (Figs. 3c; 4c). The size of these grains ranges from 6.48 to 38.1 μm, although some grains were not measured due to breakage and deformation. There are no reliable criteria for further identification and distinction between starch of cultivated and wild genera of Triticeae. Studies have shown that this type of starch is also present in the stem/leaf of Panicoideae (Liu et al., 2017). Therefore, Type III starch grains may be derived from Triticeae seeds or from Panicoideae stems/leaves. Type IV starch grains (n = 16; 6.4 % of the total; from 8 tools with 27.6 % ubiquity) are commonly found in tubers. Certain species and genera can be defined relatively based on modern tuber starch studies (Wan et al., 2011). Type IV-1 starch grains (n = 3; from 2 tools) closely resemble starch from yam (Dioscorea polystachya) (Fig. 4d) based on their size range of 22.4–40.7 μm, and their morphological features (Fig. 3d). Type IV-2 starch grains (n = 5; from one stone knife) are elongated oval in shape with radiated fissures, are extremely eccentric and size range of 9.92–27.04 μm (Fig. 3e). The morphology of these grains is similar to that of the lily family (Liliaceae). Most Liliaceae starches have a smooth surface, but some genera also have large fissures (Fig. 4e). Type IV-3, a starch grain with a size of 59.15 μm is observed (Fig. 3f), and is most similar to the lotus root (Nelumbo nucifera) (Fig. 4f). The remaining Type IV st

4.3.1. Processing tools Among the five stone mortars, the smallest one (SM3) contained only one starch grain, and the majority of the phytoliths in this mortar were mostly from stems/leaves, which were relatively fragmented, suggesting that this stone mortar was likely used for grinding adulterants rather than processing grains. The other four mortars had an unusual abun dance of phytoliths (n = 390, 31 % of the total), which were identified as belonged to the stems/leaves and husks of numerous Poaceae plants, including rice and millets. Only 18 starch grains exhibited signs of breakage, cracking (Fig. 3j), and local lamellae, which are characteris tics typically associated with processing methods such as grinding and pounding (Ge et al., 2010, 2015). The low starch extraction rate may be attributed to processing methods that did not completely crush the grains. However, it is also possible that severe environmental corrosion and damage occurred later, resulting in the decomposition of most starch grains. Only 3 starch grains were found on the grinding rod (GR1), despite the abundance of phytoliths. These 3 starch grains were identified as millet and Triticeae, whereas the phytoliths mainly originated from rice and millets, with a considerable number also belonging to the stems/ leaves of other Poaceae plants. Ethnographic studies and test analyses have shown that grinding slabs and rods were mainly used for grinding nuts, beans, or tubers and were not typically used for dehusking millets (Wang, 2008; Liu et al., 2010a–c; Robitaille, 2016). body_evidence.quote: In this study, a total of 1259 phytoliths were extracted from 29 stone tools (Fig. 5), and they predominantly belonged to the Poaceae family. Of these, five phytoliths types were particularly prevalent: elongate (31.8 % of the total, 97.3 % ubiquity), bilobate (21.8 % of the total, 75.9 % ubiquity), skeleton (13.2 % of the total, 82.8 % ubiquity), rectangle (7.1 % of the total, 58.6 % ubiquity), and bulliform (6.3 % of the total, 75.9 % ubiquity). Elongate and rectangle phytoliths are typically found in the epidermal structures of many plants, whereas bilobate, bulliform, and skeleton phytoliths are predominantly found in the stems, leaves, and husks of Poaceae. Polylobate, cross, rondel, and prickle are commonly found in the subfamilies Pooideae and Panicoideae. The mid- long saddle is common in Bambusoideae, whereas the short saddle is typical of the Eragrostis subfamily. Some Poaceae phytoliths have been identified at the species level. For example, 44 phytoliths (41.4 % ubiquity) were identified as either double-peak from rice (Oryza sativa) husks or longitudinal bilobate and

Of all the starch grains, 250 were classified into types I–VI based on their morphology, size, and extinction cross characteristics. The remaining 37 grains lacked identifiable features and were classified as unidentified. Notably, some grains were unmeasurable owing to overlap within clusters, making them difficult to observe entirely after rotation; however, they were still included in the analysis. Type I starch grains (n = 164; 65.6 % of the total; from 17 tools with 58.6 % ubiquity) closely resemble those found in Panicoideae, particu larly foxtail millet (Setaria italica) and broomcorn millet (Panicum mil iaceum) (Figs. 3a; 4a). These grains were identified based on their morphological characteristics and sizes, ranging from 4.61 to 19.5 μm. The overlap in starch characteristics between foxtail millet and broomcorn millet is relatively high, making it difficult to distinguish between them. This type of starch is also found in the stem/leaf of Panicoideae (Liu et al., 2017). Therefore, Type I is associated with millets (S. italica and P. miliaceum) starch, which likely originated from seeds and stems/leaves. Type II starch grains (n = 23; 9.2 % of the total; from 13 tools with 41.4 % ubiquity) are polyhedral with a centric hilum and normally have T- or linear-shaped fissures. Their extinction cross is “+” shaped with a bent end (Fig. 3b). These starch grains closely resemble those from Job’s tears (Coix lacryma-jobi) (Fig. 4b), based on their size (10.1–26.5 μm)

and morphological characteristics. Type III starch grains (n = 31; 12.4 % of the total; from 16 tools with 55.2 % ubiquity) are more typical of the Triticeae tribe (Figs. 3c; 4c). The size of these grains ranges from 6.48 to 38.1 μm, although some grains were not measured due to breakage and deformation. There are no reliable criteria for further identification and distinction between starch of cultivated and wild genera of Triticeae. Studies have shown that this type of starch is also present in the stem/leaf of Panicoideae (Liu et al., 2017). Therefore, Type III starch grains may be derived from Triticeae seeds or from Panicoideae stems/leaves. Type IV starch grains (n = 16; 6.4 % of the total; from 8 tools with 27.6 % ubiquity) are commonly found in tubers. Certain species and genera can be defined relatively based on modern tuber starch studies (Wan et al., 2011). Type IV-1 starch grains (n = 3; from 2 tools) closely resemble starch from yam (Dioscorea polystachya) (Fig. 4d) based on their size range of 22.4–40.7 μm, and their morphological features (Fig. 3d). Type IV-2 starch grains (n = 5; from one stone knife) are elongated oval in shape with radiated fissures, are extremely eccentric and size range of 9.92–27.04 μm (Fig. 3e). The morphology of these grains is similar to that of the lily family (Liliaceae). Most Liliaceae starches have a smooth surface, but some genera also have large fissures (Fig. 4e). body_evidence.quote: 3.1.1. Type I starch grains The results revealed that 684 Type I starch grains shared common features, including their polyhedral shape, centric hilum, and the absence of lamellae. These grains could be classified into three subtypes based on differences in size, surface morphology, and fissure type. (1) Type I-1 starch grains. A total of 621 starch grains fell into Type I- 1. All of them had deeply crossed, winged to Y-shaped or stellate fissures cutting through the hilum and surfaces with short lines radiating from the centre to the edges (Fig. 3(a)–(d)). Type I-1 grains ranged in length from 7.3 to 27.0 μm, with an average diameter of 15.5 ± 3.5 μm. Pre vious studies on the starch grains of modern plants, such as foxtail millet (Setaria italica), broomcorn millet (Panicum miliaceum), and Panicum bisulcatum (Yang et al., 2012b), have shown that Type I-1 starch grains have the morphological characteristics of millet starch grains. The common occurrence of both carbonised foxtail millet and broomcorn millet in the Haidai region during the Longshan period (An et al., 2021) indicated that Type I-1 starch grains were from foxtail millet and broomcorn millet. (2) Type I-2 starch grains. This type included 29 starch grains with polyhedral or spheroidal shape, centric hilum, and no lamellae. Most of them had deep stellate fissures with dense lines radiating towards the periphery (Fig. 3(e) and (f)). The lengths of type I-2 grains ranged from 12.3 to 24.0 μm, with an average diameter of 17.4 ± 3.1 μm. According to a crop harvesting simulation study (Yang et al., 2014), foxtail mil

3.1.2. Type II starch grains A total of thirteen starch grains were classified as Type II. The common features of Type II starch grains included their polyhedral structures, closed centric hilum, absence of lamellae, and X-shaped extinction crosses (Fig. 3(i) and (j)). These grains were smaller, measuring 4.3–9.0 μm, with an average diameter of 6.6 ± 1.3 μm. Ac cording to Wei et al.’s (2008) investigation of modern rice starch grains and Yao et al.’s (2016) description of the morphological characteristics of modern rice starch grains, Type II starch grains likely originated from the genus Oryza.

12.2 to 18.2 μm, with an average diameter of 14.8 ± 1.6 μm (Fig. 3(k) and (l)). Modern reference collections show that the hilum of a starch grain from roots and tubers is typically extremely eccentric (Wan et al., 2011). Accordingly, Type III starch grains were determined to be from roots and tubers. As only a small number of these starch grains were identified, we could not determine the species or genus from which they originated.

3.1.4. Type IV starch grains Five starch grains were classified as Type IV, which had a biconvex shape, centric hilum, and indistinct lamellae (Fig. 3(m) and (n)). The starch grains were olivary and had a longitudinal dent when rotated, measuring 13.8–23.0 μm, with an average diameter of 19.8 ± 3.9 μm. Type IV starch grains had similar characteristics to the starch grains of the tribe Triticeae. Furthermore, the criteria proposed by Piperno et al. (2004) and Yang and Perry (2013) to identify the starch grains of the tribe Triticeae showed that Type IV starch grains were highly similar to the starch grains of the genus Hordeum.

body_evidence.quote: We found starch granules on all sampled stone tools except GS 1, the grinding slab from Phase I. Among the 972 recovered starch granules (Table 2 and Fig. 3; Fig. 4 shows modern starches in our reference), 788 starch granules show identifiable features consistent with our modern plant references, classified into 9 types (detailed in Section 3.1.2). Since we found no starch granules on GS 1, we excluded it from the following discussion. Three noticeable patterns emerge from the starch result. First, Pan icoideae starch granules, likely from broomcorn (Panicum milliaecum) or foxtail (Setaria italica) millets, are present on all stone tools. And they account for a significant portion (30 %) of the overall count. This result is consistent with the macrobotanical record that millet agriculture progressed during Phase II. Second, wild plant resources, especially various kinds of underground storage organs (USOs), are ubiquitous in Phase II. Despite their small quantity, yam (Dioscorea sp.), snakegourd (Trichosanthes kirilowii) root, lily (Lilium sp.) bulb, and lotus (Nelumbo nucifera) root are identified on multiple sampled tools. Their presence suggests that wild plants were still part of the diet when millet agri culture developed. Third, 276 granules (28 % of the total) are incom plete or fractured, which are characteristics of damage. They resemble starch granules after grinding, as shown in previous studies (Babot, 2003). Therefore, the eight stone tools could all be used in grinding activities.

body_evidence.quote: 2.1.1. Phytoliths in pottery residues. In total, 4248 phytoliths were recovered from residues on 11 out of 12 sherds, except for the cooking vessel (POT). Of these phytoliths, 2704 (63.7% of the total) were classified into seven taxonomic types. The majority of phytoliths in the residues are spheroid ornate, constituting a percentage of 53.8% with a ubiquity of 91.7%. In particular, fermentation vessels and serving vessels generally exhibit a higher percentage of spheroid ornate phytolith compared to the large basins and cooking pot, reaching up to 100% and 93.8% in JAR3 and JAR5, respectively. The second phytolith type, derived from rice husks (3.7%), was present in nearly half of the pottery residue samples (ubiquity of 41.7%), but in minor proportions (0.2 to 2.10%) across most samples, except for JAR7 (33.5%) and BWL (23.1%), which were used specifically for fermentation and serving. Bulliform phytoliths from rice leaves have a relatively high ubiquity of 41.7% but are present in low quantities (0.3%). The mean percentage of rice bulliforms with ≥9 fish-scale facets in the CUP, JAR6, and JAR2 is 45.5% (56 out of 123) (Fig. 3 and SI Appendix, Table S2; bulliform identification method, SI Appendix). 2.1.2. Phytoliths in pottery clay. In total, 4672 phytoliths were recovered from pottery clay, with 1309 (28.0%) identifiable into specific taxonomic categories. The most prevalent phytolith types are those from Panicoideae, constituting a percentage of 7.8%, with ubiquity of 75.0%, followed by rice husk (6.7% in percentage), common bulliform (6.4%), woody (2.0%), and Pooideae

counts, measurements, and morphological features are docu mented in SI Appendix, Tables S3 and S4 . Type I rice starches (Oryza sp.) were present in all 12 vessels, typically appearing in a compound form comprising multiple small granules, with some isolated single granules. A total of 436 rice compounds and single granules were recorded, and 812 granules were measured for size. Most individual granules exhibited blurry birefringence without an extinction cross, although a few displayed a clear extinction cross, indicative of fermented rice ( Fig. 4 :1-4, compared with SI Appendix, Fig. S2 :1-4). The quantity of Type I starch is calculated from rice compounds and isolated individual granules, resulting in the highest count of all starch Types (41.0% of the total), with 100% ubiquity through the assemblage. Type II Job’s tears starches (Coix lacryma-jobi ) were identified in eight vessels (n = 59; 5.6% of the total; 66.7% ubiquity). The size range and starch morphologies of Type II starches align with Job’s tears ( Fig. 4 :5, compared with SI Appendix, Fig. S2 :5 and ﻿SI Appendix, Fig. S3 ). Type III Panicoideae starches were present in 11 vessels (n = 28; 2.6% of the total; 91.7% ubiquity). These granules, resembling barnyard grass (Echinochloa sp.), are small, circular, or polygonal, particularly consistent with Echinochloa colona in shape and size range ( Fig. 4 :6, compared with SI Appendix, Fig. S2 :6 and

﻿SI Appendix, Fig. S3 ). However, some Type III starches may poten tially be small Job’s tears granules, similar to barnyard grass in form. E. colona , a weed found in damp places, is widely distributed in warm regions throughout China ( 32 :515-518). Type IV, Triticeae wild grass starches were found in six vessels (n = 10; 0.9% of the total; 50.0% ubiquity), with some displaying enzymatic digestion ( Fig. 4 :7; compared with SI Appendix, Fig. S2 :7). Type V acorn starches, identified in 10 vessels (Fagaceae; n = 111; 10.4% of the total; 83.3% ubiquity), exhibit diverse forms and sizes comparable to various acorn species in our reference database, includ ing Cyclobalanopsis fleuryi , Lithocarpus brevicaudatus , Lithocarpus glaber , and Quercus fabri ( Fig. 4 :8-11, compared with SI Appendix, Fig. S2 :8-11 and SI Appendix, Fig. S3 ). These oak species are prev alent in southern China, including Zhejiang ( 33 ). Most starches (n = 927; 87.2% of the total) exhibit various forms of damage, classified into two categories. 1) Damage attrib uted to enzymatic digestion (n = 596; 56.1% of the total), show ing random pitting, deep channels, broken edges, central depression, and lacking extinction cross, but remaining weakly birefringent ( Fig. 4 :3,6,7,10). Such altered forms can result from various factors, including fermentation. Our experiment indicates that during the brewing process, most rice granules become blurry or disappear, and only a few remain recognizable (SI Appendix, Fig. S2 :1-4). 2) Gelatinization due to high-heat cooking (steam ing or boiling; n = 331; 31.1% of the total), characterized by evenly expanded surfaces, with starch grains tending to fuse into large masses ( Fig. 4 :13). Additionally, some starches (n = 414; 38.9% of the total) that are too damaged or gelatinized, or too lacking in any diagnostic features, are classified as unidentifiable (UNID) and gelatinized mass (SI Appendix, Table S3 ). When the trypan blue staining method was applied to subsam ples, more gelatinized starches were identified, while some dis played recognizable granules, resembling those found in rice-compound granules ( Fig. 4 :14,15). These alterations align with our reference database (SI Appendix, Fig. S2 :15,16), as well as with samples from other experimental fermentation and cook ing ( 27 , 30 , 31 ). body_evidence.quote: Regardless of the brewing method, yeast is essential for converting sugars into alcohol; its presence is therefore a key indicator of alcoholic fermentation. Yeast cells can survive and be preserved in the residues of fermented beverages, and their morphology can be directly examined under a light microscope. Traditional brewing utilizes various yeast species, with Saccharomyces cerevisiae being the most common. These cells are typically round to oval, measuring approximately 5–10 μm in length. Yeast primarily reproduces by budding, whereby a small protrusion develops on the cell surface, enlarges to the size of a mature cell, and then separates from the parent to form an independent cell [32,33] (pp. 143–149) (Figure 2(A1)). Our brewing experiments show that yeast cells typically retain a clearly defined cell wall, and although some internal organelles may still be visible, they cannot be readily identified. The presence of cells in the budding stage is the most reliable criterion for identifying yeast; however, these are infrequently preserved in archaeological residues. Accordingly, the observation of round or oval cells—particularly when two or more remain connected—provides strong evidence for yeast. We also observed that, after fermentation is complete, yeast cells often occur in clusters (Figure 2(A2,A3)).

A total of 66 yeast cells were identified, representing two morphological types: spher- ical or oval forms (N = 56; 4.22–11.5 μm in length) and elongated oval forms (N = 10; 7.48–12.68 μm in length) (Table 1). The cells occur either as single units or in clusters. Several exhibit budding characteristics, indicated by small protrusions emerging from the parent cell or by pairs of cells remaining connected, suggesting an active stage of reproduction comparable to modern reference examples (Figure 2(4–9); cf. 2 and 3).

Type I (sorghum, Sorghum sp.): A total of 46 examples were identified, round or polygonal in shape, measuring 4.79–25.07 μm in length. Some appeared singly, while others were found in compound clusters. Most exhibited damage, such as deep fissures, central voids, blurred extinction cross, and mild gelatinization, consistent with fermentation- related enzymatic activity (Figure 3(1,2,6,9); cf. Figure 4(1–3)). Type I starch morphologies broadly resemble those of several species under Panicoideae subfamily, such as foxtail millet (Setaria italica), broomcorn millet, maize, and sorghum. However, maize and millets can be excluded: maize was not introduced to China until the 16th century [37], and millet starch granules are considerably smaller than the size range observed in Type I. In our reference database, broomcorn millet starches measure 4.81–10.86 μm; and foxtail millet starches measure 4.04–16.85 μm. By contrast, Type I starches most closely match modern sorghum in both morphology and size range of 5.90–26.81 μm (Table 2). This identification is further supported by the detection of sorghum components in the aforementioned mass spectrometry analysis.

• Type II: More than 20 granules from XLZ-7 and XLZ-13 belong to this type (Figure 5D–F). They are polygonal or near-circular, with a centric hilum and frequent fissures, and a size range of 8.03–21.18 μm. They likely belong to the Panicoideae family, such as foxtail millet (Setaria italica) and broomcorn millet (Panicum miliaceum), as well as pos- sibly smaller granules from Job's tears (Coix lacryma-jobi L.) (Liu, Ma, and Cui 2014; Yang et al. 2012).

• Type III: One granule from XLZ-13 belongs to this type (Figure 5H). It has a near-circular shape, a centric hilum, and pressure depressions, and measures 20.09–23.6 μm. These characteristics suggest it is likely from the Triticeae tribe, such as the genus Agropyron and Elymus (Yang and Perry 2013).

body_evidence.quote: These food legumes starch granule retrieved from 12 artifacts of 6 archaeological sites are showed in Fig. 4, which can be divided to two sub-groups. Type A, contained 43 elliptic starch granules usually with longitudinal fissure and clear-cut lamellae. The range of length was 23.09–47.21 μm, and the mean length of these starch granules is 30.07 μm. Type B, contained 13 round starch grains usually with radiating fissure and inconspicuous lamellae. The range of length was 15.84–22.19 μm, and the mean length of these starch granules is 20.59 μm. The length of all ancient starch granules ranged from 15.84 to 47.21 μm, with a mean value of 27.87 μm and a standard deviation of 6.25 μm.

Although precise taxonomic identification of the extracted ancient starch granules at the species level remains challenging, comparative analysis was conducted by examining granule size distributions of modern food legume starches from different genera or taxa sharing geographic origins. Modern starch data from 18 food legume species were categorized into four groups: Group 1: Genus Phaseolus; Group 2: Genus Pisum and Genus Vicia; Group 3: Genus Vigna; Group 4: Seven remaining legume species. Kernel density estimation (KDE) analysis of modern and ancient starch granule length data is presented in Fig. 5. Among modern samples, Group 1 and Group 2 exhibit similar KDE profiles, both peaking near 30 μm. Groups 3 and 4 show comparable distribution patterns, though Group 4 displays a higher frequency of larger granules. The ancient starch granules were classified as Type I and Type II based primarily on granule size thresholds, a distinction re flected in their KDE distributions. Modern reference data demonstrate that starch granules from a single legume species typically exhibit bimodal size distributions, collectively forming a complete starch assemblage (Wang et al., 2013). Consequently, combining Type I and Type II reveals that the merged KDE profile (Type I + II) aligns most closely with Group 3.

body_evidence.quote: A total of 116 phytoliths were identified in 24 pottery vessels, with counts ranging from 1 to 17 per vessel and an average of 5 phytoliths per vessel. No phytoliths were found in 18 vessels (Supplementary mate rial). The recovered morphotypes are primarily associated with Poaceae family and include bilobate, polylobate, cross, rondel, bulliform, and elongate forms, with one—an opaque perforated platelet possibly derived from the Asteraceae family (Fig. 6). body_evidence.quote: Laboratory observations and identification were carried out using an Olympus BM53 light microscope equipped with a polarizing optic. Photographs and measurements were taken using the Olympus DP74 imaging system. To facilitate taxonomic comparisons, we collected starch grains from modern common edible plants (Fig. 4). We also reviewed published data on modern starch grains (Yang et al., 2009, 2010; Ge et al., 2010; Ge, 2010; Wan et al., 2011; Yang and Perry, 2013; Liu et al., 2014; Wan et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022b). The identification and classification of phytoliths referred to the standards established by Wang and Lu (1993), and were compared with the rele vant published data (Lu et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2018; Ge et al., 2020; Wang and Lu, 2022).

2018: Fig. 3. m-n; Fig. 4. m-r). Based on our observations of starch grains from commonly encountered modern USOs, this particular subtype closely resembles the bell-shaped grains observed in several USO spe cies, such as Trichosanthes kirilowii (Fig. 4h, h’), Pseudostellaria hetero phylla (Fig. 4i, i’), and Fallopia multiflora, among others.

Type A (n = 464): This type was characterized by a polyhedral or rounded polyhedron shape, as well as semicircular form with rounded edges in three-dimensional shape. They were identified within the subfamily Panicoideae based on modern starch morphology and repre sent the most abundant type. The identifiable ones were categorized into sub-types AI and AII.

Type AII (n = 105): This sub-type included subcircular, rounded polygonal, rounded rectangular and rounded semicircular shapes, with usually rounded contours. Hila were centered or slightly eccentric and visible. Fissures were radial, Y-shaped, linear-shaped and star-shaped. The birefringence crosses were vertical or X-shaped, with nearly all of them featuring Z-shaped arms. The size range was 13.15~29.88 μm, and the average size was 20.25 ± 3.74 μm (Fig. 5b, b’). The aforemen tioned characteristics are predominantly found in Job’s tears (Coix lacryma-jobi), although it cannot be entirely ruled out that they may also appear in foxtail millet (Setaria italica) (Yang et al., 2010; Ge et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2014). According to the two-step identification method pro posed by Liu et al. (2014), three preliminary identification standards are effective for singling out the most readily diagnosed grains of job’s tears from those of millets, including (1) being larger than 21.17 μm in size, (2) having an eccentricity ratio greater than 1.47, and (3) having a Z- shaped arm on the extinction cross for grains >12.8 μm. Type AII starch grains comply with at least one of these three identification standards (see Fig.S2). Taking all factors above into consideration, starch grains of type II were classified as job’s tears.

body_evidence.quote: Type AII (n = 105): This sub-type included subcircular, rounded polygonal, rounded rectangular and rounded semicircular shapes, with usually rounded contours. Hila were centered or slightly eccentric and visible. Fissures were radial, Y-shaped, linear-shaped and star-shaped. The birefringence crosses were vertical or X-shaped, with nearly all of them featuring Z-shaped arms. The size range was 13.15~29.88 μm, and the average size was 20.25 ± 3.74 μm (Fig. 5b, b’). The aforemen tioned characteristics are predominantly found in Job’s tears (Coix lacryma-jobi), although it cannot be entirely ruled out that they may also appear in foxtail millet (Setaria italica) (Yang et al., 2010; Ge et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2014). According to the two-step identification method pro posed by Liu et al. (2014), three preliminary identification standards are effective for singling out the most readily diagnosed grains of job’s tears from those of millets, including (1) being larger than 21.17 μm in size, (2) having an eccentricity ratio greater than 1.47, and (3) having a Z- shaped arm on the extinction cross for grains >12.8 μm. Type AII starch grains comply with at least one of these three identification standards (see Fig.S2). Taking all factors above into consideration, starch grains of type II were classified as job’s tears.

Type C: Starch grains of this type were polyhedral or round poly hedral in shape with the centric hila closed, and they were common for the multigrain aggregation form. Nearly every starch grain classified as Type C displayed an extinction cross when observed under polarized light, devoid of any discernible fissures or lamellae, and measured approximately 5 to 7 μm in length. These starch grains were identified as originating from rice (Yang and Perry, 2013; Ge, 2010). These starch grains were exclusively observed in the M72S male’s dental calculus and the M91:25 small jar with lid (Fig. 3). A substantial quantity of type C starch grains adhered to the M72S male’s dental calculus (Fig. 5e, e’, f, f’; Fig.S3a–c’). Due to their abundance and adhesive complexity, which made accurate quantification impractical, they will be treated as a single unit for analytical simplicity. A single starch grain of this type was identified within the M91:25 small jar with a lid. body_evidence.quote: Type A (n = 464): This type was characterized by a polyhedral or rounded polyhedron shape, as well as semicircular form with rounded edges in three-dimensional shape. They were identified within the subfamily Panicoideae based on modern starch morphology and repre sent the most abundant type. The identifiable ones were categorized into sub-types AI and AII.

Type AII (n = 105): This sub-type included subcircular, rounded polygonal, rounded rectangular and rounded semicircular shapes, with usually rounded contours. Hila were centered or slightly eccentric and visible. Fissures were radial, Y-shaped, linear-shaped and star-shaped. The birefringence crosses were vertical or X-shaped, with nearly all of them featuring Z-shaped arms. The size range was 13.15~29.88 μm, and the average size was 20.25 ± 3.74 μm (Fig. 5b, b’). The aforemen tioned characteristics are predominantly found in Job’s tears (Coix lacryma-jobi), although it cannot be entirely ruled out that they may also appear in foxtail millet (Setaria italica) (Yang et al., 2010; Ge et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2014). According to the two-step identification method pro posed by Liu et al. (2014), three preliminary identification standards are effective for singling out the most readily diagnosed grains of job’s tears from those of millets, including (1) being larger than 21.17 μm in size, (2) having an eccentricity ratio greater than 1.47, and (3) having a Z- shaped arm on the extinction cross for grains >12.8 μm. Type AII starch grains comply with at least one of these three identification standards (see Fig.S2). Taking all factors above into consideration, starch grains of type II were classified as job’s tears.

Type B (n = 67): Starch grains were circular or lenticular, featuring centrally located hilum. Fissures were often absent, while lamellae were present occasionally. The extinction cross exhibited X-shaped and vague

Type C: Starch grains of this type were polyhedral or round poly hedral in shape with the centric hila closed, and they were common for the multigrain aggregation form. Nearly every starch grain classified as Type C displayed an extinction cross when observed under polarized light, devoid of any discernible fissures or lamellae, and measured approximately 5 to 7 μm in length. These starch grains were identified as originating from rice (Yang and Perry, 2013; Ge, 2010). These starch grains were exclusively observed in the M72S male’s dental calculus and the M91:25 small jar with lid (Fig. 3). A substantial quantity of type C starch grains adhered to the M72S male’s dental calculus (Fig. 5e, e’, f, f’; Fig.S3a–c’). Due to their abundance and adhesive complexity, which made accurate quantification impractical, they will be treated as a single unit for analytical simplicity. A single starch grain of this type was identified within the M91:25 small jar with a lid. Given its distinctive polyhedral morphology, characterized by well-defined and sharp edges and corners, along with its minute size of 5.7 μm, we deduced that it originated from rice (Fig.S3, d and d’).

body_evidence.quote: damage requires support from contextual archeological information, a representative number of samples, and complementary lines of evidence29. Previous brewing simulation studies have demonstrated that saccharification and fermentation tend to leave morphological changes on starch grains, including small pits and cracks, missing edges, hazy extinction crosses, enlarged fissures, expansion of the central depression, and ring-shaped structures17,30,31. These damage types are typical of brewing and distinguishable in a well-documented context. To further strengthen our interpretations, we compared the archeological starch grains with modern reference collections obtained through our brewing experiments (Fig. 4). In addition, the analysis of biomolecules preserved in archeological artifacts, using chromatographic and mass spectrometric techniques, is a powerful but controversial approach32. It is now widely accepted that the identification of ancient alcoholic beverages through organic residue analysis can be strengthened by archaeobotanical evi- dence and archeological context33–35. Moreover, residual evidence of fungi and husk phytoliths may indicate brewing and filtration techniques17,31. Based on this framework, our study integrates archaeobotanical analysis with organic residue analysis to investigate alcohol-related practices at the Shuanghuaishu site. What is more, previous studies have identified the ingredients of Neolithic alcoholic beverages in China as cereals (such as millets, rice, Triticeae, and Job’s tears), tubers, fruits, and honey8,36.
