body_evidence.quote: Results Starch grains A total of 244 starch grains were extracted from 13 of the 28 samples, and no starch grains were discovered in the other 15 samples or any of the control samples, suggesting that the analysis was not contaminated and that the 244 grains could be interpreted as valid data. Of the 244 starch grains analyzed, 77 grains were unidentified (UNID) due to damage or lack of typical characteristics. The remaining 167 starch grains, identified through comparison with modern reference materials (Fig. 5), were derived from five plant types and underground storage organs (USOs) (Fig. 6, Table 4). These include Panicoideae (include foxtail millet, common millet, and Job’s tears Coix lacryma-jobi L.), rice, Triticeae, legume (include Vigna and other legumes), snake gourd root (Trichosanthes kirilowii), and other USOs. body_evidence.quote: Starch granule identification Starch granules of different plants are characterized by their overall shape, type, size, position, form of the hilum, fissure, presence or absence of lamellae, and the appearance and projection of Maltese crosses under a polarized microscope31–33. Therefore, the comprehensive morphological characteristics of starch granules can serve as an important basis for their identification. The morphological data of modern starch granules form the basis for the analysis of ancient starch granules. To identify ancient starch granules extracted from the calculus, we referred to over 40 species from 18 genera of modern plants (Fig. 3). In addition to comparative plant samples collected by the authors, many studies about starch granule morphology of modern plants are also consulted to any further identification34–46.

Results In total, 151 starch granules were recovered from 45 dental calculus samples (Table 2). Sixty-six starch granules could not be identified owing to severe damage or diagnostic features. The remaining 85 starch granules were classified into seven types based on the above-mentioned reliable diagnostic attributes (Fig. 4). Type 1 starch granules (N = 2) are polygonal with acute angles. They are small, ranging from 4.2 μm to 5.45 μm and the average size is approximately 4.82 ± 0.73 μm. The hilum is centered without fissures or lamellae. The extinction cross is faint with an “X” shape. The two starch granules are single in the free state (Fig. 4a-a’). Although most of starch granules from rice are always aggregated47,48, processing activities can dis- perse them and these grains are able to become single.Meantime,compared with modernreference materials (Fig. 3) and research byYangetal. 49on the morphological description of rice starch granules from the Kuahuqiao site, the features of Type 1 starch grains accord with those of rice (Oryza sativa).

Considering that charred rice remains were found at the Jiangzhuang site, these starch granules are probably from rice (Oryza sativa). Type 2 starch granules (N = 9) are polygonal with a centric hilum. Their size range is from 5.7 μm to 14.3 μm, and the average size is 9.66 ± 0.54 μm. They have smooth surfaces without any lamellae. Some of the larger starch granules have “Y” or horizontal linear fissures across the hilum with a plane view. The extinction arm is clear and vertical with an “+” shape (Fig. 4b-b’). Compared with reference collections in our laboratory and published works36,37 (Fig. 3), these polygonal granules are often found in the family Poaceae, including foxtail millet (Setaria italica), commonmillet(Panicummiliaceum),rice (Oryzasativa),Job'stears (Coix lacryma-jobi),sorghum(Sorghumbicolor),andoats(Avenasativa).Starch granules from rice and oats are smaller than type 2 (Fig. 3); Job's tears starch granules always have a “Z” shaped arm on the extinction cross, particularly on larger granules38 (Fig. 3); the starch granules of sorghum are bigger with distinct lamellae (Fig. 3). The surface of Type 2 starch granules is relatively smooth with clear and vertical extinction cross, and the average size is 9.66 μm, both indicating that the Type 2 starch granules were not from rice, oat, sorghum, and Job's tears; they are likely from foxtail millet or common millet. The size of foxtail millet is 6.23–19.35 μm with an average size of 9.32 μm, and the larger granules have fissures across the hilum (Fig. 3). The hilum is centric or slightly eccentric with “-” or “Y” shape fissure. Lamellae are not evident. Under the polarized light, the extinction arm is vertical with a “Z” bent shape at the end. Some starch granules were encapsulated by calculus (Fig. 4c-c’). As mentioned above, Job's tears starch granules always have a “Z” shaped arm on the extinction cross, particularly on larger granules38 (Fig. 3). These characteristics of type 3 starch granules accord with those of Coix sp and they are probably from Coix sp. Type 4 starch granules (N = 36) are oval or nearly round in shape, with sizes ranging from 9.75–33.84 μm. The average size is 17.91 ± 1.10 μm. Ancient starch granules analysis reveals that Job's tears were an important plant food resource in the Yangtze, Yellow, Liao, Jianghuai, and Huanghuai regions during the early and Middle Holocene59–61. body_evidence.quote: Our analysis identified three types of microfossils—starch gran- ules, phytoliths, and parasite eggs—with their quantities varying across samples. Control sediment samples contained only mineral crystals, fungal spores, and pollen, suggesting minimal postdep- ositional or curation-related contamination. Detailed counts and descriptions are provided in the SI Text and SI Appendix, Tables S2 and S3 . Given that microfossils are more reliable for assessing group-level dietary patterns rather than individual diets ( 36 ), the following discussion integrates data from all specimens while con- sidering site-level differences. A total of 240 starch granules were recovered, of which 165 were taxonomically identifiable using our reference data ( Fig. 2 and SI Appendix, Text and Fig. S1 ). The identified starch types include acorns (Quercus sp., Lithocarpus sp., and Cyclobalanopsis sp.; N = 99; Fig. 2 : 1 to 3), rice [Oryza sp.; N = 15 (compound count); >82 individual granules; Fig. 2 : 4], Triticeae grasses

(N = 17; Fig. 2 : 5), Paniceae grasses (N = 10; Fig. 2 : 6), yam (Dioscorea sp.; N = 6; Fig. 2 : 7), and unidentified underground storage organs (USOs; N = 18; Fig. 2 : 8). At both sites, acorn starches are the most abundant, followed by unidentified USOs, indicating a strong reliance on wild plant resources. This pattern aligns with macrobotanical and palynological data, which show a dominance of acorns and Quercus pollen ( 33 , 34 ). Paniceae starches are present exclusively in specimens from Jingtoushan, while Dioscorea starches are limited to Kuahuqiao specimens. Notably, gelatinized starch granules were recovered at both sites, indicating the consumption of cooked plant foods (N = 43). These granules exhibit distinctive morphological changes, including swelling, distortion, and loss of the extinction cross under polarized light ( Fig. 2 : 9 to 11), consistent with heat-induced modifications such as boiling or steaming ( 37 – 39 ). Although gelatinization can obscure taxonomic identification, these granules likely derive from noncompound starches, including acorn, USOs, and Triticeae grasses. A greater proportion of Kuahuqiao suids (10 of 12) than Jingtoushan suids (8 of 20) consumed human-prepared foods, as indicated by the presence of gelatinized starches. A total of 117 phytoliths were identified, corroborating both starch and environmental data (SI Appendix, Table S3 ). body_evidence.quote: Type A: Rice starch grains (n=8; size range: 5.1–11.6 μm). The grains exhibited polygonal shape, centric hila. Their surfaces were smooth without lamellas; no cracks were observed. The extinction arm was X- shaped under orthogonal polarization with sharp angles. Combined with Yang Xiaoyan’s discussion on the single rice starch granule from the Kuahuqiao site (Yang and Jiang, 2010), we concluded that the A-type starch granules were from rice (Fig. 3a)

Type B: Job’s tears starch grains (n=26; size range: 13.3–24.9 μm). Most starch grains exhibited nearly circular polyhedral morphologies with smooth surfaces lacking lamellae, and the hila were located at or near the centers. Some grains displayed “-”, Y-shaped, or radial cracks at the hilum. Extinction arms were vertically oriented under orthogonal polarization, and some exhibited Z-shaped bending at the end of the extinction arm. According to modern reference samples, starch grains of gramineous plants (e.g., Setaria italica, Panicum miliaceum, and Coix lacryma-jobi) are generally polyhedral, and the extinction arms are vertical. However, the particle sizes of Setaria italica and Panicum mil iaceum are generally smaller, averaging 7.6 ± 1.4 μm and 9.2 ± 2.8 μm, respectively (Ge et al., 2010). In contrast, the Job’s tears starch grains have larger maximum and average particle sizes, and their extinction arms were mostly Z-shaped (Liu et al., 2014a). Based on this, we iden tified Job’s tears as the source of the Type B starch grains (Fig. 3b).

Type C: Millet starch grains (n=16; size range: 15.1–25.1 μm). The starch grains exhibitedpolyhedral structureswith centrally located hila, and some hila were depressed. There were “-”-shaped, T-shaped, Y- shaped, or radial cracks at the hilum. Compared with modern reference samples, the collected grains’ morphological characteristics were similar to those of gramineous starch grains (Yang et al. (2010b). Analysis of Setaria italica, Panicum miliaceum, and their wild relatives revealed that Type C starch grains extracted from the samples lacked diagnostic specificity, precluding further taxonomic classification. Based on the above analysis, we concluded that Type C starch grains originated from millet (Fig. 3c).

Type D: Triticeae starch grains (n=24; size range: 11.3–30.1 μm). The frontal projection appears round or oval, while the side projection is thin and long, and nearly olive-shaped. The hilum is located at or near the center. There is no cracks at the hilum. The extinction arms are either vertical or X-shaped under orthogonal polarization, exhibiting diffuse extinction. Some larger starch grains have clear lamellae (Fig. 3d). smaller granules are nearly circular or polygonal with a centered hilum, and there is no cracks at the hilum (Fig. 3e). body_evidence.quote: After the observation under the microscope, a large number of starch grains with fermentation damage characteristics were found. According to current literatures, these damaged starch grains were likely related to alcoholic beverages making (Liao et al., 2022a; Liu et al., 2021b). In this case, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis was conducted to verify whether human at the site had already engaged in wine-brewing activities. For LC-MS analysis, ten common organic acids in fermented drinks were selected as detection targets including lactic, acetic, butyric, succinic, tartaric, pyruvic, fumaric, malic, citric, and oxalic acid (Gong, 2023). During the experiment, standard reagents were also tested with the same procedure to ensure all tests were not contaminated in the laboratory. The specific organic acid reagent used were as follows: L-lactic acid (85 %, AR), glacial acetic acid (99 %, AR), butyric acid (99 %, AR), succinic acid (99 %, AR), tartaric acid (L (+) -tartaric acid, 99 %, AR), pyruvic acid (98 %, AR); fumaric acid (99 %, AR); DL-malic acid (99 %, AR); citric acid (99 %, AR) acid (99 %, AR). The tartaric acid was produced by Shanghai McLin Biochemical Tech nology Co., Ltd., the DL-malic acid was produced by Tianjin Fuchen Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd., and all remaining organic acid reagents were produced by the State Pharmaceutical Group Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.

However, the particle sizes of Setaria italica and Panicum mil iaceum are generally smaller, averaging 7.6 ± 1.4 μm and 9.2 ± 2.8 μm, respectively (Ge et al., 2010). In contrast, the Job’s tears starch grains have larger maximum and average particle sizes, and their extinction arms were mostly Z-shaped (Liu et al., 2014a). Based on this, we iden tified Job’s tears as the source of the Type B starch grains (Fig. 3b).

Type C: Millet starch grains (n=16; size range: 15.1–25.1 μm). The starch grains exhibitedpolyhedral structureswith centrally located hila, and some hila were depressed. There were “-”-shaped, T-shaped, Y- shaped, or radial cracks at the hilum. Compared with modern reference samples, the collected grains’ morphological characteristics were similar to those of gramineous starch grains (Yang et al. (2010b). Analysis of Setaria italica, Panicum miliaceum, and their wild relatives revealed that Type C starch grains extracted from the samples lacked diagnostic specificity, precluding further taxonomic classification. Based on the above analysis, we concluded that Type C starch grains originated from millet (Fig. 3c).

body_evidence.quote: whether these four potteries are related to fermented drinks was not discussed in this paper. Notably, multiple organic acids were detected from the other six potteries. Among them, acetic and butyric are com mon in various fermented beverages, and they originate from different organic substances through acetic acid bacteria’s fermentation (BARATA et al., 2012). Tartaric acid is an iconic organic acid existing widely in grain or fruit wine (Ding and Xia, 2014), and malic acid is very common in fermented drinks except distilled liquor (Li, 2017b). Com bined with the result of starch grain analysis, it can be concluded that five pottery Jiandiping (Sample 1: 2022LCT32175; Sample 3: 2022LCT2917H1595; Sample 4: 2022LCTG2H1620; Sample 5: 2022LCTG23; Sample 7: 2022LCT32164) should to be related to alcoholic beverages. For sample 10 (pottery cup: 2022LCT2917H1595), it is difficult to determine whether the organic acid residues came from alcoholic beverage because only malic acid was found in the cup apart from acetic and butyric. In addition, in the starch grain analysis on two potteries (one is Jiandiping numbered 2019LCT15305, the other is a large-mouth round bottom jar numbered 2019LCT2119H599) which were both unearthed at Chengyan site in 2019, 164 starch grains with fermented damage characteristics were observed (Wang et al., 2017a) (Fig. 8), and these damage features included disappearance of partial edge (Fig. 8a), small pits on the surface (Fig. 8b), blurred cross extinc tion arm (Fig. 8c), recessed hilum (Fig. 8a and b), and ring-shaped rim (Fig. 8d,e,f) (Liao et al., 202

After the observation under the microscope, a large number of starch grains with fermentation damage characteristics were found. According to current literatures, these damaged starch grains were likely related to alcoholic beverages making (Liao et al., 2022a; Liu et al., 2021b). In this case, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis was conducted to verify whether human at the site had already engaged in wine-brewing activities. For LC-MS analysis, ten common organic acids in fermented drinks were selected as detection targets including lactic, acetic, butyric, succinic, tartaric, pyruvic, fumaric, malic, citric, and oxalic acid (Gong, 2023). body_evidence.quote: Type I rice (Oryza sp.) starches are present in all ten samples and represent the most abundant category (39.1%; 100% ubiquity). They occur mainly as compound aggregates of small polygonal granules (n = 110 measured; 2.99–7.06 μm), with some isolated granules. A total of 188 rice starches were recorded. Many display blurred birefringence and lack extinction crosses, consistent with experimentally fermented rice (Fig. 4: 1–3, 15; cf. Fig. 3: 1–3; Table 1).

Type II Paniceae starches occur in four samples (n = 15; 3.1%; 40% ubiquity). These granules are polygonal (6.05–16.3 μm), centric hila, and mostly exhibit enzymatic damage characterized by hollowed cen ters with relatively well-preserved peripheries (Fig. 4:4,5; Table 1).

millet produce predominantly polyhedral starch granules with occa sional spherical forms, but they exhibit different size ranges, with foxtail millet generally larger (5.29–21.17 μm) than broomcorn millet (3.03–12.34 μm) (Liu et al., 2014: Table 1). The Xiying Type II starches fall within the reported shape and size ranges of millet starches (Fig. 3:4,5; cf. Fig. 4:4,5). Type III Triticeae starches are rare (n = 3; 0.6%; 30% ubiquity) and occur in three samples. These lenticular granules (24.01–40.59 μm) all exhibit enzymatic damage (Fig. 4: 6; cf. Fig. 3: 8; Table 1), suggesting processing prior to deposition. Taxonomic resolution finer than the tribe level is not possible.

body_evidence.quote: A total of five starch granules were identified in the sealed chicken drumstick shaped vase (Figure 5a–e). Based on their morphological characteristics, these granules were classified into four distinct types. Type 1 (n = 2) exhibited a smooth sur- face, polygonal to nearly circular shape, prominent extinction arms in a near-vertical orientation, and a central navel with a straight crack, with an average particle size of 22.58 μm. Type 2 (n = 1) was characterized by a polyhedral shape, concave navel, no visible layering, and perpendicular extinction arms, with a particle size of 21.20 μm. Type 3 (n = 1) was nearly circular with a lens-shaped side, no central navel cracks, visible layered pat- terns, and “X”-shaped dispersed extinction arms, with a particle size of 18.45 μm. Type 4 (n = 1) had a polyhedral shape, closed navel, sharp contact surfaces, no obvious cracks or layers, and “X”-shaped extinction arms under polarized light, with a parti- cle size of 8.23 μm (Appendix S9). Comparative analysis of mor- phology, grain size, and existing studies suggests that these four types of starch originate from Trib. Paniceae (n = 2), foxtail mil- let (Setaria italic) (n = 1), Triticeae (n = 1), and rice (Oryza sativa) (n = 1), respectively (Ge et al. 2010; Yang et al. 2016; Yang and Perry 2013).

A total of 211 phytoliths are identified across 12 distinct mor- photypes within 100 fields of view, including Ω-type from in- florescence bracts of foxtail millet, OPAQUE PERFORATED PLATELETS from Asteraceae, BULLIFORM FLABELLATE, SMOOTH-ELONGATE, ELONGATE-ECHINATE, ACICULAR, BILOBATE, SHORT SADDLE, RONDEL, WAVY TRAPEZOID, and other epidermal cells. Among these, the calculable con- centrations were 6.79 grains/mL for Ω-shaped and 413.96 grains/mL for OPAQUE PERFORATED PLATELETS from Asteraceae. Additionally, 145 round cleistothecia from fungi (with a calculated concentration of 492 grains/mL), and eight Artemisia spp. pollen grains (27.14 grains/mL) are observed in the same 100 fields of view (Figure 5f–ac; Appendix S9).

Ancient DNA analysis in this study revealed that Proteobacteria, and Bacteroidetes, dominate the bacterial community, whereas Ascomycota and Basidiomycota are prevalent among fungi, and Thaumarchaeota are prominent in the archaeal population of the chicken drumstick shaped vase (Figure 4). Existing stud- ies have identified Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, Firmicutes, and Bacteroidetes as the predominant bacterial phyla in mod- ern cellar mud, mash, and liquor (Duan 2016; Huang, Huang, et al. 2017; Huang, Xiong, et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2012; Yang et al. 2017). In the context of fungal microbiology, Ascomycota and Basidiomycota, along with Aspergillus species, dominate the modern brewing process. These microorganisms have been reported to account for relative abundances of 98.95% and 99.67% in flavor compound formation within Chinese yellow wine (Mou 2015). Certain fungal genera including Aspergillus, Mucor, Fusarium, and Alternaria have been identified at vary- ing abundance levels across different Chinese yellow wine starter samples (Cao et al. 2008; Fang et al. 2006; Niu 2020). Notably, our investigation revealed a high concentration of Ascomycota cleistothecia in the liquid (Figure 5f–i), linked to qu brewing fermentation (Liu et al. 2019, 2024), aligning with ancient DNA analysis results. body_evidence.quote: Experimental studies have shown that starch granules in malt-based brewing un- dergo enzymatic hydrolysis during grain germination, followed by additional modification during mashing. These processes produce a series of distinctive microscopic alterations, including pitting, deep fissures, exposed lamellae, broken edges, loss of birefringence, central depressions, mild gelatinization, and hollowed centers surrounded by relatively intact peripheries. The latter two morphologies, particularly the “pizza crust-shaped” form, are especially characteristic of Triticeae (wheat and barley) starch granules subjected to mashing at 65–70 ◦C [48] (Figure 4). In traditional North Shaanxi millet beer, we identified three characteristic types of damaged starch granules: enzymatically digested starches produced during grain germination, “pizza crust-shaped” starches formed during mashing, and heavily gelatinized aggregates resulting from steaming. In contrast, qu was traditionally prepared from uncooked or semi-cooked cereals (such as rice or wheat) inoculated with fungal cultures and subsequently combined with boiled or steamed starchy ingredients to initiate saccharification and fermentation [2,3] (Figure 3). Experimental and ethnographic studies of qu-based brewing have shown that the resulting fermented beverages contained diverse microbial communities [50,60,61]. Type I rice starches (Oryza sp.) were identified in 13 vessels, making them the most ubiquitous starch type in the assemblage (86.7% ubiquity). They typically occurred as compound starches composed of multiple small polygonal granules. A total of 94 rice compound starches and isolated single granules were recorded, accounting for 20.8% of the total assemblage. Measurements of 142 individual granules yielded sizes ranging from 2.9 to 7.04 μm (mean = 4.72 μm), consistent with those of modern reference rice starches

Type II Panicoideae taxa starches were recovered in seven vessels (n = 31; 6.9% of the total assemblage; 46.7% ubiquity). The granules are small and predominantly polygonal, with a few spherical forms, ranging in size from 7.65 to 18.88 μm (mean = 12.10 μm). Their morphology and size range are consistent with several Panicoideae taxa, including foxtail millet (Setaria italica), broomcorn millet (Panicum miliaceum), barnyard grass (Echinochloa sp.), and small granules of Job’s tears (Coix lacryma-jobi) (Figure 5: 4; cf. Figure 6: 2–5; Figure 7). Consequently, individual granules cannot be assigned confidently to a more specific taxon based on starch morphology alone. However, phytolith analysis provides complementary information that permits more confident taxonomic interpretation (see below). Carbonized barnyard grass seeds have previously been recovered from Jiahu [62], and Job’s tears starches have been identified at the nearby Lingjing (ca. 14,000–11,000 cal. BP) and Shunshanji (ca. 8500–7000 cal. BP) sites in the Ying River region [63]. Although millet micro- and macrobotanical remains have been reported from several Peiligang culture sites (ca. 8000–7000 cal. BP), including Tanghu [64] and Peiligang [65], this study provides the first evidence for millet starch remains at Jiahu. Type III Job’s tears starch (Coix lacryma-jobi) was recorded in one vessel (n = 1; 0.2% of the total assemblage; 6.7% ubiquity). A total of 452 starch granules were recovered, of which 209 (46.2% of the total) were assigned to nine taxonomically diagnostic types. Slightly more than half of the assemblage (n = 243; 53.8%) was classified as unidentifiable (UNID) granules or gelatinized masses because the starches were too damaged, gelatinized, or lacked diagnostic morphological features (Table 3). body_evidence.quote: A total of 337 phytoliths were recovered from 15 vessels. Most phytoliths were concentrated in two vessels, P4 bottle (n = 204) and P8 jar (n = 62), whereas each of the remaining vessels contained only 1–12 phytoliths. The phytolith assemblage is dominated by morphotypes associated with Poaceae. The phytolith assemblage from P4 bottle is morphologically diverse and includes elongate forms, bilobates, saddles, common bulliforms, Phragmites bulliforms, hair cells, and opaque perfo- rated platelets. In contrast, P8 jar contains primarily husk phytoliths, most of which are highly fragmentary and can therefore only be broadly assigned to the Paniceae tribe. However, a few specimens can be tentatively identified as broomcorn millet η-type (n = 4), foxtail millet Ω-type (n = 1), possible barnyard grass β-type (n = 3), and Triticeae dendriform phytoliths (n = 1). In addition, crenate or columellate phytoliths derived from grass seed husks or inflorescences were also identified (n = 9) (Table 5; Figure 9). The presence of husk phytoliths from two millet taxa and possibly barnyard grass is consistent with the identification of Panicoideae starch granules that may have derived from these taxa. The P8 jar sample also contained abundant microcharcoal fragments, indicating repeated exposure to high-temperature heating.

These contrasting phytolith assemblages indicate that different categories of plant materials were probably processed in these two vessels. P4 bottle appears to have contained leafy plant materials, whereas P8 jar was more directly associated with cereal processing. Notably, most phytoliths recovered from P8 jar exhibit varying degrees of discoloration, ranging from light brown to dark brown or black (Figure 9: 9–11, 14), most likely resulting from heat-induced alteration [73,74]. The sand-tempered fabric of the P8 jar (Supplementary Materials Table S2), together with the abundant microcharcoal fragments and heat-altered phytoliths, is consistent with repeated exposure to high temperatures. In addition, hair cells, epidermal tissues, and tracheary elements were recovered from 11 vessels (73.7%). Yeast cells and Monascus remains were observed attached to these plant tissues, suggesting that the tissues formed part of the fermented residue matrix (Figure 8: 4, 8, 9). Among the control samples, the interior of the P1 basin yielded 111 phytoliths, whereas the absence of starch granules and fungal elements. The remaining control samples from pottery exteriors and adhering soil contained only negligible numbers of phytoliths (0–3 per sample) (Table 5). body_evidence.quote: In addition, 12 occurrences of aggregated starch were observed (Fig. 3b–b'). Individual granule outlines remain visible in places and extinction crosses are partially preserved, although they are severely degraded and obscured. Morphologically, these aggregates match Type A1 and are most likely derived from millets. Heating experiments show that boiling foxtail and broomcorn millet in water causes granule swelling, progressive loss of extinction crosses, and the formation of aggregates that are distinct from natural compound granules(Ge et al., 2010a,b). With continued heating, granules lose their polygonal out lines, appear subround, and eventually lose all visible contours, becoming uniformly dark under crossed polars. The Miaodigou aggre gates are consistent with this pattern of gelatinization.

Type B (n 1⁄4 151) Type B granules are oval to subround (Fig. 3d–d'). When the cover slip is gently tapped, granules rotate and appear biconvex. Hila are central and lack fissures. Some granules have clear lamellae, whereas in others lamellae are faint. Extinction is diffuse and typically X-shaped. Granule size ranges from 10.95 to 34.26 μm, with a mean of 19.41 μm. In light of comparative work (Wan et al., 2016; Wan et al., 2011a,b), Type B is attributed to Triticeae grasses.

Type D (n 1⁄4 35) Type D granules are oval, with eccentric, closed hila or Y-shaped fissures. Extinction is X-shaped and lamellae are absent. Granule size ranges from 13.97 to 19.99 μm, with a mean of 15.58 μm (Fig. 3h–h'). These traits are consistent with nut starch (X. Yang et al., 2009). val granules of this type are common in oak (Quercus) and

Type E (n 1⁄4 19) Type E granules are reniform to oval, with surface pitting, clear lamellae, and fissures. Under crossed polars, lamellae remain visible and extinction is X-shaped. Granule size ranges from 15.52 to 69.39 μm, with a mean of 28.58 μm (Fig. 3g–g'). Legume starch (Fabaceae) is typically oval, reniform, or rounded-triangular, with clear lamellae and branched, Y-shaped, linear, or wing-like fissures (Q. Wang et al., 2013). On this basis, Type E is assigned to legumes.

body_evidence.quote: Type A: Starch granules belonging to the subfamily Panicoideae (n = 137; 19.88% of the total; 91.67% ubiquity) were identified. They occur predominantly as single granules, though three clusters were also observed. One cluster of granules exhibits partial gelatinization and is interwoven with fungal hyphae and a red cleistothecium (Fig. 3:2). In dividual granules measure 5.39–20.59 μm in length, with an average of 13.05 μm. These starches likely derive from foxtail millet, broomcorn millet, and small granules of Job’s tears (Fig. 3:1; cf. Fig. 4: 1,2). The starches of the two millets are morphologically very similar, differing primarily in size range (Fig. 5), while the smaller granules of Job’s tears closely resemble those of millet, making them difficult to distinguish (Liu, et al., 2014). For this reason, they are considered together here. Type A starches exhibit the highest ubiquity in the assemblage.

Type B: Starch granules identified as Job’s tears (Coix lacryma-jobi) (n = 48; 6.97% of the total; 66.67% ubiquity) were observed. In contrast to millet starches, they exhibit diagnostic features characteristic of Job’s tears, including larger granule size (8.84–26.23 μm), an eccentric hilum, and zigzag-shaped arms of the extinction cross (Liu, et al., 2014) (Fig. 3:3; cf. Fig. 4:3; Fig. 5). The earliest Job’s tears starches have been reported from the Lingjing site (11,500–9000 BP) and have been iden tified at numerous Neolithic sites in the Central Plains (Yang, et al., 2016).

Type D: Rice (Oryza sp.) starches were identified. The granules are relatively small and most commonly occur as compound grains (n = 22; 66.67% ubiquity). Most exhibited enzymatic and cooking damage; therefore, only 115 starch granules with identifiable morphologies were recorded (16.69% of the total) with size measurements (3.46–9.13 μm) (Fig. 3:5; cf. Fig. 4:5). The earliest evidence of rice in the Central Plains comes from the Jiahu site, dating to ca. 9000 cal. BP, and rice was widely cultivated in the region throughout the Neolithic (Yang, et al., 2016). Notably, rice was not only a common food crop but also served as the principal raw material for producing red rice qu starters during the Neolithic period in the Yellow River region (Liu, 2023), highlighting its pivotal role in the brewing practices represented at Pingliangtai.

Type E: Starch granules originating from the root of snake gourd (Trichosanthes cucumerina) (n = 13; 1.89% of the total; 41.67% ubiquity) were identified (Fig. 3:6; cf. Fig. 4:6). This root was used as both food and medicine, as documented in medical texts such as the Materia Medica (Li, 1981 [original 1578]). Starch from this plant has been re ported on artifacts from the Lingjing site (11,500–9000 BP) in the Central Plains (Yang, et al., 2016), as well as from numerous later Neolithic sites (Liu, et al., 2013; Liu, et al., 2018). These finds suggest that snake gourd root was a common food resource in ancient times.

body_evidence.quote: In addition to the abovementioned production steps, some of the fibers were also dyed. Previous studies have revealed the presence of dyed fibers in pink, blue and black colors at the Upper Paleolithic Shi zitan site in Shanxi (L. Liu et al., 2026) and at the early Neolithic Pei ligang site in Henan (L. Liu et al., 2024). Ethnographic and historical records show that dyeing materials in ancient China primarily included both minerals and plants (Jin and Wu, 2012; Li, 2020; Tan, 2009). Mineral-based dyes were often used for decorative applications, whereas plant-based dyes were typically applied through exhaust dyeing in dye solutions (Chen, 1984). The relatively uniform colors observed in the Shimao fibers (Fig. 4c–f), together with modern reference samples (Fig. S2n–p), suggest that some fibers may have been dyed with plant- based materials. Potential local dye sources include madder root (Rubia cordifolia) for red hues, Chinese indigo (Polygonum tinctorium) or Chinese woad (Isatis indigotica) for blue, and acorn caps (Quercus sp.) for black dyes (L. Liu et al., 2024, 2026). The Shimao evidence therefore suggests continuity in dyeing practices in north China from the Upper Paleolithic onward.

body_evidence.quote: There were 100,218 grains attributed to broomcorn millet. These starch grains ranged in maximum length from 4.62 to 12.79 μm (n = 58), with an average of 7.46 μm. Morphologically, most were polygonal, with a smaller number appearing sub-rounded. Both the size range and shape were consistent with those of modern broomcorn millet starch grains (Ge et al., 2010). The assemblage includes intact starch grains (Fig. 6a)
as well as damaged ones exhibiting hilum depressions (Fig. 6b), indi cating starch degradation following seed germination (Wang et al., 2017).

A total of 8,352 Triticeae starch grains were identified, which exhibited the A-type morphology (Peng et al., 1999). These grains range in length from 12.10 to 37.65 μm (n = 56), with an average length of 22.84 μm. The grains were generally sub-rounded and exhibited a characteristic biconvex appearance when rotated under the microscope (Fig. 6d), a diagnostic feature of Triticeae starch (Ge et al., 2024). Although some grains remained intact (Fig. 6c), the majority showed varying degrees of degradation, including fracturing, hilum collapse, and alterations in surface morphology. These alterations included enhanced visibility of lamellae (Fig. 6f) and partial to complete loss of the extinction cross under cross-polarised light (Fig. 6e). The breakage of starch grains likely resulted from mechanical stress, whereas hilum deformation and the loss of birefringence were more plausibly attributed to microbial activity and enzymatic degradation (Wang et al., 2017). In a subset of grains, the enhanced lamellae patterns radiating from the hilum resembled those observed in experimental heating under high- moisture conditions (Ge et al., 2010, Henry et al., 2009), suggesting that some Triticeae starch grains may have undergone thermal pro cessing prior to deposition.

A few phytoliths derived from cereal glumes were observed, exhib iting morphological features (thickened cell walls and rounded, sinuous outlines) consistent with long cells from the husks of Triticeae, such as wheat or barley (Rosen, 1992) (Fig. 6g). While the precise distinction between wheat and barley glume phytoliths based solely on long-cell morphology remains challenging, their presence provides supporting evidence for the use of Triticeae cereals in the beverage.

body_evidence.quote: The microfossils in the sediment sample can be divided into five types based on their morphological features. Five starch grains that could be identified were extracted from the sample. Type A (Millet starches, n = 3, size 16–22.4 μm) are polygonal and have centric hilum with clear and straight extinction cross under a polarized microscope. The lamellar is not visible, and the centered hilum shows depressed and clear linear-shaped fissures. The existence of type A proves the presence of millet in the sample. In addition, compared with modern reference samples in literature (Ge, 2010), the type A starch has rounder shape and more likely is foxtail millet. Type B (Coix lacryma-jobi, n = 1, size 21.1 μm) is also polygonal, but has no lamellae. Its features are similar to

those of Type A, but it has a clear and curing extinction cross. Type C (Tubers, n = 1, size 22.2 μm) is oval and has an eccentric hilum, as well as lamellae of large sizes. Type D (Poaceae pollen, n = 1, size 29.3 μm) is nearly round, with obvious pores on the surface, a characteristic of Poaceae pollen. Type E (suspected Saccharomyces cerevisiae, n = 2, size 4.6–7.1 μm) is highly similar to yeast cells in previous study (Li, et al., 2023), which is consistent with the detection of ergosterol derivatives by Py-GC/MS. In addition, Type A and Type C displayed damage consistent with gelatinization and fermentation, including small pits, missing edges and hazy extinction crosses, etc.

body_evidence.quote: Sporangiophores, a long stalk supporting sporangia, are often un branched (Fig. 2c) and grouped in tufts with large aseptate or few- septate hyphae (Fig. 2e) (St-Germain and Summerbell, 2011, 5, 225). Some of the molds in the black substance are more fragile. Spor angiospores, characterized by a round shape and brown color, are de tached and dispersed heavily from sporangia (Fig. 2d). For those without sporangiospores, columella and apophysis, as main structures of sporangia, can be clearly observed (Fig. 2g). The size range of sporangia and hyphae are 41.04–135.61 μm and 7.78–35.04 μm, respectively. In

addition, starch granules present typical features caused by enzymatic digestion. They have concaved channels, pitting and fissures in bright field and blurry birefringence in polarized light (Fig. 2a-b).

body_evidence.quote: The low temperature big starter from Congtai Distillery is yellowish brown in color (Fig. 1(1)E). After being cultured for five days, the molds are primarily black with some white spots (Fig. 1(2)e). Under micro scopic observation, the raw materials in this starter are wheat, similar to the homemade wheat starter, the high temperature starter and medium temperature starter as mentioned above (Fig. 5f). Filamentous fungi include Rhizopus sp. and possibly Mucor sp. in morphology (Fig. 5g, h).

Small starter is commonly made from rice as the raw material, and the color is white (Fig. 1(1)F, Fig. 1(2)f). Due to low incubation tem perature, it has a less diverse microbial community, majorly including filamentous fungi Rhizopus sp. and Mucor sp. (Sakandar et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020). In our culturing sample, Rhizopus molds were detected (Fig. 5j-k). The absence of Mucor sp. may be caused by diverse factors in the culturing environment or human artificial control of what types of fungi is added in the starter making process. In addition, heavily damaged unidentified fungal parts were also detected (Fig. 5l). In brightfield, rice granules are commonly in clusters (Fig. 5i). In polarized light, the birefringence is a little blurry. The size range of the granules (n = 145) is 2.37–8.81 μm with the average of 4.70 μm.

body_evidence.quote: Nuruk is a starter prevalently used in alcohol making in Korea. The starter is yellowish brown in color (Fig. 1(1)G). After being cultured for five days, the molds are primarily black with some white spots (Fig. 1(2) g). Nuruk starter contains a variety of substances, including wheat, molds, and yeasts. Previously published studies have revealed that the most primary filamentous fungi in Nuruk include Aspergillus sp., Rhizopus sp., Mucor sp., and Lichtheimia sp., etc. (Carroll et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2011). In our experiment, the observed major filamentous fungi include Aspergillus sp. and Rhizopus sp. (Fig. 6a-d). No obvious Mucor sp., or Lichtheimia sp. are detected.

Microscopic observation shows that rice starch granules in the cultured koji sample are predominantly arranged in compounds. Under polarized light, some starch granules exhibit clear birefringence, whereas others show blurred or weakened birefringence, reflecting varying degrees of enzymatic hydrolysis (Fig. 6e).

The leavened wheat flour dough was made by a farmer family, which can be used for making Chinese steaming buns or alcohol, since this kind of dough include natural yeasts (Fig. 1(1)I, Fig. 1(2)i). First, starch granules reveal evident enzymatic features − concentric channels, pitting and fissures in brightfield and blurry birefringence in polarized light (Fig. 6i). The size range of wheat starch granules (n = 139) is 11.43–33.03 μm with an average of 21.95 μm. Second, yeast cells are characterized by a round, oval, or elongate shape with budding repro duction features. Some are in clusters (Fig. 6j-k). These yeast cells do not have color in brightfield or birefringence in polarized light. The size range of the yeasts (n = 128) is 2.76–9.42 μm with an average of 5.29 μm. Yeasts are a kind of eukaryotic microbes, preferring an acidic environment with sugar and water. After division, some cells are still connected with the parent cells, resembling chains. In this process, pseudohyphaes can be formed (Fig. 6l). The circular and oval yeast cells

observed in this sample are morphologically consistent with S. cerevisiae, which is a type of yeast commonly involved in East Asian alcohol pro duction (Bai et al., 2022; Li et al., 2014). The typical size range of S. cerevisiae (2.5–10 μm) overlaps with the measurements in this study. However, species-level identification cannot be confirmed without further genetic analyses. Budding features with scars, formed during reproduction, are visible as protrusions on the yeast cell surfaces (Fig. 6j- k) (Cen and Cai, 2017, 73-85; St-Germain and Summerbell, 2011, 228- 229). In addition, there are long yeast cells. However, we cannot identify their taxonomy based on morphology only.

body_evidence.quote: In the foxtail millet experiment, starch granules exhibit polygonal, sub-spherical, or spherical shapes. During porridge-making, the starch granules become heavily gelatinized, primarily existing in an amor phous state (Fig. 7c). Wheat starch from Nuruk serve as an additional nutrient source and display enzymatic damage such as pitting, fissures, and loss of extinction crosses (Fig. 7a-b) (Kavanagh, 2017, 3). Congo red staining reveals broken wheat starch granules turn red (Fig. 7b).

Across both millet- and rice-based fermentations, the dominant fungi are Rhizopus sp. and Aspergillus sp., distinguishable by their morpho logical features (Fig. 7d-e, h; Fig. 8d, i). Many fungal structures are fragmented, with only sporangium or hyphae remaining (Fig. 7f, j; Fig. 8e-g). During fermentation, fungi, starch granules, spores, and yeasts become interwoven (Fig. 7g, 8h). The number of yeasts has increased rapidly in both samples (Fig. 7i). In millet alcohol, they pro duce pseudohyphae (Fig. 7j).

body_evidence.quote: In the rice experiment, steaming causes most starch granules to gelatinize and lose extinction crosses, rendering them amorphous under bright field. Unlike millet, however, some rice starch granule com pounds retain birefringence and relatively clear extinction crosses (Fig. 8a), while others show faint birefringence or appeared heavily gelatinized and amorphous (Fig. 8c).

Some rice starch clusters stain blue, and in certain cases form web structures (Fig. 8h). This web-like morphology is characteristic of starch retrogradation, a process in which gelatinized starch gradually reasso ciates into a more ordered and less soluble state during cooling. The retrogradation process, driven primarily by the reassociation of amylose and to a lesser extent amylopectin molecules, results in an amorphous network structure under bright field, and blurred or faint birefringence under polarized light (Tang and Copeland, 2007). Wheat starch granules derived from Nuruk undergo enzymatic digestion, including pitting, fissures, and disappearance of extinction crosses, though some intact granules are also observed (Fig. 8b-c).

Across both millet- and rice-based fermentations, the dominant fungi are Rhizopus sp. and Aspergillus sp., distinguishable by their morpho logical features (Fig. 7d-e, h; Fig. 8d, i). Many fungal structures are fragmented, with only sporangium or hyphae remaining (Fig. 7f, j; Fig. 8e-g). During fermentation, fungi, starch granules, spores, and yeasts become interwoven (Fig. 7g, 8h). The number of yeasts has increased rapidly in both samples (Fig. 7i). In millet alcohol, they pro duce pseudohyphae (Fig. 7j).

body_evidence.quote: Similar to rice starch granules in the steamed rice and Nuruk starter alcohol making, most rice starch granules are observed as bulky clusters in an amorphous form due to high-temperature processing (Fig. 9a, c, e), resembling a web-like structure with blurred birefringence remaining under polarized light. Also, intertwined structures containing rice clus ters and Aspergillus sp. are observed (Fig. 9c, e). Various forms of Aspergillus sp. are also observed at different stages of fermentation (Fig. 9b, d). For example, vesicles surrounded by metulae and phialides and connected to a conidiophore are observed (Fig. 9b). And most of them are very fragile, with only a short partition of conidiophore or a bold vesicle left in the sample. Throughout the fermentation process, the yeast population gradually increased (Fig. 9f). Dyeing experiments reveal that both gelatinized starch granules and fungi can be dyed with both Congo red and trypan blue (Fig. 9g-j).

body_evidence.quote: Millet starch grains are the most abundant category, with 1,393 grains identified. They exhibit faceted shapes with four to six angular or rounded edges, a centric hilum, and fissures radiating from the center, often as star-shaped patterns (Fig. 3a–c′). Under polarized light, extinction crosses are typically “+”-shaped, with occasional twisted arms. Lamellae are generally not visible (Gong et al., 2025). Grain sizes range from 6.38 to 23.23 μm, overlapping with modern foxtail millet (11.21–16.75 μm) and broomcorn millet (5.92–13.00 μm). Because starch grains from these two taxa are morphologically similar, they are collectively identified as millets.

A total of 285 starch grains were assigned to Job’s tears. These grains are polygonal to sub-rounded and commonly display Y-, V-, or linear- shaped fissures. Hilum positions are centric or eccentric, and lamellae are generally not visible. Under polarized light, the grains show extinction crosses with straight or zigzag arms, most commonly forming a characteristic “Z”-shaped extinction (Fig. 3d–f′) (Liu et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2016b). Grain sizes range from 6.87 to 26.78 μm.

A total of 32 starch grains were identified as rice. These grains are predominantly polyhedral or round-polyhedral, with a closed centric hilum. Under polarized light, they display an “×”-shaped extinction cross; fissures and lamellae are absent (Fig. 3g–i′) (Khan et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2021). Grain sizes range from 5.74 to 12.13 μm, consistent with modern domesticated Oryza sativa.

Thirty-one starch grains were identified as acorns. These grains are ovate or spheroid, with a centric hilum and a slightly bent “×”-shaped extinction cross. Fissures and lamellae are absent (Fig. 3j–l′). Grain sizes range from 9.74 to 24.93 μm, consistent with Quercus species (Faga ceae), which are documented as an important food resource in South China (Wan et al., 2012).

body_evidence.quote: damage. Partially gelatinized starch grains attributable to Job's tears or millets were identified (Fig. 10a), further supporting this interpretation.

Several starch grains show cracking and fragmentation (Fig. 10b, d), consistent with mechanical stress from grinding, stirring, or mashing (Liu et al., 2010; del Babot, 2003; Guan et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020b). Such damage may result from routine culinary handling during cooking. Overall, the co-occurrence of gelatinized, cracked, and enzymatically altered grains supports the interpretation that pottery at Zhaizishan was used for multiple food processing activities, including cooking, me chanical processing, and possibly fermentation. These damage patterns also strengthen the argument that the starch assemblage reflects culi nary residues rather than post-depositional contamination.

body_evidence.quote: Identification of grain species All identifiable starch granules come from the tribe Triticeae. (Table 4, Fig. 3 & Fig. 4) Bradford method

comparable to that of the tribe Triticeae. The surfaces of the items under consideration are faceted, with a circular configuration. The hilum is centric and exhibits depression patterns. Fissures are a relatively com mon occurrence, manifesting predominantly as a radiating pattern to wards the periphery. The extinction cross is typically “+” shaped, and only a small number of crosses exhibit a twisted pattern at the extremity of the arm. Lamellae are invariably visible (Fig. 3a, 3b, Fig. 4a, and 4b). The size range of the particles is 6.5–35.5 μm, which is divided into large and small groups. In addition to single granules, which were by far the most prevalent, starches were occasionally observed to occur in clusters within the residues from the samples (Fig. 3c and 3d). These features are comparable to Triticeae.

State IV disintegrated, starry, degraded granular residues with starch- like morphology (P4 and P5); State III a granule showing a spongy- looking appearance (P6). Some starches extracted exhibit damage pat terns indicative of fermentation, such as central depressions and pitting related to enzyme digestion (Fig. 3c and 3d), as well as hollow or swollen granules resulting from the disappearance of extinction crosses caused by gelatinization during fermentation (Fig. 3e and 3f). Some of these patterns are almost identical to the experimental results (Fig. 3e, 3f, 4d, 4e and 4j). This suggests that the damaged features of the starch grains are related to fermented drinks. State IV is present in both archaeolog ical and simulated specimens (Fig. 3g, 3 h, 4 g and 4i), exhibiting a starry dispersion pattern with a high population density. This may indicate that the granules have been fully lysed.

body_evidence.quote: Identification of grain species All identifiable starch granules come from the tribe Triticeae. (Table 4, Fig. 3 & Fig. 4) Bradford method

comparable to that of the tribe Triticeae. The surfaces of the items under consideration are faceted, with a circular configuration. The hilum is centric and exhibits depression patterns. Fissures are a relatively com mon occurrence, manifesting predominantly as a radiating pattern to wards the periphery. The extinction cross is typically “+” shaped, and only a small number of crosses exhibit a twisted pattern at the extremity of the arm. Lamellae are invariably visible (Fig. 3a, 3b, Fig. 4a, and 4b). The size range of the particles is 6.5–35.5 μm, which is divided into large and small groups. In addition to single granules, which were by far the most prevalent, starches were occasionally observed to occur in clusters within the residues from the samples (Fig. 3c and 3d). These features are comparable to Triticeae.

Starches No starch granules were recovered from the control samples. Therefore, the 213 granules identified are interpreted as use-related residues (Table 3). Of these, 94 granules were unidentifiable due to severe damage, lack of diag- nosticfeatures,orabsenceofmatchesinthemodernreferencedatabase.The identifiable granules were categorised into nine types (A-I) based on mor- phology and size. TypeA(Fig.5a)wasmostnumerous(n = 57).Thegranules(sizerange: 5.4–19.9 μm, mean: 10.4 μm) were predominantly single, spherical, or spherical-cap-shaped, often with pressure facets. Some compound granules consisted of two bell-shaped granules joined at the base or three forming a rounded triangle. The granule surfaces were smooth, occasionally with linear fissures, and lacked visible lamellae. This morphology is common in USOs, such as Amorphophallus spp.(konjac), and Pueraria lobata (kudzu), as well as some woody plants like Cycas spp. and Artocarpus altilis (breadfruit). Given the granule size, an origin from USOs growing forest margins and shaded understories is most likely.

body_evidence.quote: Four yeast cells, appearing attached to an epidermis fragment, were identified on slab 14-GS3. They are round or oval, with a size range of 6.99–10.57 μm. Two cells appear to be in the budding process, indicated by the presence of small protrusions on the mother cells (Fig 7e). During retting processes, various microorganisms, including bacteria, molds, and yeasts (and the pectinolytic enzymes they produce), play a role in breaking down pectin and other substances binding the fibers to other plant material [95]. The presence of yeast on this slab might be the result of pounding retted fibers on the tool.
retting. The presence of yeast cells attached to an epidermis fragment on 14-GS3 further supports a connection to the retting process (S6 Table; Fig 7e).

Among the seven slabs, 14-GS3 shows the most diverse array of microfossil remains associated with fiber pounding. These include not only microfibers and microfiber bundles but also various related elements such as crystals, hair cell phytoliths, epidermis fragments, pitted vessel cells, and yeast cells likely linked to the retting process (Figs 5, Fig 7a and 7c–7g; S6 Table).

body_evidence.quote: tools (SI Appendix, Table S6). They were classified into six types based on the morphological characteristics and size, five of which were taxonomically distinctive (Fig. 5). The unidentifiable starches lack diagnostic morphological features and may be identified in the future based on the expansion of modern reference collections. Throughout this study, ubiquity refers to the occurrence frequency of a specified form of residue or use- wear evidence, calculated as the percentage of analyzed artifacts within each comparison group on which that evidence was identified (SI Appendix, section 2.2).

1. Type 1 starch (np = 11, nn = 61, 4.84 to 16.65 μm), is compa rable to Panicoideae grasses (Panicoideae subfamily). Granules are mainly polyhedral with centric hila. Some show fissures that can be short linear, stellate, Y- shaped, or circular (Fig. 5(1, 2)). Panicoideae starches may occur in large clusters (Fig. 5(3)). Examples of typical wild and domesticated species include wild Setaria, foxtail millet (Setaria italica), and broomcorn millet Panicum miliaceum). Early Neolithic Panicoideae starches show larger granules (81.63% are over 11 μm, with a maximum size of 16.65 μm) and Y- shaped fissures, suggesting the presence of foxtail millet (Setaria italica) (52). 2. Type 2 starch (np = 0, nn = 11, 3.85 to 6.67 μm) is comparable to rice (Oryzeae). Granules are polyhedral or round polyhe dral, with centric hila and “X”- shaped crosses (Fig. 5(4)). They often occur in clusters due to amyloplast formation (53). The morphology and size of rice starch do not significantly differ between wild and domesticated species (54), but their presence indicates rice exploitation since the early Neolithic.

3. Type 3 starch (np = 0, nn = 14, 12.76 to 22.70 μm) is com parable to Job’s tears (Coix lacryma- jobi). These starches are polyhedral or spherical with centric hila. Fissures are commonly linear or T/Y- shaped (Fig. 5(5)). Diagnostic features include a Z- shaped arm and an eccentric ratio over 1.47, as well as a relatively larger size compared to Panicoideae (55). 4. Type 4 starch (np = 7, nn = 13, 9.72 to 22.40 μm) is comparable to Triticeae grasses (Triticeae tribe). Granules are round or dis coid, with a flat surface. When turned, they become elongated oval or lenticular. Fissures are unclear, but the hila are centric, and lamellae are visible (Fig. 5(6, 7)). Common wild Triticeae grasses in the study area include Agropyron, Elymus, and Leymus. 5. Type 5 starch (np = 9, nn = 18, 9.76 to 32.54 μm) is comparable to USOs (underground storage organ, or tubers). These tuber starches vary in size and shape but share eccentric hila and bent extinction arms (Fig. 5(8, 9)). Due to the lack of distinguishing features, they cannot be identified beyond this general category.

body_evidence.quote: The number of identified starches is low on the Paleolithic artifacts, a pattern consistent with the relatively small artifact sizes, less intensive use, and preservation conditions. The starches were mainly identified from artifacts with a relatively sharp cutting edge, such as blades and microblades. One microblade (PLGP- MB19) revealed 10 starches in three types (Panicoideae, Triticeae, and USO). A few scrapers and flakes also yielded a limited number of starches, indicating they may have contacted starchy plants sporadically. The total ubiquity of starch processing in the Upper Paleolithic sample is low, only 16.88%. Flaked tools were still used for processing starch resources during the early Neolithic, and the ubiquity of starch acquisition in flake tools did not increase significantly (23.08%) compared to the Upper Paleolithic. On the ground- edged tools, however, starches occurred more frequently (53.33% ubiquity) with a larger variety, indicating increased focus on plants compared to the Paleolithic. 2.3.2. Phytoliths. Phytoliths were not identified from the Paleolithic artifacts. In the experiments, phytoliths were recovered in sub stantially lower quantities than starch grains and in numbers comparable to microfibers (Section 2.1 and Fig. 3). This pattern may reflect differences in the abundance of these microremains in the processed plant tissues, their adherence and retention on tool surfaces, or their recovery during extraction.
